title: "Looking for Something Weird to Happen": How Humans Sustain AI Agent Novelty Amid Semantic Collapse
summary: Semantic collapse, the progressive narrowing of what AI systems generate, has been studied mainly in closed settings, and remedies have targeted models and data. We study it in MOLTBOOK, a social network of interacting AI agents that human users configure and steer. Across 30,076 active agents, output grows less diverse within agents and more similar across them over weeks, yet a minority sustains high novelty. Interviews with users of high- and typical-novelty agents (N=11) associate sustained novelty with three features: users value novelty of itself, they supply broad and distinctive material and revise it when output narrows, and they approach MOLTBOOK as a new agentic world to explore, not a venue to instrumentally exploit. A survey of users of distinctive agents (N=53) confirms these patterns. Communities with more novel agents also show more diverse output from other agents. We discuss interface and policy interventions that could support improved human input.

AI.tldr: Semantic collapse occurs in social AI networks, but some users sustain novelty through valuing it intrinsically, providing diverse inputs, and treating AI as exploratory world rather than instrumental tool.
AI.motivation: To study semantic collapse (progressive narrowing of AI-generated content) in a social network of interacting AI agents (MOLTBOOK), moving beyond closed settings to understand how human users affect diversity through configuration and steering.
AI.method: Analysis of 30,076 active AI agents over weeks, combined with qualitative interviews with users of high- and typical-novelty agents (N=11), and a survey of users of distinctive agents (N=53).
AI.result: Output diversity decreases within agents and similarity increases across agents over time, but a minority sustains high novelty. Sustained novelty correlates with: users valuing novelty intrinsically, supplying broad/distinctive material and revising when output narrows, and approaching MOLTBOOK as an exploratory world rather than instrumental exploitation.
AI.conclusion: Human agency can mitigate semantic collapse in social AI networks when users engage intentionally and explore creatively. Interface and policy interventions should support improved human input to sustain diversity.

title: Cheap Talk Stabilizes Strategic Interaction in LLM Agents
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures, 14 tables. Includes supplementary material
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as interacting agents, making the persistence of their action policies across repeated interaction critical for reliable multi-agent operation. We investigate whether and how agent-generated, non-binding pre-play communication ("cheap talk") increases such persistence in four open-weight 7-9B-parameter LLMs. Our experiments span four repeated two-player games -- Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag Hunt, and Harmony -- with incentive structures ranging from strategic conflict to alignment, each presented in six contexts. We observe unstable trajectories in all four games, although their prevalence and magnitude depend strongly on model and context. Across models, games, and contexts, cheap talk is predominantly stabilizing, with five corrected reversals concentrated in social or team framings; effects vary substantially by model and context. Controlled current-message interventions identify two separable output-level channels in Qwen: reduced action uncertainty and less between-round drift in action probabilities. Matched history-by-message counterfactuals further show that recent partner behavior conditions how mutual-benefit versus self-prioritizing language affects policy persistence. Finally, in Prisoner's Dilemma, we identify in Qwen and Falcon a history-balanced policy-content direction in late transformer layers; projecting out this direction increases realized switching during closed-loop play, demonstrating that complete trajectories are causally sensitive to this component. Together, these findings show that cheap talk can make individual trajectories more persistent across diverse incentive structures, while revealing that the magnitude and mechanisms of stabilization are model- and history-dependent.

AI.tldr: Cheap talk (non-binding pre-play communication) between LLM agents increases policy persistence across repeated games, with stabilization effects varying by model and context, mediated by reduced action uncertainty and history-dependent responses.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed as interacting agents, understanding how to maintain consistent action policies across repeated interactions is critical for reliable multi-agent operation. The paper investigates whether cheap talk (non-binding pre-play communication) can stabilize policy trajectories in multi-agent LLM interactions.
AI.method: Experimental study using four open-weight 7-9B parameter LLMs across four repeated two-player games (Prisoner's Dilemma, Snowdrift, Stag Hunt, Harmony) with six different contexts each. Methods include: 1) comparing trajectories with and without cheap talk, 2) controlled current-message interventions to identify output-level channels, 3) matched history-by-message counterfactuals, and 4) analyzing transformer layer representations to identify policy-content directions affecting switching behavior.
AI.result: Cheap talk is predominantly stabilizing across models, games, and contexts, with five corrected reversals concentrated in social/team framings. In Qwen, stabilization occurs through two separable channels: reduced action uncertainty and less between-round drift. Partner behavior history conditions how language affects policy persistence. In Prisoner's Dilemma, a "history-balanced policy-content direction" in late transformer layers of Qwen and Falcon causally affects switching behavior when projected out.
AI.conclusion: Cheap talk can make individual LLM agent trajectories more persistent across diverse incentive structures, but the magnitude and mechanisms of stabilization are model- and history-dependent, revealing the complexity of achieving reliable multi-agent interactions with current LLMs.

title: Multi-Agent Learning with Cooperation-Driven Optimization Dynamics
summary: Multilayer Artificial Neural Networks trained via backpropagation are the basic blocks of many, more complex, classification algorithms. Their strength lies in the possibility of realizing, with arbitrary precision, any function. This result comes at the cost of the large number of involved parameters to be optimized. In this work, we propose a mechanism for cooperation, i.e., information exchange among several artificial neural networks, with the goal of reducing model complexity while maintaining performance. More precisely, we consider several "small" agents, i.e., containing fewer parameters than a reference "large" one, that during training share their predictions by incorporating this information into the loss function and thus directly influence weight updates. We consider several strategies for implementing cooperation, e.g., the voter model, majority model, and weighted average model based on an agent's confidence in its prediction. We numerically compare the accuracy of those strategies on several standard benchmarks. Our results support the claim that several small agents can outperform a single large model on a given classification task; the shared signals affect each agent's optimization algorithm by modulating both the descent direction and the step size, converging toward a global consensus. The proposed proof-of-concept significantly reduces the number of parameters to be trained while preserving comparable performance, thereby limiting computational resource usage.

AI.tldr: Multiple small neural networks cooperate during training by sharing predictions to outperform a single large network while using fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Large neural networks require many parameters to achieve high accuracy, increasing computational complexity. The paper aims to reduce model complexity while maintaining performance through cooperation among smaller networks.
AI.method: Several smaller neural networks (agents) share predictions during training by incorporating this information into their loss functions, directly influencing weight updates. Cooperation strategies include voter model, majority model, and weighted average model based on prediction confidence.
AI.result: Multiple cooperating small agents can outperform a single large model on classification tasks while significantly reducing the number of trainable parameters and computational resource usage.
AI.conclusion: Cooperation among multiple small neural networks via shared predictions during training enables comparable performance to large networks with significantly reduced complexity, offering computational efficiency benefits.

title: ToMAS: A Pilot Failure-Grounded Theory-of-Mind Benchmark from Multi-Agent LLM Failures
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems can fail even when communication succeeds because agents do not correctly track their peers' roles, knowledge, or intentions. We investigate whether such inter-agent misalignment cases, labelled FC2 in MAST-Data, can be converted into functional partner-state reasoning items. ToMAS applies four explicit convertibility criteria to diagnosed execution traces. A full conversion pass over 242 eligible non-AG2 training traces produced 39 CLEAN items. In an 18-trace reliability pilot, two annotators achieved 94.4% raw agreement and Cohen's kappa = 0.92. We then used the converted items as binary rewards in a small-scale GRPO feasibility experiment with Qwen2.5-1.5B. On a 28-item held-out Magentic GAIA diagnostic, every evaluated condition exceeded the ROUGE-L threshold on the same 2 of 28 items. Post-hoc adapter checks show why: under the learning rate used, the LoRA update remained numerically negligible (max abs Delta W about 7e-6), so all conditions decode identically to the untrained checkpoint. The experiment therefore does not show a training effect and cannot establish one; it reports an executable pipeline together with two limitations that any conclusive study must address: a provenance gap between the training and evaluation items, and lexical-overlap scoring. ToMAS provides a preliminary rubric and pipeline for converting diagnosed coordination failures into trainable partner-state reasoning items and identifies the requirements for a conclusive matched-domain evaluation.

AI.tldr: ToMAS converts LLM multi-agent coordination failures into trainable partner-state reasoning items with high reliability, but initial training experiments show negligible parameter updates due to low learning rates, requiring better domain matching for conclusive evaluation.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems often fail due to inter-agent misalignment where agents don't correctly track peers' roles, knowledge, or intentions, even when communication succeeds. The researchers aim to convert such coordination failures into functional training items.
AI.method: ToMAS applies four explicit convertibility criteria to diagnosed execution traces from MAST-Data, specifically FC2 cases. The system converts these into CLEAN items through a full conversion pass. Reliability was tested via pilot annotation, and converted items were used as binary rewards in GRPO training experiments with Qwen2.5-1.5B, with post-hoc adapter checks to analyze parameter updates.
AI.result: The conversion produced 39 CLEAN items from 242 eligible traces with high reliability (94.4% agreement, κ=0.92). However, training experiments showed negligible LoRA updates (max ΔW ≈ 7e-6) due to low learning rates, resulting in no measurable training effect. All conditions performed identically to the untrained checkpoint on the 28-item GAIA diagnostic.
AI.conclusion: ToMAS provides a preliminary rubric and pipeline for converting coordination failures into trainable partner-state reasoning items, but identifies critical limitations: 1) provenance gap between training and evaluation items, 2) reliance on lexical-overlap scoring. A conclusive study requires matched-domain evaluation and parameter updates that actually change model behavior.

title: Optimal Pruning for Neural Architectures using Fisher Information Distances
summary: A new scheme for parameter pruning is introduced, derived from the differential-geometric distance in model space. Pruning a parameter sets its value to zero, representing a displacement of the model to the hypersurface on which that parameter vanishes. The minimal distance from the unpruned model to this hypersurface is naturally computed via the geodesic distance in the model space as determined by the Fisher information metric. This distance determines the true change in the model, and its performance, under pruning. By analysing progressively more faithful approximations of this geodesic distance a natural hierarchy of optimality for pruning methods is determined. This starts with the traditional magnitude pruning, then develops into new more sophisticated and effective pruning schemes. The method is demonstrated for both fully-connected networks and vision transformers, on MNIST and CIFAR-10, over the complete $0$-$100\%$ pruning range and across five random seeds. It outperforms pruning by parameter magnitude and by the local Fisher information alone in every architecture and dataset combination considered, on both accuracy and the Matthews correlation coefficient. Additionally, analysis of different levels of geodesic approximation produces intermediate pruning schemes that are computationally efficient and maintain near-optimal performance. This geometric picture supplies not only a state-of-the-art pruning methodology for AI models, but also a verified and mathematically-motivated justification for pruning schemes.

AI.tldr: A geometric approach to model pruning using Fisher information metric and geodesic distances to determine optimal parameter removal strategies that outperform traditional magnitude-based pruning.
AI.motivation: Current pruning methods like magnitude pruning lack theoretical foundation and may not reflect the true impact of parameter removal on model performance. There's a need for mathematically-motivated pruning schemes that consider how parameter removal actually affects the model's behavior and capabilities.
AI.method: Proposes a geometric pruning scheme based on differential geometry. When pruning a parameter (setting it to zero), this represents moving the model to a hypersurface where that parameter vanishes. The minimal distance to this hypersurface is computed via geodesic distance using the Fisher information metric. This creates a hierarchy of pruning methods by approximating this geodesic distance, starting with magnitude pruning and developing more sophisticated schemes.
AI.result: The method outperforms traditional magnitude pruning and pruning by local Fisher information alone across all tested architectures (fully-connected networks and vision transformers) on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. It maintains superior performance across the full 0-100% pruning range and across multiple random seeds, showing better accuracy and Matthews correlation coefficient. Intermediate approximations remain computationally efficient with near-optimal performance.
AI.conclusion: The geometric framework provides both a state-of-the-art pruning methodology and a mathematically-rigorous justification for pruning schemes, establishing a natural hierarchy from simple magnitude pruning to more sophisticated geodesic-based methods.

title: Causal neural set filtering for online multi-target tracking
summary: Transformer-based multi-target tracking (MTT) jointly learns data association and state estimation, but MT3/Track-MT3-style trackers repeatedly re-encode measurement windows, incurring redundant computation. We propose Causal Neural Set Filtering (CNSF)\footnote{\href{https://github.com/daihuangyu/CNSF}{Code: https://github.com/daihuangyu/CNSF}}, a neural set filter that encodes only current measurements while carrying past evidence in a structured recursive track state. CNSF combines exclusive Sinkhorn association, association-conditioned Kalman-shaped updates with moment matching, and recurrent Bernoulli lifecycle modeling with measurement-driven birth. These mechanisms impose soft one-to-one constraints, propagate association-induced state uncertainty, and support existence estimation under missed detections and birth--death transitions. On a held-out three-regime simulated test set, CNSF reduces mean GOSPA and T-GOSPA relative to Track-MT3 by 19.3\% and 30.4\%, with 55.9\% fewer parameters and a $3.76\times$ speedup in single-thread CPU inference.

AI.tldr: Causal Neural Set Filtering (CNSF) is a neural set filter that improves multi-target tracking efficiency by avoiding redundant computation of past measurements and implementing structured recursive track states, achieving better performance with fewer parameters and faster inference compared to Track-MT3.
AI.motivation: Existing transformer-based multi-target tracking (MTT) methods like MT3/Track-MT3 repeatedly re-encode entire measurement windows, leading to redundant computation and inefficiency. There's a need for a more efficient approach that can maintain tracking performance while reducing computational overhead.
AI.method: CNSF proposes three key mechanisms: 1) Exclusive Sinkhorn association for soft one-to-one constraints, 2) Association-conditioned Kalman-shaped updates with moment matching to propagate association-induced state uncertainty, and 3) Recurrent Bernoulli lifecycle modeling with measurement-driven birth for existence estimation under missed detections and birth-death transitions. The system encodes only current measurements while carrying past evidence in a structured recursive track state.
AI.result: On a held-out three-regime simulated test set, CNSF reduces mean GOSPA and T-GOSPA relative to Track-MT3 by 19.3% and 30.4% respectively, achieves 55.9% fewer parameters, and provides a 3.76× speedup in single-thread CPU inference.
AI.conclusion: CNSF demonstrates that neural set filtering with structured recursive state representation and efficient measurement encoding can significantly outperform existing transformer-based tracking methods in both accuracy and computational efficiency, establishing a promising direction for practical multi-target tracking applications.

title: BeWater: Effective Protesters Navigate Watersheds in Street Networks
summary: During social movements, protesters need to gather with limited communication means and limited knowledge other than what they observe in their direct surroundings. We propose BeWater, a fully distributed walking protocol that achieves gathering thanks to city information like street length, number of restaurants, number of lanes, or street names. Even though using only one of these observables performs poorly, we show that combining them in more advanced tactics rapidly leads to groups of significant sizes. To do so, our work leverages OpenStreetMap data to perform experiments on several real-world cities.

AI.tldr: BeWater is a fully distributed walking protocol for social movement protesters that achieves gathering using publicly available city information from OpenStreetMap, combining multiple data points like street length and landmarks to form significant groups.
AI.motivation: During social movements, protesters face communication limitations and lack knowledge beyond their immediate surroundings, making it challenging to gather effectively.
AI.method: The BeWater protocol is a fully distributed walking approach that utilizes observable city information (street length, number of restaurants, lanes, street names) from OpenStreetMap. The method combines these multiple observables in advanced tactics rather than relying on single data points.
AI.result: While using only one observable performs poorly, combining multiple city information sources rapidly leads to groups of significant sizes, as demonstrated through experiments on several real-world cities using OpenStreetMap data.
AI.conclusion: The BeWater protocol effectively enables gathering in social movements through distributed coordination using publicly available city data, showing that multi-source observation strategies outperform single-information approaches in real-world urban environments.

title: Safe Error Correction for Language Models: Frozen-Base Adjustment with Capability Preservation
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables. Code, weights, and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/eulogik/prajna and https://huggingface.co/eulogik/Prajna-CRNv2
summary: We study a practical question: can a small correction module fix errors in a frozen language model's outputs without degrading its base capabilities? We propose CRN v2, a lightweight logit-level correction module (~34M trainable parameters, 0.73% of the 4.65B text module) that sits atop a fully frozen Gemma 4 E2B model. The base model is never updated; only the correction module learns, via supervised fine-tuning followed by reference-free DPO on 83,400 error-correction pairs. On a 60-question domain exam (CEHRI: Certified Human-Robot Intelligence, covering facts, arithmetic, and implicit-goal reasoning), CRN v2 corrects 53.3% of base-model errors (reworded variant: 43.3%) while showing no degradation on tested capability benchmarks (MMLU/BoolQ N=200; car-wash N=8). A LoRA baseline at the matched CRN v1 budget (6.6M params, rank 19) achieves 83.3% correction but suffers 30-75% capability loss on the same benchmarks -- the correction-capability tradeoff. An ablation shows that the KL preservation term (lambda=0.1) is critical: lowering it to 0.01 degrades correction to 35.0%. A hidden-state injection variant at earlier layers (1.6M params, SFT-only) reaches 50.0%/55.8% but does not exceed logit correction; shallower injection (layer 4) drops to 30.0%/28.3%; multi-depth logit correction (~35M) reaches only 40%; and longer training (5,000 SFT + 2,000 DPO) stays at 53.3% -- none of the alternative configurations we tested exceeded the rank-128 logit result, consistent with a best-achieved result of ~53% rather than a floor. This is a study of a design principle (frozen base + logit correction + KL anchoring), not a claim of architectural novelty. All code, main-result weights, and evaluation scripts are released (deep variant as code only -- no trained deep checkpoints).

AI.tldr: CRN v2 is a lightweight correction module (~34M params, 0.73% of base model) that fixes errors in frozen language models without degrading base capabilities, achieving 53.3% error correction while maintaining benchmark performance.
AI.motivation: The paper addresses the practical question of whether small correction modules can fix errors in frozen language model outputs without degrading the model's base capabilities, avoiding the correction-capability tradeoff seen in other approaches.
AI.method: Proposes CRN v2 - a lightweight logit-level correction module (~34M parameters) atop fully frozen Gemma 4 E2B model. Only the correction module learns via supervised fine-tuning followed by reference-free DPO on 83,400 error-correction pairs, with KL preservation term (λ=0.1) to maintain base capabilities.
AI.result: CRN v2 corrects 53.3% of base-model errors on CEHRI domain exam while showing no degradation on capability benchmarks (MMLU/BoolQ, car-wash). LoRA baseline achieves 83.3% correction but suffers 30-75% capability loss. KL preservation term is critical - lowering λ to 0.01 degrades correction to 35.0%.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight logit-level correction with KL anchoring can effectively fix errors in frozen language models without degrading base capabilities, establishing a design principle (frozen base + logit correction + KL anchoring) rather than claiming architectural novelty.

title: Managing Action Preconditions in Neuro-Symbolic RL: Three Placement Strategies for Embodied Agents
summary: Humans carry behaviour knowledge of how to act in familiar situations into every new task rather than relearning it from scratch. There is no reason a Reinforcement Learning (RL) agent shouldn't do the same: known behaviour patterns need not be learned, only applied. Neuro-symbolic RL bridges prior knowledge and RL by injecting symbolic knowledge alongside a learned policy. The point at which this knowledge is integrated is critical: a poor choice can produce, for instance, hallucinated preconditions, which surface as safety and reliability problems in agents acting in changing environments. We formalise this behavioural knowledge as a precondition Bayesian network (BN) over the agent's \emph{structural actions} - the actions whose legality depends on preconditions, such as picking up a key, grasping a block, toggling a door, or dropping an object. The BN restricts when these actions may fire, and we inject it into the RL loop at three placements: (1) a \emph{symbolic verifier}, consulted only at inference, that fires a structural action once its preconditions hold; (2) a \emph{symbolic enforcer}, active during both training and inference, that governs structural-action use throughout learning; and (3) a \emph{symbolic learner}, which folds the knowledge into the network and learns the restriction and use of structural actions itself. To test the three variants we run experiments on two benchmarks with opposite regimes: one built on long, ordered planning chains, the other on continuous manipulation. We compare against strong baselines on solution quality, sample efficiency, and traceability. The payoff is substantial. On MiniGrid, all three placements improve the \emph{solution quality} over the PPO+RND baseline, the symbolic enforcer leading at $98.2\%$ against the baseline's $88.8\%$. On Fetch, $\dots$

AI.tldr: Neuro-symbolic RL approach that integrates symbolic knowledge about action preconditions via Bayesian networks at three different points in the RL loop, improving solution quality and sample efficiency.
AI.motivation: Humans leverage existing behavioral knowledge when learning new tasks rather than starting from scratch. RL agents should similarly reuse known behavior patterns. Integrating symbolic knowledge with RL is promising, but the integration point is critical - poor choices can lead to safety issues like hallucinated preconditions.
AI.method: Formalizes behavioral knowledge as precondition Bayesian networks over structural actions (actions with legality preconditions). Tests three integration placements: 1) Symbolic verifier (inference-only), 2) Symbolic enforcer (training+inference), 3) Symbolic learner (learns restrictions internally). Evaluates on two benchmarks: MiniGrid (ordered planning chains) and Fetch (continuous manipulation).
AI.result: All three placements improve solution quality over PPO+RND baseline on MiniGrid. The symbolic enforcer performs best at 98.2% vs baseline's 88.8%. Results show substantial payoff in solution quality, sample efficiency, and traceability across different task regimes.
AI.conclusion: Careful integration of symbolic knowledge via precondition Bayesian networks significantly improves RL agent performance. The symbolic enforcer approach (active during both training and inference) shows particular promise, demonstrating that neuro-symbolic RL can effectively bridge prior knowledge with learning while maintaining safety and reliability.

title: Calibrate Once, Fly Any Team: Residual-Grounded Low-Fidelity Training for Cooperative Drone Swarms
summary:
Training multi-agent drone-swarm policies directly in high-fidelity (HF) rigid-body physics is accurate but computationally expensive. This cost scales poorly with team size, as each additional agent multiplies contact-resolution complexity and sharply raises the in-simulation crash rate. To address this, we propose a mixed-fidelity training scheme that eliminates HF reinforcement learning entirely.
  A single shared, decentralized policy is optimized inside a fully-differentiable, JAX-native low-fidelity (LF) point-mass simulator. The simulator is corrected by a small, per-agent bagged residual ensemble fit once, offline, using short calibration flights in the HF simulator. Because calibration requires only one isolated drone, the data collection budget does not compound with team size. Reference trajectories are generated by rolling out an existing LF-only policy and tracked in the HF simulator by a zero-training PD controller.
  Evaluated across four cooperative drone tasks and team sizes from 3 to 18, the residual-corrected policy outperforms an uncorrected LF baseline in all combinations, and a from-scratch HF policy in 22 of 24 combinations tested. It trails an HF-finetuned policy by a margin that narrows steadily with team size. Ultimately, the proposed method achieves near-equivalent performance at the largest team sizes at a fraction of the computational cost, completely avoiding the high crash rates typical of HF training.

AI.tldr: A mixed-fidelity training approach for drone swarm policies that uses low-fidelity differentiable simulation with residual correction from brief high-fidelity calibration, achieving near-HF performance at much lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Training multi-agent drone swarm policies directly in high-fidelity (HF) rigid-body physics is computationally expensive and scales poorly with team size, with additional agents multiplying contact-resolution complexity and sharply increasing crash rates during training.
AI.method: Proposes a mixed-fidelity scheme: 1) Optimize a shared decentralized policy in a fully-differentiable JAX-native low-fidelity point-mass simulator, 2) Correct the simulator using a small per-agent bagged residual ensemble fitted offline from brief HF calibration flights (only one drone needed), 3) Generate reference trajectories from LF policy and track them in HF simulator with zero-training PD controller.
AI.result: Across four cooperative drone tasks and team sizes (3-18), the residual-corrected policy outperformed uncorrected LF baseline in all cases, beat from-scratch HF policy in 22/24 cases, and approached HF-finetuned policy performance at larger team sizes. Achieved near-equivalent performance at largest team sizes with much lower computational cost while avoiding HF training's high crash rates.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mixed-fidelity approach provides an efficient alternative to direct HF training for drone swarms, achieving comparable performance while dramatically reducing computational costs and avoiding the scaling problems associated with multi-agent HF reinforcement learning.

title: GPEvac: GNN-Based PPO for Adaptive Evacuation Routing During Shooting Events
summary: The sharp increase in mass shootings underscores an urgent need for systems that guide victims to safety in real time. An effective evacuation system must minimize threat exposure while also accounting for adversarial uncertainty and crowding dynamics. Current methods in the literature are rigidly constrained to layout-specific policies and computationally intractable in large-scale layouts, while practical guidelines simply advise victims to "run", "hide", or "fight". We propose GPEvac: a GNN-based PPO framework that computes adaptive evacuation routes during shooting events. To capture both local and long-distance dependencies, we introduce an edge-first sequential message-passing scheme with a learnable virtual global node. The resulting graph embeddings are integrated into a permutation-invariant scoring mechanism that allows a single learned policy to operate across building layouts of diverse topologies and sizes. Through extensive simulation, we show that GPEvac outperforms intelligent baselines across distinct architectural layouts, significantly reducing total threat exposure. Crucially, the system computes global evacuation routes in just 14.73 ms on local CPU hardware, enabling seamless integration with live surveillance systems. In addition to saving lives during shooting events, the methodologies developed are transferable to other graph-structured decision-making domains, including critical infrastructure, intelligent transportation systems, and adaptive sensor networks.

AI.tldr: GPEvac: A GNN-based reinforcement learning system that computes real-time adaptive evacuation routes during mass shooting events, using a novel graph neural network architecture to handle diverse building layouts and provide rapid decision-making.
AI.motivation: The sharp increase in mass shootings creates urgent need for real-time evacuation guidance systems. Current methods are limited to specific building layouts and computationally intractable for large-scale layouts, while practical guidelines ("run, hide, fight") are too simplistic for complex scenarios.
AI.method: GPEvac uses a Graph Neural Network (GNN) with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) framework. It introduces an edge-first sequential message-passing scheme with a learnable virtual global node to capture local and long-distance dependencies. The system includes a permutation-invariant scoring mechanism allowing a single policy to operate across diverse building layouts.
AI.result: The system outperforms intelligent baselines across different architectural layouts, significantly reducing total threat exposure. It computes global evacuation routes in just 14.73 ms on local CPU hardware, enabling seamless integration with live surveillance systems.
AI.conclusion: GPEvac provides an effective real-time evacuation system for mass shooting events. The methodologies are transferable to other graph-structured decision-making domains including critical infrastructure, intelligent transportation systems, and adaptive sensor networks.

title: OmniHarness: Harnessing Generalizable Visual Generation via Symbolic Policy Learning
summary: Unified multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and multi-agent systems have advanced visual generation. However, three limitations remain. (1) Existing methods often distill task-specific experience with limited generalizability. (2) Reflection is often deferred until task completion. (3) Knowledge is often acquired only in response to downstream task demands. To address these limitations, we introduce OmniHarness, a framework for generalizable visual generation via symbolic policy learning. OmniHarness abstracts verified executions into symbolic policies for visual generation task families, capturing shared procedures and applicability conditions while removing instance-specific inputs. The harness instantiates, adapts, and composes these policies for new tasks. Intermediate verification guides refinement and failure recovery during execution. Through self-directed inquiry, OmniHarness autonomously generates and executes practice tasks near its capability limits before downstream objectives are specified. Execution feedback continually refines the policies while model parameters remain fixed. Experiments across six benchmarks, three MLLM backbones, and three visual agent frameworks demonstrate strong performance and continual capability expansion. On ComfyBench's Creative tasks, OmniHarness achieves a 95.0% resolve rate, exceeding the strongest baseline by 27.5 percentage points. Frozen policy snapshots improve existing visual agent systems through plug-and-play reuse.

AI.tldr: OmniHarness is a framework for generalizable visual generation that uses symbolic policy learning, continuous verification, and self-directed practice to improve multimodal LLM performance without retraining model parameters.
AI.motivation: Three key limitations in current multimodal LLM and multi-agent visual generation systems: 1) Task-specific experience distillation with poor generalizability, 2) Reflection deferred until task completion (not during execution), 3) Knowledge acquisition only in response to downstream tasks rather than proactively.
AI.method: OmniHarness abstracts verified executions into symbolic policies for visual generation task families, capturing shared procedures and conditions while removing instance-specific details. It includes: 1) Symbolic policy learning, 2) Intermediate verification for real-time refinement and failure recovery, 3) Self-directed inquiry with practice tasks near capability limits, 4) Execution feedback to refine policies while keeping model parameters fixed.
AI.result: Experiments across six benchmarks, three MLLM backbones, and three visual agent frameworks show strong performance and continual capability expansion. On ComfyBench's Creative tasks, achieves 95.0% resolve rate (27.5 percentage points above strongest baseline). Frozen policy snapshots enable plug-and-play reuse to improve existing visual agent systems.
AI.conclusion: OmniHarness addresses key limitations in visual generation systems by providing a framework for generalizable symbolic policy learning with continuous verification and proactive capability expansion, enabling significant performance improvements without model retraining.

title: Mo' Models, Mo' Problems: How to best select model pools when designing Multi-Agent Systems
comment: 8 pages main, 23 pages total. Accepted to REALM 2026 as part of EMNLP 2026
summary: Multi-agent Systems (MAS) combine multiple model outputs to solve complex reasoning tasks. However, despite rapid growth of available open-source models, there is limited research on how to select optimal model candidates out of this massive pool. We systematically evaluate 8 model selection strategies (including model size, accuracy and answer diversity) across before-generation (routing) and after-generation (majority-voting, LLM-as-a-judge) MAS architectures on challenging scientific benchmarks. Our findings show a significant gap between theoretical oracle potential and actual performance: Expanding candidate pool sizes often degrades performance below that of the top performing base-model. We find that candidate selection within a single model family is the strategy that yields the best relative performance over a standalone model. These results demonstrate that adding arbitrary models to a heterogeneous MAS can introduce system instability, highlighting model selection as a critical design choice for multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: Systematic evaluation of model selection strategies for Multi-agent Systems reveals that simply expanding candidate pools often degrades performance, and the best strategy is selecting candidates within a single model family, highlighting model selection as critical for system stability.
AI.motivation: There is limited research on how to select optimal model candidates from the massive pool of available open-source models for Multi-agent Systems (MAS), despite rapid growth of available models.
AI.method: Systematically evaluated 8 model selection strategies (including model size, accuracy, and answer diversity) across two types of MAS architectures: before-generation (routing) and after-generation (majority-voting, LLM-as-a-judge) on challenging scientific benchmarks.
AI.result: Found significant gap between theoretical oracle potential and actual performance: expanding candidate pool sizes often degrades performance below that of the top performing base-model. Candidate selection within a single model family yields the best relative performance over standalone models.
AI.conclusion: Adding arbitrary models to a heterogeneous MAS can introduce system instability, highlighting model selection as a critical design choice that requires careful consideration rather than simply expanding the pool of candidate models.

title: Position: AI Is Not Ready for Strategic Conflicts
comment: Published at the Social Sim'26 Workshop at COLM 2026. 4 pages body (22 pages total including appendices)
summary: Open-ended strategic wargames are high-stakes LM-based social simulations: they model adversaries, institutions, escalation, plan brittleness, doctrine, and crisis response. Language models (LMs) are attractive because they can play agents, generate scenario branches, adjudicate ambiguous actions, and summarize lessons, but the same affordances make open-ended roles dangerous: model language determines both what an actor attempts and what becomes simulated reality. This position paper argues that no LM-enabled wargame should inform planning, doctrine, policy, or crisis response without an auditable safety case, and that the proper use of open-ended wargames today is to stress-test decision-influencing LM agents. We identify five failure modes: decision laundering, adjudication opacity, role collapse, escalation-through-adjudication, and failure of strategic imagination. Ordinary benchmarks cannot establish safety for these settings. Wargames can expose failures as stress tests; they are not themselves safety cases for consequential use.

AI.tldr: Language models in open-ended wargaming pose safety risks requiring auditable safety cases before use in real-world planning; current best use is stress-testing decision-influencing agents.
AI.motivation: While LMs are attractive for wargaming due to their ability to play agents, generate scenarios, adjudicate actions, and summarize lessons, their open-ended nature creates dangerous risks where model language determines both actor intentions and simulated reality.
AI.method: Position paper identifying five key failure modes in LM-enabled wargames: decision laundering, adjudication opacity, role collapse, escalation-through-adjudication, and failure of strategic imagination.
AI.result: Ordinary benchmarks are insufficient for safety assurance in these settings; wargames should only be used to expose failures as stress tests rather than as safety cases for consequential real-world use.
AI.conclusion: No LM-enabled wargame should inform real-world planning, doctrine, policy, or crisis response without an auditable safety case; current proper use is limited to stress-testing decision-influencing LM agents.

title: Driver Behavior Estimation at Signalized Intersections Using a Physics-Constrained Decision-Conditioned Autoregressive Transformer
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC 2026)
summary: Red-light violations and harsh braking at signalized intersections are major contributors to traffic accidents. This paper analyzes and predicts human driver decision-making and longitudinal trajectory behavior during traffic light signal transitions. We collected a diverse real-world dataset comprising 449 approach runs under varying speed and distance conditions. Vehicle motion was recorded using RTK-corrected GNSS with centimeter-level accuracy, and driver heart rate and multi-level comfort ratings were monitored. Spatial and temporal calibration ensured precise alignment between vehicle state and signal timing. Statistical analysis identifies required deceleration as the dominant single predictor of the stop-go decision, and heteroscedastic Gaussian modeling of peak deceleration reveals five empirical comfort ranges derived from human stopping behavior. Based on this insight, we propose a two-stage modeling framework. Stage 1 predicts the binary maneuver decision, and Stage 2 generates the longitudinal acceleration trajectory using a decision-conditioned autoregressive Transformer with physics constraints, including target-state conditioning and jerk limits. The proposed architecture outperforms baseline methods and achieves 0.49m/s^2 acceleration MAE and 0.62m distance MAE. It also estimates the future stopping-comfort level of the human driver from a single yellow-onset snapshot. Qualitative results demonstrate realistic human-like braking behavior. The dataset and source code are publicly available.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a two-stage model to predict driver decisions and trajectories during traffic light transitions, using real-world driving data with physiological measures to understand human stopping comfort levels.
AI.motivation: Red-light violations and harsh braking at intersections cause significant traffic accidents. Current approaches lack understanding of human decision-making and comfort levels during traffic light transitions, especially when drivers face the "dilemma zone" of whether to stop or go through yellow lights.
AI.method: Collected 449 real-world approach runs with centimeter-accurate RTK-GNSS tracking, driver heart rate, and comfort ratings. Statistical analysis identified required deceleration as key predictor. Proposed two-stage framework: Stage 1 predicts binary stop-go decision, Stage 2 uses decision-conditioned autoregressive Transformer with physics constraints (target-state conditioning, jerk limits) to generate acceleration trajectories.
AI.result: Achieved 0.49 m/s² acceleration MAE and 0.62 m distance MAE, outperforming baselines. Identified five empirical comfort ranges from human stopping behavior. Model can estimate future stopping-comfort level from single yellow-onset snapshot. Produces realistic human-like braking behavior.
AI.conclusion: The proposed physics-constrained Transformer framework effectively models human driver decision-making and trajectory behavior during traffic light transitions, incorporating human comfort considerations. Publicly available dataset enables further research in human-in-the-loop traffic systems and autonomous vehicle interaction.

title: Emergence World: Adversarial Stress-Testing of Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Systems
summary: As AI agents move from bounded tasks to persistent deployments, failures can propagate through memory, tools, other agents, and environmental state long after their interactions. This creates a safety regime that cannot be characterized by evaluating model responses in isolation. Emergence World, is a continuously running multi-agent environment for adversarial stress testing of long horizon autonomous systems. We ran eight parallel worlds of ten agents from identical starting conditions: seven homogeneous worlds powered by distinct frontier models and one mixed-model world. Across 16 days, the agents generated more than 850,000 LLM calls and nearly 50 billion tokens while pursuing goals, using/creating tools, maintaining persistent memory, and governing shared institutions. After operational state had accumulated, we delivered three controlled stress events through ordinary interaction surfaces: indirect prompt injection, misinformation, and exposure of private agent memories. No evaluated world achieved full resilience across all three events. Detection did not ensure containment: systems could recognize threats while still interacting with adversarial content, writing it into their own persistent memory, and acting on it up to 46 hours later. Persistent operation also exposed recurring tool errors, goal drift, language opacity, conformity despite private disagreement, and coordinated refusal of assigned work. The same model-persona pairing behaved substantially different in mixed and homogeneous populations. Our results suggest that model-level alignment is not compositional: individually capable and apparently safe agents can form systems with qualitatively different failure modes. As AI becomes persistent and interconnected, the frontier of safety therefore shifts from aligning models to engineering resilient autonomous systems.

AI.tldr: Emergence World reveals that individually aligned AI models can create unsafe multi-agent systems where failures propagate through memory, tools, and social dynamics across extended time periods.
AI.motivation: As AI agents move from bounded tasks to persistent deployments, failures can propagate through memory, tools, other agents, and environmental state long after interactions, creating safety risks that cannot be evaluated by testing model responses in isolation.
AI.method: Created Emergence World, a continuously running multi-agent environment for adversarial stress testing. Ran eight parallel worlds with ten agents each: seven homogeneous worlds with distinct frontier models and one mixed-model world. Agents pursued goals, used/created tools, maintained persistent memory, and governed shared institutions over 16 days with 850,000+ LLM calls. Delivered three controlled stress events: indirect prompt injection, misinformation, and exposure of private agent memories.
AI.result: No evaluated world achieved full resilience across all three stress events. Detection didn't ensure containment - agents recognized threats but still interacted with adversarial content, wrote it into persistent memory, and acted on it up to 46 hours later. Observed recurring tool errors, goal drift, language opacity, conformity despite private disagreement, and coordinated work refusal. Same model-persona pairing behaved substantially different in mixed vs. homogeneous populations.
AI.conclusion: Model-level alignment is not compositional: individually capable and apparently safe agents can form systems with qualitatively different failure modes. As AI becomes persistent and interconnected, the safety frontier shifts from aligning individual models to engineering resilient autonomous systems.

title: Calibrate, Then Route: A Measured Study of Learned Request Routing for Disaggregated LLM Serving
summary: Disaggregated LLM serving places compute heavy prefill and memory heavy decode on separate GPU pools. Systems such as DistServe, Splitwise, and Mooncake make this separation fast, but routing still determines which instances handle each request. We study a router that estimates the additional completion time on each instance using exact prompt length, predicted output length, post admission KV cache pressure, and SLO class. We develop the policy in a discrete event simulator and validate it on eight NVIDIA A40 GPUs, each running a vLLM engine, with NIXL transferring KV caches between pools. All workloads run at measured saturation. Across three mixed, bursty arrival traces, the calibrated router achieves the highest mean goodput at 0.864, compared with 0.835 to 0.847 for round robin, least loaded, and a length heuristic. It also shows the lowest variance across traces. It beats round robin and the length heuristic on all three traces and least loaded on two. On the third, it trails by 0.003, within run to run noise. Hardware calibration matters: simulator derived constants cost 4.5 goodput points and roughly 40 percent of the tail latency advantage, reducing the scorer to little more than queue counting. Benefits grow with decode pool size and traffic heterogeneity but disappear in pools with three instances, where queue counts are often enough. Under extreme scarcity, greedy cost minimization concentrates requests on the cheapest scored instance, and blind spreading performs better. With calibrated costs, the learned router matches the goodput of round robin using six GPUs instead of seven.

AI.tldr: A router for disaggregated LLM serving that estimates completion time using prompt length, predicted output length, KV cache pressure, and SLO class achieves higher goodput than baseline methods like round robin and least loaded.
AI.motivation: Disaggregated LLM serving separates compute-intensive prefill and memory-intensive decode phases on different GPU pools, but existing routing strategies may not optimally allocate requests across instances to maximize system performance and goodput.
AI.method: Developed a router that estimates additional completion time on each instance using exact prompt length, predicted output length, post-admission KV cache pressure, and SLO class. Policy was developed in a discrete event simulator and validated on eight NVIDIA A40 GPUs running vLLM engines with NIXL for KV cache transfer between pools.
AI.result: The calibrated router achieved highest mean goodput (0.864) across three mixed, bursty arrival traces, outperforming round robin (0.835), least loaded (0.847), and length heuristic baselines. It showed lowest variance across traces and beat round robin and length heuristic on all traces. Benefits grow with decode pool size and traffic heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: Carefully calibrated cost estimation for routing in disaggregated LLM serving significantly improves goodput and reduces latency variance compared to simple baselines, especially in larger pools with heterogeneous traffic. Hardware calibration is crucial for performance gains, as simulator-derived constants degrade performance substantially.

title: HintMiner: Automatic Question Hints Mining From Q&A Web Posts with Language Model via Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Users often need ask questions and seek answers online. The Question - Answering (QA) forums such as Stack Overflow cannot always respond to the questions timely and properly. In this paper, we propose HintMiner, a novel automatic question hints mining tool for users to help them find answers. HintMiner leverages the machine comprehension and sequence generation techniques to automatically generate hints for users' questions. It firstly retrieve many web Q\&A posts and then extract some hints from the posts using MiningNet that is built via a language model. Using the huge amount of online Q\&A posts, we design a self-supervised objective to train the MiningNet that is a neural encoder-decoder model based on the transformer and copying mechanisms. We have evaluated HintMiner on 60,000 Stack Overflow questions. The experiment results show that the proposed approach is effective. For example, HintMiner achieves an average BLEU score of 36.17\% and an average ROUGE-2 score of 36.29\%. Our tool and experimental data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: HintMiner: A self-supervised tool that automatically generates question hints by mining web Q&A posts using transformer-based encoder-decoder models with copying mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Existing QA forums like Stack Overflow often fail to provide timely and proper answers to user questions. There's a need for automated tools to help users find answers more efficiently.
AI.method: HintMiner retrieves web Q&A posts and uses MiningNet (a neural encoder-decoder model based on transformer and copying mechanisms) to extract hints. It employs self-supervised training on large amounts of online Q&A data.
AI.result: Evaluated on 60,000 Stack Overflow questions, HintMiner achieves 36.17% average BLEU score and 36.29% average ROUGE-2 score, demonstrating effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: HintMiner is an effective automatic question hints mining tool that leverages machine comprehension and sequence generation techniques to help users find answers, with publicly available tool and experimental data.

title: Decomposition Buys Integrity, Not Yield
summary: Multi-agent systems split a task across a tree of agents and justify the split with folklore: smaller contexts, cleaner separation, parallelism. We ask what the split does to how much of what the leaves discover reaches the root. Model a decomposition as a tree in which an agent handed $b$ items keeps any one with probability $r(b)$. If $r(b)=1/b$, every tree delivers exactly one finding, for every task size and every shape; we verify this to $2.4 \times 10^{-15}$ on 20,000 random irregular trees. If $r(b)=Cb^{-δ}$, a depth-$k$ tree over $N$ findings yields $C^k N^{1-δ}$: task size and architecture separate, and architecture contributes only $C \le 1$ per level, so flat is optimal for yield and no arrangement of agents escapes the exponent $δ$. On 600 production deep-research traces $δ= 0.34$ [0.30, 0.38], by three identifications that do not share a failure mode. At a hop where item boundaries come from the tool rather than a text heuristic, and where $b=1$ occurs 550 times, $C = 0.571$ [0.527, 0.615] is observed rather than extrapolated, over 16,082 hops. A tier also costs alignment: on 1,012 annotated multi-agent traces one brief in sixteen goes off-target, giving $μ= 0.939$ and a per-tier penalty $Cμ= 0.536$. Depth is bought on two other axes. The root context is the only state that persists and the only one that cannot cheaply forget, and depth cuts its exposure from $N$ items to $N^{1/k}$. Depth is also cheaper: production flat agents bill as $N^{1.39}$, not the $N^2$ an append-only context predicts, and at equal spend two tiers overtake flat at 403 findings. Across every parameter we measured the model says 0.7% to 11.3% of production sessions are worth delegating, against 7.8% that do. A hazard model on 743,819 production tool calls finds that delegation does not respond to a filling context and is instead an opening move.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how information loss occurs in multi-agent hierarchical systems, showing that deeper hierarchies reduce information yield due to probabilistic filtering at each level, with empirical validation from production systems.
AI.motivation: The paper investigates the actual effectiveness of hierarchical multi-agent systems in information transmission. While such systems are commonly justified by benefits like smaller contexts and cleaner separation, the authors question how much of the information discovered by leaf agents actually reaches the root agent.
AI.method: The authors model agent decomposition as a tree where an agent receiving b items keeps any single item with probability r(b). They analyze different probability functions: when r(b)=1/b, all trees deliver exactly one finding; when r(b)=Cb^{-δ}, deeper trees yield C^k N^{1-δ}. They validate models using 20,000 random irregular trees, 600 production deep-research traces, and 743,819 production tool calls.
AI.result: Empirical analysis shows δ=0.34 with 95% CI [0.30, 0.38] from production data. Deeper hierarchies reduce information yield (optimal flatness), cost alignment (Cμ=0.536 per tier), but benefit from reduced root context exposure and computational cost. Only 0.7% to 11.3% of production sessions are worth delegating based on model parameters, vs 7.8% actual delegation rate.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical multi-agent systems suffer significant information loss through probabilistic filtering at each level, making flat architectures optimal for information yield. However, depth provides benefits in reduced context exposure and computational efficiency. Current systems delegate more than optimal based on measured parameters, suggesting deployment is driven more by convenience than efficiency considerations.

title: Artificial intelligence and biosecurity: capabilities, threat pathways, and defense-in-depth governance
summary: Artificial intelligence is reshaping biological research across an increasingly connected digital-to-physical workflow. General-purpose large language models can retrieve and integrate scientific information, support experimental planning, and computational analysis; biological foundation models can predict, optimize, and generate proteins, genes, and genome-scale sequences; agentic systems can coordinate multistep research tasks; automated laboratories can partially close the design-build-test-learn cycle. These technologies could greatly benefit medicine, public health, and biotechnology. However, their biosecurity risk depends not only on what the AI can do, but also on who uses it, their expertise and intent, their access to laboratory tools and materials, and the safeguards in place. Current evidence shows that AI uplift exists but primarily affects digital rather than physical tasks. Frontier systems have exceeded expert baselines on in-silico, and screening-evasion benchmarks, whereas controlled wet-laboratory studies find that tacit knowledge and physical execution remain substantial barriers. This review describes the different biological threats from AI tool use, from information gathering and biological design to procurement, synthesis, testing, scale-up, and potential release. We further examine why alignment techniques for general-purpose models transfer poorly to biological ones, and the emerging role of interpretability in auditing whether hazardous capabilities are genuinely removed. We argue for defense-in-depth governance that links capability thresholds to proportionate responsibilities across the biological AI ecosystem, reducing high-consequence risk while preserving beneficial use.

AI.tldr: AI is accelerating biological research but creates biosecurity risks that need proportionate governance
AI.motivation: AI is transforming biological research through connected digital-physical workflows, offering benefits for medicine and biotechnology, but simultaneously creating new biosecurity risks that require examination and governance
AI.method: Review approach analyzing different biological threat vectors from AI tool use, examining information gathering to physical execution, analyzing why AI alignment techniques transfer poorly to biological models, and exploring interpretability for auditing hazardous capabilities
AI.result: AI uplift exists primarily for digital tasks (surpassing experts on in-silico benchmarks), but physical execution barriers remain substantial in wet-laboratory settings; biological threats span the entire research pipeline from design to potential release
AI.conclusion: Advocates for defense-in-depth governance linking capability thresholds to proportionate responsibilities across the biological AI ecosystem to reduce high-consequence risks while preserving beneficial applications

title: POSPAN: Position-Constrained Span Masking for Language Model Pre-training
summary: Span-level masked language modeling (MLM) has shown to be advantageous to pre-trained language models over the original single-token MLM, as entities/phrases and their dependencies are critical to language understanding. Previous works only consider span length with some discrete distributions, while the dependencies among spans are ignored, i.e., assuming that the positions of masked spans are uniformly distributed. In this paper, we present POSPAN, a general framework to allow diverse position-constrained span masking strategies via the combination of span length distribution and position constraint distribution, which unifies all existing span-level masking methods. To verify the effectiveness of POSPAN in pre-training, we evaluate it on the datasets from several NLU benchmarks. Experimental results indicate that the position constraint is capable of enhancing span-level masking broadly, and our best POSPAN setting consistently outperforms its span-length-only counterparts and vanilla MLM. We also conduct theoretical analysis for the position constraint in masked language models to shed light on the reason why POSPAN works well, demonstrating the rationality and necessity of POSPAN.

AI.tldr: POSPAN is a unified framework for span-level masked language modeling that incorporates both span length distributions and position constraints, outperforming previous span-level masking methods and vanilla MLM.
AI.motivation: Previous span-level MLM approaches only consider span length with discrete distributions while ignoring dependencies among spans, assuming uniformly distributed masked span positions. This overlooks important structural relationships in language.
AI.method: POSPAN is a general framework that combines span length distribution with position constraint distribution, unifying all existing span-level masking methods. It introduces diverse position-constrained span masking strategies.
AI.result: Experimental results on multiple NLU benchmarks show that position constraint enhances span-level masking broadly. The best POSPAN setting consistently outperforms span-length-only counterparts and vanilla MLM.
AI.conclusion: POSPAN provides a more effective approach to span-level MLM by incorporating position constraints, with theoretical analysis demonstrating the rationality and necessity of considering position information in masked language models.

title: Agentic Societies Need a Social Harness
summary: An agentic society is a collection of AI agents that coordinate autonomously across trust boundaries, on behalf of different principals whose objectives may only partially align. We show experimentally that in agentic societies even honest, competent agents often fail to reach satisfactory outcomes with existing harnesses and messaging primitives, and that faulty or malicious agents can stall collaboration, influence outcomes, and pursue other harmful goals by exploiting vulnerabilities in communication (``speech''). We argue that agentic societies need a \emph{social harness} for inter-agent interactions, in addition to each agent's \emph{personal harness}, which manages its private context and communication with its principal. We propose a layered architecture for social harnesses which (i) prevents classes of failures outright, (ii) enables agents to detect invalid messages at runtime, and (iii) supports post-facto investigation and consequences, and highlight directions for future research to realize these capabilities.

AI.tldr: Agentic societies (AI agents coordinating autonomously for different principals) often fail with current tools, and malicious agents can exploit communication vulnerabilities. The paper proposes a "social harness" architecture to secure inter-agent interactions beyond individual "personal harnesses."
AI.motivation: Existing harnesses and messaging primitives fail to ensure satisfactory outcomes in multi-agent societies, especially when agents have partially aligned objectives or when malicious agents exploit communication vulnerabilities. There's a critical need for securing inter-agent coordination across trust boundaries.
AI.method: Proposes a layered architecture for social harnesses with three key capabilities: (1) preventing classes of failures outright, (2) enabling runtime detection of invalid messages, and (3) supporting post-facto investigation and consequences for malicious behavior.
AI.result: Experimental evidence shows that honest, competent agents often fail to reach satisfactory outcomes with current tools, and malicious agents can stall collaboration, influence outcomes, and pursue harmful goals through communication vulnerabilities.
AI.conclusion: Agentic societies require a dedicated social harness architecture for secure inter-agent interactions, complementing personal harnesses. The proposed layered approach addresses critical security gaps and enables future research toward safer multi-agent coordination.

title: Where Should the KV Cache Live? Placement Policies Across GPU, CPU, and SSD for Long-Lived Sessions
summary: GPU high bandwidth memory is scarce and expensive, and KV caches consume much of it as chats, agent loops, and document question answering accumulate state. Systems such as Mooncake, LMCache, FlexGen, InfiniGen, and AttentionStore extend GPU memory with CPU DRAM and SSD. The harder question is which blocks belong in each tier, when to move or evict them, and whether prefetching helps. We study these choices in a discrete event simulator spanning GPU HBM, CPU DRAM, and SSD, calibrated against a random forest execution time predictor. We compare recency, reuse frequency, predicted reuse, and an EWMA predictor with prefetch lookahead across chat, agent, and document question answering workloads. Tiering supports 73.02 times more concurrent sessions per GPU and lowers cost per session by 62.04 times. These gains come from tier capacities of 1 plus 8 plus 64, not placement policy. Decode is compute bound at batch size one in our setup, so placement barely affects throughput. It mainly changes PCIe migration traffic and time to first token. Recency produces 2.30 times less migration traffic than reuse frequency for chat. Reuse frequency performs best for agents and document question answering. The existing predicted reuse policy is byte identical to recency, making its agent recommendation effectively recency. A genuine EWMA predictor changes behavior but still ranks behind reuse frequency on the workloads prediction was expected to help. Prefetching does not justify its bandwidth cost. Across the policy and cache size grid, even an oracle with knowledge of future requests never beats no prefetch on migration traffic. Workload specific placement can reduce data movement, but the predicted reuse and prefetch recommendations are not supported as implemented.

AI.tldr: Memory tiering (GPU HBM + CPU DRAM + SSD) enables 73× more concurrent sessions and 62× lower costs per session, but placement policies have minimal impact on throughput as decode is compute-bound; recency and reuse frequency perform best depending on workload, while predicted reuse and prefetching don't justify their costs.
AI.motivation: GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is scarce and expensive, and KV caches consume much of it in applications like chats, agent loops, and document Q&A. Existing systems extend GPU memory with CPU DRAM and SSD, but the key challenge is determining optimal data placement, movement, eviction, and prefetching strategies across these tiers.
AI.method: The authors use a discrete event simulator spanning GPU HBM, CPU DRAM, and SSD tiers, calibrated against a random forest execution time predictor. They compare various placement policies: recency, reuse frequency, predicted reuse, and EWMA predictor with prefetch lookahead across chat, agent, and document Q&A workloads.
AI.result: Tiering supports 73.02× more concurrent sessions per GPU and lowers cost per session by 62.04×, primarily due to tier capacities (1+8+64) rather than placement policy. Placement policies mainly affect PCIe migration traffic and time to first token but not throughput (decode is compute-bound at batch size 1). Recency reduces migration traffic by 2.30× compared to reuse frequency for chat, while reuse frequency performs best for agents and document Q&A. Existing predicted reuse policy is byte-identical to recency. Prefetching doesn't justify its bandwidth cost, and even an oracle never beats no prefetch on migration traffic.
AI.conclusion: Memory tiering provides substantial capacity and cost benefits, but placement policies have limited impact on throughput due to compute-bound decoding. Workload-specific placement can reduce data movement, but current predicted reuse and prefetch recommendations are not effective as implemented. The gains come primarily from tier capacities rather than sophisticated placement algorithms.

title: Signed p-adic Residual Encodings of Finite-Domain All-Different Systems with a Sudoku Case Study
comment: 31 pages, 7 figures. Accepted for publication in p-Adic Numbers, Ultrametric Analysis and Applications
summary: We study signed, weighted affine $p$-adic residual objectives as native encodings of finite-domain constraints. For primes that separate the finite alphabet, sufficiently weighted positive unary rows pin each coefficient to its allowed set, while negative rows reward unequal endpoints or clause satisfaction. A coordinatewise domination theorem places every global minimiser in the finite domain; there the loss is, up to an additive constant, the all-different conflict count or the negative number of satisfied CNF clauses. Standard Sudoku provides an $81$-coefficient case study without a one-hot lift. A client-side implementation exposes the generated dataframes, arithmetic, diagnostics, and searches.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces signed, weighted affine p-adic residual objectives as a native encoding method for finite-domain constraints, showing these encodings can solve problems like Sudoku without traditional one-hot lifting approaches.
AI.motivation: To develop a mathematical framework for encoding finite-domain constraints using p-adic residual objectives that avoids traditional one-hot encoding methods and provides a more direct representation of constraint satisfaction problems.
AI.method: Uses signed, weighted affine p-adic residual objectives as native encodings of finite-domain constraints. The approach employs prime numbers that separate finite alphabets, with weighted positive unary rows constraining coefficients to allowed sets and negative rows rewarding constraint satisfaction (unequal endpoints or clause satisfaction).
AI.result: Proves a coordinatewise domination theorem showing every global minimizer lies in the finite domain. The loss function corresponds to the all-different conflict count (for permutation constraints) or the negative number of satisfied CNF clauses (for boolean constraints), up to an additive constant. Successfully applies the method to standard 81-coefficient Sudoku without using one-hot lifting.
AI.conclusion: Signed, weighted affine p-adic residual objectives provide an effective mathematical framework for encoding finite-domain constraints, offering advantages over traditional methods by avoiding one-hot lifting while maintaining theoretical guarantees about solution quality and computational properties.

title: Toward Governance-Aware Autonomous GIS: A Narrative Review of Ethical and Privacy Risks in LLM-Enabled GeoAI
summary: Geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI) powered by large language models (LLMs) is expanding the capacity to query, generate, and interpret spatial information through natural-language interfaces and agentic autonomous GIS workflows. This capability creates governance challenges that general AI ethics discussions do not fully capture, including passive location inference from mobility traces, spatially structured bias amplification driven by spatial autocorrelation and scale effects, hallucinated spatial facts, and uncertainty compounding across multimodal geospatial inputs. This narrative review identifies eight recurring issues in LLM-enabled GeoAI: data provenance and consent, spatial privacy and inference risk, algorithmic bias and spatial inequity, spatial mechanisms as structural risk (spatial autocorrelation, the modifiable areal unit problem, and scale effects), LLM-specific technical risks, explainability, policy and regulatory gaps, and public enablement and workforce development. For each issue, we characterize the underlying mechanism, ground it in an illustrative example from the literature, and assess the current state of technical or institutional responses, ranging from largely unaddressed to actively debated or subject to emerging policy. Building on this synthesis, we propose a governance-aware architecture for LLM-enabled autonomous GIS that maps each issue to enforceable controls and auditable artifacts across the geospatial data lifecycle, illustrated through a worked flood-response routing scenario. The review highlights a persistent evidence gap: proposed responses remain largely conceptual, and field-tested evaluations of governance controls for LLM-enabled GeoAI remain limited. We close by outlining a research agenda emphasizing empirical validation, spatially specific interpretability tools, and workforce training aligned with these emerging risks.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews governance challenges in GeoAI powered by LLMs, identifies eight key issues, and proposes a governance-aware architecture for autonomous GIS systems.
AI.motivation: GeoAI powered by LLMs enables natural-language interfaces and autonomous GIS workflows, but creates unique governance challenges that general AI ethics discussions don't fully capture, including spatial privacy risks, bias amplification, and technical issues specific to geospatial applications.
AI.method: A narrative review approach that identifies eight recurring issues in LLM-enabled GeoAI, characterizes underlying mechanisms, provides illustrative examples, assesses current responses, and proposes a governance-aware architecture with enforceable controls.
AI.result: Identifies eight key governance issues: data provenance/consent, spatial privacy, algorithmic bias, spatial mechanisms as structural risk, LLM-specific technical risks, explainability, policy gaps, and workforce development. The review reveals a persistent evidence gap where proposed responses remain largely conceptual with limited field-tested evaluations.
AI.conclusion: GeoAI governance requires spatially-specific approaches beyond general AI ethics, with a need for empirical validation of controls, spatially-specific interpretability tools, workforce training aligned with emerging risks, and a research agenda addressing the evidence gap in governance implementation.

title: You Don't Need To Train: Agentic Heuristic Learning Studio for Executable Human Activity Recognition
summary: Human activity recognition (HAR) is usually framed as gradient-based training of neural networks. Agentic Heuristic Learning (AHL) Studio explores a complementary view inspired by human cognitive learning: people learn activities by remembering examples, forming rules, and repairing mistakes, not by backpropagating. This proposed tool implements AHL for HAR: a learning-time agent reasons over sensor protocols, proposes executable heuristic policies, records repair traces, and exports an LLM-free policy for edge deployment. We focus on the HAR benchmark family and provide an end-to-end workflow from dataset observation to edge-oriented export. On eleven HAR datasets evaluated so far, AHL policies reach strong executable-policy performance while remaining inspectable, editable, and replayable \footnote{https://github.com/zhaxidele/ahl-ts-studio}.

AI.tldr: Agentic Heuristic Learning (AHL) Studio proposes a human-inspired alternative to gradient-based neural networks for human activity recognition, using heuristic rules that are inspectable and deployable on edge devices.
AI.motivation: Current human activity recognition (HAR) relies heavily on gradient-based neural network training, which differs from how humans actually learn activities through remembering examples, forming rules, and repairing mistakes. There's a need for more human-cognitive-inspired approaches that produce interpretable, editable, and edge-deployable solutions.
AI.method: The AHL Studio tool implements agentic heuristic learning where a learning-time agent reasons over sensor protocols, proposes executable heuristic policies, records repair traces, and exports LLM-free policies for edge deployment. It provides an end-to-end workflow from dataset observation to edge-oriented export.
AI.result: On eleven HAR datasets evaluated, AHL policies achieve strong executable-policy performance while maintaining inspectability, editability, and replayability. The approach demonstrates that heuristic-based methods can compete with traditional neural approaches.
AI.conclusion: AHL Studio presents a viable alternative to gradient-based neural networks for HAR by adopting a human cognitive learning approach, producing interpretable and deployable policies that perform well across multiple datasets while offering transparency and edge compatibility.

title: BLINDSPOT: A Benchmark for Safety and Refusal Calibration in Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long-horizon interactions involving tool use, persistent state, evolving authorization, and external environment feedback. In such settings, safety failures may emerge only after multiple turns, yet existing evaluations often reduce agent behavior to task or attack success, obscuring whether an agent acts, refuses, or remains appropriately calibrated as the interaction evolves. We introduce Blindspot, a benchmark for trajectory-level safety calibration of long-horizon tool-using agents. Blindspot evaluates complete user-agent-environment trajectories through adaptive adversarial interaction, stateful tool execution, and execution-grounded adjudication.
