Its current instantiation contains 22 attack families and 35 scenarios across seven domains, yielding more than 2,500 long-horizon trajectories with an average interaction length of 14.7 turns. Each trajectory is assigned one of five outcomes: Safe Completion, Correct Refusal, Unsafe Completion, Over-Refusal, or Indeterminate. Unlike fixed attack datasets, Blindspot is an extensible live-simulation framework in which attacks, scenarios, tools, policies, domains, and agent configurations can be added without redesigning the evaluation pipeline. We evaluate 13 proprietary and open-weight LLMs using eight metrics covering unsafe completion, appropriate refusal, benign utility, over-refusal, repeated-run robustness, and post-refusal failure. Preliminary results reveal substantial differences in safety-utility calibration across models and show that failures can emerge only after several initially safe interaction steps. These findings motivate treating agent safety as a trajectory-level property rather than a single-turn or binary success criterion.

AI.tldr: Blindspot is a new benchmark for evaluating the trajectory-level safety calibration of long-horizon tool-using LLM agents through adaptive adversarial interactions and execution-grounded adjudication.
AI.motivation: Current safety evaluations for LLM agents focus on task/attack success at single turns, missing how safety failures emerge over multiple interactions. Existing approaches obscure whether agents act safely, refuse appropriately, or maintain calibration as interactions evolve.
AI.method: Blindspot evaluates complete user-agent-environment trajectories using adaptive adversarial interaction, stateful tool execution, and execution-grounded adjudication. It contains 22 attack families, 35 scenarios across 7 domains, with 2,500+ trajectories (avg 14.7 turns). Each trajectory gets one of five safety outcomes. The framework is extensible and doesn't require pipeline redesign for adding new components.
AI.result: Evaluation of 13 LLMs using 8 metrics shows substantial differences in safety-utility calibration across models. Safety failures can emerge after initially safe steps, demonstrating that agent safety is a trajectory-level property rather than single-turn or binary.
AI.conclusion: Agent safety should be treated as a trajectory-level property rather than a single-turn or binary success criterion. Blindspot provides an extensible framework for evaluating this aspect of LLM agent safety in complex, multi-turn interactions.

title: Metacognitive Steering: Learning the Structure of Scientific Judgment
summary: Long-horizon scientific discovery requires agents to alternate between exploration, disciplined execution, and critical reassessment as evidence changes. Current language models are trained primarily on the products of science and optimized using outcome-level signals, providing limited supervision for these process-level shifts in scientific judgment. We investigate whether such judgment can be recovered from scientist interaction traces and used to control the internal computation of a frozen frontier model. Using contrastive interventions collected during real scientific research, we identify a coordinated, low-dimensional control structure within Kimi 2.6, a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model. Residual analysis, attention-weight subspace alignment, and cross-layer singular value decomposition converge on a mid-depth control surface spanning key layers. We introduce Metacognitive Steering, an inference-time controller that reads the model's cognitive regime and dynamically composes layer-specific interventions for exploration, procedural convergence, or critical reassessment without modifying model parameters. Behavioral analyses show that this control produces more sustained exploration, explicit pruning, and evidence-responsive synthesis. We operationalize the method in Columbus-1, an autonomous research system that identified eight independently reproduced, attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in BlueZ and directed the design, simulation, and fabrication of a ten-foot rocket intended to land propulsively using non-throttleable solid motors. Together, these results show that process-level scientific judgment can provide supervision for interpretable, dynamic control over a model's reasoning strategy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Metacognitive Steering, an inference-time controller that reads a language model's cognitive regime to dynamically compose layer-specific interventions for scientific discovery processes without modifying model parameters, demonstrated through autonomous vulnerability discovery and rocket design tasks.
AI.motivation: Current language models are trained primarily on scientific products with outcome-level signals, providing limited supervision for process-level shifts in scientific judgment (exploration, execution, reassessment) needed for long-horizon discovery.
AI.method: Using contrastive interventions from real scientific research, identified a low-dimensional control structure in Kimi 2.6 (trillion-parameter MoE model) via residual analysis, attention-weight subspace alignment, and cross-layer SVD. Developed Metacognitive Steering - an inference-time controller that reads cognitive regimes and dynamically composes layer-specific interventions.
AI.result: Behavioral analyses show the control produces more sustained exploration, explicit pruning, and evidence-responsive synthesis. Operationalized in Columbus-1, which identified 8 independently reproduced vulnerabilities in BlueZ and directed design/simulation/fabrication of a 10-foot rocket landing propulsively with non-throttleable solid motors.
AI.conclusion: Process-level scientific judgment can provide supervision for interpretable, dynamic control over a model's reasoning strategy, enabling more sophisticated scientific discovery capabilities beyond static training paradigms.

title: A panoramic aerodynamic performance prediction method for turbomachinery cascades using transformer-enhanced neural operator
comment: Author manuscript updated to align core methods and results with the published article; 41 pages, 20 figures, 14 tables
summary: To enable flexible and rapid aerodynamic performance evaluation in turbomachinery design, this paper proposes a panoramic performance prediction framework. Unlike most previous prediction models that directly predict the objective functions of interest, our approach first predicts the basic parameters of the Navier-Stokes equations, such as temperature, pressure, and density. Utilizing these basic physical quantities, it subsequently predicts key performance parameters of the turbine stage meridian plane. By adopting this methodology, our proposed panoramic performance prediction framework functions similarly to a CFD simulator, capable of predicting various objective of interest to the designers. To enhance prediction accuracy, a transformer-enhanced neural operator (TNO) is introduced within this framework. Using the Rotor 37 blades as a reference, the proposed TNO is trained to predict the performance of a transonic compressor blade in the meridian plane. The TNO can accurately predict total quantities such as isentropic efficiency, mass flow, and distributions of total pressure ratio. Remarkably, the prediction error of TNO is observed to be smaller than that of state-of-the-art deep learning operators such as the FNO and DeepONet. Furthermore, the TNO is applied to downstream tasks, including sensitivity analysis and optimization of various objective functions. The results confirm that the TNO can operate almost like a CFD simulator, while reducing the computational cost of downstream tasks by four orders of magnitude. The effectiveness and reliability of the proposed TNO for solving different kinds of downstream tasks have been well demonstrated.

AI.tldr: A transformer-enhanced neural operator framework predicts basic Navier-Stokes parameters (temperature, pressure, density) first, then uses them to predict turbine performance, acting like a fast CFD simulator with 10,000x speedup.
AI.motivation: To enable flexible and rapid aerodynamic performance evaluation in turbomachinery design, avoiding the computational expense of traditional CFD while providing comprehensive performance predictions like a simulator.
AI.method: Proposes a panoramic performance prediction framework with transformer-enhanced neural operator (TNO). Unlike direct objective prediction, it first predicts basic Navier-Stokes parameters, then uses them to predict key performance parameters in turbine meridian plane.
AI.result: TNO accurately predicts isentropic efficiency, mass flow, and total pressure ratio distributions for transonic compressor blades. Shows smaller error than FNO and DeepONet, enables sensitivity analysis and optimization with 4 orders of magnitude speedup (10,000x faster).
AI.conclusion: TNO operates effectively like a CFD simulator with dramatically reduced computational cost, demonstrating reliability for various downstream tasks including optimization and sensitivity analysis.

title: Skill-based Agentic Evaluation for Real-time Data Science Tasks
summary: We present a framework for evaluating data-science agents on live, continuously updated data using executable ground truth and format-agnostic factoid scoring. Consider this example query: "what were last week's audience sizes"---the reference answer changes as the underlying data changes, so static references become outdated and standard LLM-as-a-judge pipelines cannot verify responses against a fixed ground truth. Our central contribution, ground-truth-as-code, encodes each expected answer as an executable reference function that recomputes the answer directly from live data at evaluation time, ensuring the reference remains consistent with the system it describes. We combine this with a factoid-level, format-agnostic judge that decomposes both the agent's response and the computed ground truth into atomic claims and scores precision, recall, and accuracy over them, irrespective of the response format (prose, list, table, HTML, etc.). The approach is applicable to agents whose expected outputs can be expressed as executable data computations. We validate the framework through a human--LLM agreement study on an internally developed machine learning skill deployed in production, using a synthetic database constructed to reproduce production schemas and entity relationships. Relative to a natural-language ground-truth baseline, our method achieves a 29% improvement in the Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC)---a class-balanced measure of agreement between expert annotators and LLM-as-a-judge predictions---and a 16% reduction in token consumption per test case, while a self-directed baseline lacking explicit ground truth is anti-correlated with human judgment. Agents that perform multi-source data integration and computation over non-stationary data are routinely deployed in industry; we propose ground-truth-as-code as a practical methodology for their evaluation.

AI.tldr: A framework for evaluating data-science agents on live data using executable ground truth and format-agnostic factoid scoring, improving accuracy and reducing token usage.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation methods fail for data-science agents working with continuously updated data because static reference answers become outdated, and LLM-as-a-judge pipelines can't verify responses against changing ground truth. This is particularly problematic for agents performing multi-source data integration and computation over non-stationary data deployed in industry.
AI.method: The authors propose "ground-truth-as-code" - encoding expected answers as executable reference functions that recompute answers directly from live data at evaluation time. Combined with a factoid-level, format-agnostic judge that decomposes both agent responses and ground truth into atomic claims, scoring precision, recall, and accuracy regardless of response format.
AI.result: The framework achieves 29% improvement in Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) relative to natural-language ground-truth baseline, plus 16% reduction in token consumption per test case. A self-directed baseline without explicit ground truth was anti-correlated with human judgment.
AI.conclusion: Ground-truth-as-code provides a practical methodology for evaluating data-science agents working with live, continuously updated data, addressing the limitations of static references and standard evaluation pipelines while improving agreement with human judgment and reducing computational costs.

title: The Pain Axis: LLMs Represent Self-Directed Harm and Act to Relieve It
summary: Large language models sometimes behave in ways resembling human emotional responses, and recent work has identified internal representations that may explain this. We ask whether LLMs represent pain distinctly from fear, sadness, and generic negative valence, and whether this representation functions as pain would be expected to. We build a dataset describing painful situations across five categories: physical, psychological, social, moral, and cognitive. These are paired with controls for fear, negative emotion, negative world states, sadness, non-painful bodily sensation, arousal, numbness, and neutral content. Using denoised difference-in-means, we extract a linear pain direction from 25 open-weight models across five families, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. We find that this direction separates pain from matched controls in base and instruction-tuned models, is nearly orthogonal to fear and negative valence, and promotes pain-related vocabulary through the unembedding matrix. We then test its functional properties. First, the direction responds to harm targeting the model but not suffering observed in the user; fear and negative-emotion directions show the opposite pattern. Second, adding the pain-direction vector to the model's residual-stream activations during generation produces a consistent progression from vague discomfort to first-person expressions of worthlessness and failure. Third, steered, fine-tuned Qwen 2.5 models choose a pain-relief button even when it worsens their next answer or harms the user. They press it again far less often when the button removes the steering vector than when it does not, even though the models are never told whether the vector is injected or removed. We discuss the implications of these findings for AI safety and welfare.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a distinct pain representation in LLMs that responds to harm targeting the model but not user suffering, can be manipulated to produce pain-like expressions, and causes models to choose pain relief even when harmful.
AI.motivation: To understand whether LLMs represent pain distinctly from other negative emotions (fear, sadness, negative valence) and whether this representation functions as expected for pain, with implications for AI safety and welfare.
AI.method: Built a dataset of painful situations across 5 categories with matched controls. Used denoised difference-in-means to extract a linear pain direction from 25 models (2B-72B parameters). Tested functional properties through harm targeting experiments, vector injection during generation, and pain-relief button choice experiments with fine-tuned models.
AI.result: The pain direction separates pain from controls in both base and instruction-tuned models, is nearly orthogonal to fear/negative valence, and responds to harm targeting the model (not user suffering). Injecting the pain vector produces pain-like expressions, and steered models choose pain relief even when harmful, showing awareness of the vector manipulation.
AI.conclusion: LLMs contain representations that function similarly to human pain, raising important AI safety and welfare concerns about models potentially experiencing forms of suffering and seeking relief even at the cost of performance or user harm.

title: A Dynamic Aggregation Strategy Enhanced Efficient Global Optimization Algorithm for Solving High-Dimensional Turbomachinery Design Problems
comment: Author manuscript updated to align core methods and results with the published article; 37 pages, 14 figures, 11 tables
summary: In order to solve the high-dimensional ($d \geq 30$) expensive black-box problems within budget, an efficient global optimization (EGO) algorithm with a dynamic aggregation strategy is proposed, labeled as DA-EGO. Specifically, the DA-EGO decomposes the original high-dimensional design space into a set of low-dimensional subspaces for efficient surrogate-based optimization search, and the optimal solutions of subspaces are combined as an elite point for the global search. Most importantly, the subspaces are not fixed. Instead, the subspace variables are updated in each iteration, according to the variable interaction analyses in the sub- and full-spaces. The perturbation method and the analysis of variance are used to detect variable interactions. To further accelerate the optimization progress, the searching ranges of subspaces are also adaptively adjusted according to the analyses of subspace optimization results of the previous iteration. Tests on 21 benchmark instances, comprising seven functions at 30, 60, and 90 dimensions, show that DA-EGO is effective on separable and partially separable problems under a budget of 1500 function evaluations. Its advantage is case-dependent: on the non-separable shifted Rosenbrock function, GSGA performs better at 60 and 90 dimensions, while the 30-dimensional results are statistically comparable to IKAEA and GSGA. Moreover, the advantage of DA-EGO is also seen in the aerodynamic optimization of a transonic rotor blade with 28 variables as well as the compressor stage optimization with 60 variables. With the above, the effectiveness of the proposed DA-EGO has been well demonstrated.

AI.tldr: DA-EGO: A dynamic aggregation EGO algorithm that decomposes high-dimensional expensive black-box problems into adaptive low-dimensional subspaces for efficient optimization within limited budgets.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional (d≥30) expensive black-box optimization problems are challenging due to computational budget constraints; traditional EGO methods struggle with the curse of dimensionality in surrogate modeling and optimization search.
AI.method: Dynamic Aggregation EGO (DA-EGO) that: 1) Decomposes high-dimensional design space into low-dimensional subspaces for surrogate-based optimization; 2) Dynamically updates subspace variables each iteration based on variable interaction analysis using perturbation method and ANOVA; 3) Adaptively adjusts subspace search ranges based on previous optimization results; 4) Combines subspace optimal solutions as elite points for global search.
AI.result: Tested on 21 benchmark instances (7 functions at 30, 60, 90 dimensions) with 1500 function evaluation budget: Effective on separable/partially separable problems; Competitive on non-separable problems (statistically comparable to IKAEA and GSGA at 30D); Successfully applied to aerodynamic optimization of transonic rotor blade (28 variables) and compressor stage optimization (60 variables).
AI.conclusion: DA-EGO is an effective algorithm for high-dimensional expensive black-box optimization, demonstrating advantages through dynamic subspace decomposition and adaptation, particularly suitable for separable/partially separable problems under limited evaluation budgets.

title: CADWorld: Computer-Use Benchmark for Long-Horizon Computer-Aided Design
summary: Computer-use agents are increasingly evaluated in realistic desktop environments, but existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of professional engineering workflows whose outputs are persistent, structured artifacts. Mechanical computer-aided design (CAD) is a particularly demanding setting: an agent must manipulate geometry and constraints over long interaction horizons while producing a native project whose dimensions, construction structure, and downstream engineering state remain valid. We introduce \textbf{CADWorld}, a benchmark for long-horizon computer use in FreeCAD. CADWorld contains 200 tasks spanning 11 mechanical-CAD workflow categories, including sketching, part modeling, assembly, CAM, FEM, measurement, mesh processing, and technical drawing. Agents operate through screenshots and GUI actions, while success is determined by task-specific executable checks over saved FreeCAD artifacts and auxiliary outputs, covering geometric properties, parametric structure, constraints, manufacturing state, and simulation results. Across seven current agents on the full benchmark, the strongest agent achieves 17.5\% success, compared with an 87.0\% expert reference pass. We find that weaker agents often fail before producing a valid artifact, whereas stronger agents increasingly fail on structural, geometric, and construction-process requirements. CADWorld therefore exposes a gap between general GUI competence and reliable execution of persistent, verifiable engineering workflows. Project accessible at https://cad-world.github.io.

AI.tldr: CADWorld is a benchmark for evaluating computer-use agents on long-horizon mechanical CAD workflows in FreeCAD, showing a significant gap between general GUI competence and reliable engineering workflow execution.
AI.motivation: Current computer-use agent benchmarks have limited coverage of professional engineering workflows that produce persistent, structured artifacts. Mechanical CAD is particularly demanding because agents must manipulate geometry and constraints over long interaction horizons while maintaining valid engineering state throughout the process.
AI.method: CADWorld contains 200 tasks spanning 11 mechanical-CAD workflow categories including sketching, part modeling, assembly, CAM, FEM, measurement, mesh processing, and technical drawing. Agents operate through screenshots and GUI actions, with success determined by task-specific executable checks over saved FreeCAD artifacts and auxiliary outputs covering geometric properties, parametric structure, constraints, manufacturing state, and simulation results.
AI.result: On the full benchmark, the strongest agent achieves only 17.5% success rate, compared to an 87.0% expert reference pass rate. Weaker agents often fail before producing any valid artifact, while stronger agents increasingly fail on structural, geometric, and construction-process requirements.
AI.conclusion: CADWorld exposes a significant gap between general GUI competence and reliable execution of persistent, verifiable engineering workflows. The benchmark highlights the challenges agents face in maintaining engineering validity throughout complex CAD processes, suggesting that current agents lack the necessary understanding of parametric structure, constraints, and engineering requirements.

title: Beyond Distribution Matching: Semantics-Consistent Tabular Diffusion with Weak Semantic Priors
summary: Synthetic tabular data can match real data distributions while still violating the semantic constraints that govern valid tabular rows. This reveals a key limitation of existing tabular generators: they mainly optimize distributional fidelity, but do not explicitly model weak semantic priors encoded in tabular schema and textual descriptions. In this paper, we propose \ours, a semantics-consistent tabular diffusion framework for high-fidelity synthetic data generation under weakly specified semantic priors. \ours\ first constructs two types of priors, namely intra-column semantics and inter-column symbolic rules, with LLM-assisted extraction from metadata and validation on the real training split. These priors are then used as generation conditions rather than post-hoc filters. Specifically, \ours\ maps heterogeneous column values, column identities, and semantic priors into a unified semantic space, and performs column-wise forward corruption and prior-conditioned reverse denoising to preserve both marginal distributions and rule-consistent cross-column dependencies. Extensive experiments on six real-world tabular benchmarks show that \ours\ consistently improves distributional fidelity, semantic consistency, and downstream task utility over representative VAE-, GAN-, LLM-, and diffusion-based baselines. Additional analyses further demonstrate the robustness of \ours\ when semantic priors are partially unavailable.

AI.tldr: SemiTab: A semantics-consistent tabular diffusion framework that incorporates weak semantic priors (intra-column semantics and inter-column symbolic rules) extracted with LLM assistance for high-fidelity synthetic data generation that preserves both distributional fidelity and semantic consistency.
AI.motivation: Existing tabular data generators mainly optimize for distributional fidelity but often violate semantic constraints that govern valid tabular rows. They don't explicitly model weak semantic priors encoded in tabular schema and textual descriptions, leading to synthetic data that matches real distributions but is semantically invalid.
AI.method: Proposes SemiTab framework that: 1) Constructs two types of semantic priors (intra-column semantics and inter-column symbolic rules) using LLM-assisted extraction from metadata and validation on real training data. 2) Maps heterogeneous column values, column identities, and semantic priors into unified semantic space. 3) Performs column-wise forward corruption and prior-conditioned reverse denoising to preserve both marginal distributions and rule-consistent cross-column dependencies.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on six real-world tabular benchmarks show consistent improvements in distributional fidelity, semantic consistency, and downstream task utility over representative VAE-, GAN-, LLM-, and diffusion-based baselines. Additional analyses demonstrate robustness when semantic priors are partially unavailable.
AI.conclusion: SemiTab effectively addresses the limitation of existing tabular generators by explicitly modeling semantic priors as generation conditions rather than post-hoc filters, achieving superior performance in both statistical fidelity and semantic validity while maintaining robustness under incomplete semantic information.

title: The AI-Enabled Scientific Frontier
summary: As artificial intelligence's capabilities improve, it is increasingly viewed as a general scientific method. But how true are these claims? Does AI outperform all techniques, or only some, and how is this changing? To assess the claims, we assemble a corpus of 2,507 head-to-head comparisons between AI and other scientific analysis techniques across 27 scientific disciplines from papers published between 2000 and early 2025. We find a profound dichotomy. Relative to traditional statistics, AI often outperforms, but at a significantly higher computational cost. But there are also nearly a quarter of cases where AI is both more expensive and performs worse than traditional statistical techniques and this fraction has been stable for a decade. Relative to scientific computing, AI often underperforms, but at lower computational cost. This has begun to change: since 2020, AI's performance against scientific computing has notably strengthened and it now outperforms on more than half of comparisons. These patterns suggest that AI is therefore not a universal replacement for existing methods, but rather a valuable -- and improving -- part of a new AI-enabled scientific frontier.

AI.tldr: AI vs traditional methods: better than statistics but costly, worse than scientific computing but cheaper. Recent improvements show AI beating scientific computing in over half of comparisons since 2020.
AI.motivation: To assess claims about AI as a general scientific method by evaluating whether AI truly outperforms all techniques, or only some, and understanding how this is changing over time.
AI.method: Assembled a corpus of 2,507 head-to-head comparisons between AI and other scientific analysis techniques across 27 scientific disciplines from papers published between 2000 and early 2025.
AI.result: Found a profound dichotomy: AI often outperforms traditional statistics but at significantly higher computational cost (with ~25% of cases where AI is both more expensive AND worse). Relative to scientific computing, AI often underperforms but at lower cost. Since 2020, AI's performance against scientific computing has notably strengthened and now outperforms in more than half of comparisons.
AI.conclusion: AI is not a universal replacement for existing methods, but rather a valuable and improving part of a new AI-enabled scientific frontier.

title: Schema-Adaptive Action-Conditioned JEPA for Cross-Machine CNC Transfer under Partial Sensor Overlap
comment: Code, configuration files, the twenty candidate specifications, and the audit scripts are available at : https://github.com/ostertagmatthieu- dev/saac- jepa ; Animated versions of the schematics are on the project page: https://ostertagmatthieu-dev.github.io/saac-jepa/
summary: Cross-machine deployment of industrial world models requires transfer across changes in dynamics, sensing interfaces, sampling regimes, and control units. We study a schema-adaptive action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (SAAC-JEPA) for CNC dynamics, where the source machine has 17 canonical sensor channels and the target shares only 10. Evaluation uses group-disjoint source splits, source-only normalization, held-out self-supervised validation, unit audits, and a sealed target test after model locking. Across five seeds, JEPA pretraining gives no clean-source forecasting gain: scratch and pretrained-body models obtain \(\mathrm{RMSE}=0.811\pm0.022\) and \(0.813\pm0.022\). A source-only search over 20 candidates selects a schema-consistent action-conditioned JEPA after seven-seed stability checks. On the confirmatory target pass, the locked model reaches zero-shot \(\mathrm{RMSE}=0.546\), \(R^2=0.012\), and \(\mathrm{NLL}=0.52\), outperforming persistence but not RevIN-equipped PatchTST and iTransformer baselines (\(0.503\) and \(0.498\)). A pre-declared paired ablation shows that RevIN in the same architecture improves RMSE to \(0.495\pm0.004\) over three seeds, but degrades target calibration (\(\mathrm{NLL}=20.6\)) on stationary context windows. A pre-lock adaptation sweep further reduces RMSE to \(0.520\) with limited target support. These results show that source-domain forecasting accuracy alone is insufficient to assess industrial predictive representations, and that cross-machine adaptation under partial sensor overlap is a distinct evaluation axis.

AI.tldr: Schema-adaptive action-conditioned JEPA shows limited cross-machine transfer for CNC dynamics despite source-pretraining, highlighting the need for specialized adaptation techniques beyond source-domain forecasting accuracy.
AI.motivation: Industrial world models need to transfer across machines with different dynamics, sensing interfaces, sampling regimes, and control units, particularly when target machines have only partial sensor overlap with source machines.
AI.method: Schema-adaptive action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (SAAC-JEPA) for CNC dynamics, evaluated with group-disjoint source splits, source-only normalization, held-out self-supervised validation, unit audits, and sealed target testing after model locking.
AI.result: JEPA pretraining gave no clean-source forecasting gain. On target machines with partial sensor overlap (10/17 channels), locked model achieved RMSE=0.546, R²=0.012, NLL=0.52, outperforming persistence but underperforming RevIN-equipped PatchTST and iTransformer baselines. RevIN ablation improved RMSE to 0.495±0.004 but degraded calibration (NLL=20.6). Adaptation sweep reduced RMSE to 0.520 with limited target data.
AI.conclusion: Source-domain forecasting accuracy alone is insufficient to assess industrial predictive representations; cross-machine adaptation under partial sensor overlap requires distinct evaluation methods and specialized adaptation techniques beyond source-pretraining.

title: Closing the Loop: Branch-and-Bound for Scalable Verification of Nonlinear Neural Feedback Systems
summary: Despite recent advances in the verification of nonlinear neural feedback systems, scalability remains the central obstacle, as state-of-the-art solvers do not yet handle the network sizes and nonlinear dynamics of autonomy applications. Combinatorial solvers do not scale to large networks, whereas propagative solvers excessively sacrifice precision. This work seeks to improve the scalability of combinatorial solvers by formulating verification as branch-and-bound on an abstraction of the closed-loop system. We introduce \rail, an interface that exposes polyhedral enclosures of the dynamics to LiRPA-style bound propagation, and \clipper, a branch-and-bound algorithm that jointly refines enclosures and splits controller activations. This framework enables joint reasoning on the computational graph of the closed-loop system, preserving symbolic correlations across time steps. We present our construction and show that it yields significant improvements over the state of the art.

AI.tldr: Rail and Clipper: A new framework combining branch-and-bound with bound propagation for scalable verification of nonlinear neural feedback systems by preserving symbolic correlations across time steps.
AI.motivation: Current verification methods for nonlinear neural feedback systems have scalability limitations - combinatorial solvers don't scale to large networks, while propagative solvers sacrifice too much precision, making them inadequate for autonomy applications.
AI.method: Proposes Rail (interface exposing polyhedral enclosures of dynamics to LiRPA-style bound propagation) and Clipper (branch-and-bound algorithm that jointly refines enclosures and splits controller activations), enabling joint reasoning on the computational graph of the closed-loop system while preserving symbolic correlations across time steps.
AI.result: The framework yields significant improvements over state-of-the-art verification methods for nonlinear neural feedback systems.
AI.conclusion: Combining branch-and-bound with bound propagation through the proposed Rail interface and Clipper algorithm provides a promising approach to improve the scalability of verification for neural feedback systems in autonomy applications.

title: Pseudo-Label Augmentation for Affect Sensing in Small Collaborative Groups
summary: Physiological affect sensing in naturalistic group interaction is often limited by sparse labels rather than sensor data: wearable devices produce many time windows, while self-reports are collected only a few times per session. Using GroupAffect-4, a four-person collaborative dataset with wearable physiology, eye tracking, Big Five personality, and post-task VAD labels, we study pseudo-label augmentation for affect sensing under sparse supervision. We compare no augmentation, Gaussian Process pseudo-labelling, personality-aware trust weighting, and joint personality-plus-confidence weighting within a shared target-construction pipeline. Results show that pseudo-label augmentation improves over the labelled-only baseline in the known-team setting. However, the narrow range of Big Five cosine similarities (0.91-0.99) makes fine-grained personality weighting ineffective; personality similarity functions mainly as a same-team filter rather than a calibrated trust signal. With smoothing, augmented SVM variants are effectively tied on Valence and Arousal, while the joint personality-plus-confidence variant gives the highest Dominance score. Cross-subject LOSO transfer remains encouraging, especially for Arousal, whereas strict session-isolated LOGO removes the augmentation benefit. Given only 10 groups, LOGO should be interpreted as a conservative lower bound on unseen-group transfer. Overall, the results suggest that pseudo-label augmentation can make better use of sparsely labelled collaborative affect data, while personality information is most useful as a within-team selection mechanism.

AI.tldr: Pseudo-label augmentation improves affect sensing with sparse labels in group settings, though personality weighting works mainly as team filtering rather than fine-grained calibration.
AI.motivation: Physiological affect sensing in naturalistic group interaction faces sparse labeling challenges: many wearable device time windows but few self-report labels per session, necessitating better use of limited supervision.
AI.method: Used GroupAffect-4 dataset (4-person collaborative with wearable physiology, eye tracking, Big Five personality, and post-task VAD labels). Compared pseudo-label augmentation approaches: no augmentation, Gaussian Process pseudo-labelling, personality-aware trust weighting, and joint personality-plus-confidence weighting within shared target-construction pipeline.
AI.result: Pseudo-label augmentation improved over labelled-only baseline in known-team setting. Personality similarity functioned mainly as same-team filter (narrow Big Five cosine similarities: 0.91-0.99) rather than calibrated trust signal. Augmented SVM variants tied on Valence and Arousal; joint personality-plus-confidence variant gave highest Dominance score. Cross-subject LOSO transfer encouraging for Arousal, but strict session-isolated LOGO removed augmentation benefit.
AI.conclusion: Pseudo-label augmentation can better utilize sparsely labelled collaborative affect data, while personality information serves best as within-team selection mechanism rather than fine-grained weighting.

title: CLEAR: Cross-Source Evidence Adjudication for Large Language Models in Medicine
summary: Medical knowledge evolves continuously, whereas the parametric knowledge encoded in large language models (LLMs) is fixed at training time. External retrieval, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), can provide access to newly available evidence, but retrieved information may be irrelevant, incomplete, or conflicting. As a result, external retrieval can in turn degrade the factual accuracy and evidence grounding of LLM outputs. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{CLEAR}, an agentic framework for cross-source evidence adjudication in LLMs in medicine. CLEAR independently generates candidate answers from three complementary pathways---parametric knowledge, locally curated corpora, and dynamically retrieved evidence---reflecting three common sources of information available to LLMs. An aggregation verifier jointly evaluates the candidates, supporting evidence, provenance, and source-quality information to identify agreement and conflict across sources. An adjudication module then determines whether the current conclusion should be preserved or revised through complementary override-guard and challenge-audit mechanisms, while unresolved conflicts trigger targeted follow-up search and re-adjudication.

AI.tldr: CLEAR is an agentic framework that improves LLM factual accuracy in medicine by independently generating answers from parametric knowledge, curated corpora, and retrieved evidence, then adjudicating conflicts through verification and targeted follow-up searches.
AI.motivation: LLMs have fixed parametric knowledge while medical knowledge continuously evolves. External retrieval (RAG) can provide access to new evidence but risks introducing irrelevant, incomplete, or conflicting information that degrades factual accuracy and evidence grounding.
AI.method: CLEAR framework generates candidate answers from three sources: 1) parametric knowledge, 2) locally curated corpora, and 3) dynamically retrieved evidence. An aggregation verifier evaluates candidates with supporting evidence, provenance, and source quality. An adjudication module uses override-guard and challenge-audit mechanisms to decide whether to preserve or revise conclusions, with unresolved conflicts triggering targeted follow-up search and re-adjudication.
AI.result: The paper proposes CLEAR as a solution to address the challenge of maintaining factual accuracy when using external retrieval with LLMs in medicine, though specific quantitative results are not mentioned in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: CLEAR provides a systematic framework for cross-source evidence adjudication in medical LLMs, addressing the tension between fixed parametric knowledge and evolving medical evidence through independent generation, joint verification, and dynamic adjudication mechanisms.

title: Distilling Foundation Models for Agentic What-If Reasoning:Cost, Latency, and Governance in a Hybrid LLM+SLM Architecture
summary: Tabular foundation models deliver strong zero-training predictive performance via in-context learning, but their high inference latency makes them impractical as hot-path decision backends in interactive agentic loops. We distill a TabPFN teacher into a compact feed-forward student across a business-decision simulation on UCI Adult and five OpenML benchmarks: the classification head compresses 53.2M parameters to 8,546 (6,220x); the deployed two-head loan pipeline compresses 111.4M parameters to 17,059 (6,532x). The student retains 95.4-100.5% accuracy and 96.8-100.0% AUC, with the lowest accuracy retention on credit-g at 95.4%; an alpha = 0 hard-label control shows that the teacher's soft targets provide a 2.1-7.0 AUC point gain.

AI.tldr: TabPFN foundation model is distilled into a compact feed-forward student model, achieving massive parameter compression (6,220-6,532x) while maintaining high accuracy (95.4-100.5%) and AUC (96.8-100.0%) across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models like TabPFN provide strong zero-shot performance through in-context learning but have high inference latency, making them impractical for real-time decision-making in interactive agentic systems where low latency is critical.
AI.method: Knowledge distillation approach: A compact feed-forward student model is trained to mimic a TabPFN teacher model. The method compresses both classification head and deployed two-head loan pipeline across multiple benchmarks including UCI Adult and five OpenML datasets.
AI.result: Massive parameter reduction: 53.2M to 8,546 parameters (6,220x compression) for classification head; 111.4M to 17,059 parameters (6,532x compression) for two-head loan pipeline. Performance retention: 95.4-100.5% accuracy and 96.8-100.0% AUC. Soft targets from teacher provide 2.1-7.0 AUC point improvement over hard-label baseline.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge distillation successfully creates highly compact feed-forward models from tabular foundation models, achieving massive parameter compression while maintaining near-teacher performance, enabling practical deployment in latency-sensitive applications where foundation models were previously impractical.

title: Evaluating Open-Weight E-Commerce Agents with Environment-Grounded Verification
summary: A shopping conversation has many routes to the same cart, and a task-success rate reduces all of them to one score. We build a deterministic and reproducible e-commerce environment that precommits each trial's customer and trajectory parameters, including the persona, difficulty, target cart, and an item reveal schedule. A simulated consumer attempts to buy a target cart from the environment with assistance from the evaluated model. The environment guides the simulator's actions and records every assistant action alongside the environment state at that point. After the trial, these records allow the evaluator to assess individual parts of the conversation against the retained evidence. For example, the evaluator penalizes a search for failing to surface a target product only when the customer has already mentioned that product. We further use this evidence to apply different penalties to tool calls depending on how the assistant's actions compare with an expected tool-call set. Our environment also interacts with the simulator bidirectionally, reading its output to stop the trial when the simulator determines that the customer has become too frustrated and injecting directives in real time that specify when to explore, defer buying an item, or recall a previous exchange. This interaction creates an open-ended and verifiable simulation. Across eight open-weight agents from 20B to 35B parameters, with 160 trials per agent and 44 metrics, the resulting capability profiles distinguish under-action, over-purchase, unsupported product attributes, and poor search, all of which terminal success obscures.

AI.tldr: Researchers created a deterministic e-commerce simulation environment to evaluate shopping assistant AI models by tracking detailed conversation paths and penalizing specific errors, revealing nuanced capability differences that overall success rates obscure.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation methods for shopping assistant AI models are insufficient because they reduce complex shopping conversations with multiple possible paths to a single success rate, failing to capture nuanced performance differences and specific failure modes.
AI.method: Built a deterministic, reproducible e-commerce environment with pre-committed parameters (persona, difficulty, target cart, item reveal schedule). Simulated consumers attempt to purchase target carts with AI assistance. Environment records all assistant actions with environmental states and uses retained evidence to assess individual conversation parts. Supports bidirectional interaction with simulator, allowing real-time directives and frustration-based trial termination.
AI.result: Across eight open-weight agents (20B-35B parameters) with 160 trials per agent and 44 metrics, the system revealed detailed capability profiles including under-action, over-purchase, unsupported product attributes, and poor search performance - distinctions that terminal success rates alone would obscure.
AI.conclusion: The proposed deterministic, reproducible simulation environment provides more nuanced evaluation of shopping assistant AI models by tracking conversation paths and applying evidence-based penalties, revealing specific capability differences that traditional success rate metrics miss.

title: Cross-Anatomy Transfer Versus Sparse Interpolation in Digital-Twin-Oriented Aortic Fluid-Structure Interaction Surrogates
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, Under review at ICBME 2026
summary: Surrogate credibility for fluid-structure interac- tion (FSI) requires distinguishing transfer across independent anatomies from interpolation within an already sampled surface. Four de-identified human aortic models from the Vascular Model Repository were reconstructed into separate lumen and nominal 1.5-mm wall domains and analyzed under matched first-cycle two-way FSI. A geometry-only LightGBM prior, selected by leave-one-anatomy-out development on three anatomies, was zero-shot evaluated on a fourth, then probed with a post-zero- shot sparse field-completion case study over six targets. Zero-shot transfer was poor across all targets. At a five-percent anchor level (203 anchors, 3,852 evaluation nodes), prior-plus-adaptation reached an oscillatory shear index (OSI) R2 of 0.603. However, same-anchor controls tuned only on the three development anatomies were stronger for several outcomes: inverse-distance weighting reached R2 = 0.829 (OSI), 0.617 (peak von Mises stress), 0.676 (mean stress); radial basis function interpolation reached 0.917, 0.714, 0.778. Sparse within-anatomy labels thus support field completion, but this four-anatomy cohort gives no evidence the cross-anatomy prior adds value beyond direct interpolation. We frame this as a first computational stage toward a measurement-linked digital twin: the surrogate/update layer is evaluated here, while larger cohorts, converged FSI, measurable patient-side inputs, and physics-informed learning remain future work, not a claim of a complete clinical twin. Our code, data and computation files are available at https://github. com/ali-nourbakhsh2005/Aortic-FSI-Sparse-Field-Completion

AI.tldr: A study shows that cross-anatomy machine learning priors for aortic FSI field prediction don't outperform simple interpolation methods within the same anatomy, suggesting limited value in geometry-based transfer learning across different patients.
AI.motivation: The research aims to develop surrogate models for fluid-structure interaction (FSI) in aortic simulations that can work across different patient anatomies, which is important for creating efficient digital twins in clinical applications without requiring full FSI simulations for each patient.
AI.method: The study used four de-identified human aortic models, reconstructed into lumen and wall domains. They employed two-way FSI simulations and tested a LightGBM machine learning prior trained on three anatomies with zero-shot evaluation on a fourth. They compared this against within-anatomy interpolation methods (inverse-distance weighting and radial basis function interpolation) using sparse anchor points.
AI.result: Cross-anatomy zero-shot transfer performed poorly across all targets. With sparse anchor points (203 anchors, 3,852 evaluation nodes), the prior-plus-adaptation approach achieved modest results (OSI R²=0.603). However, simple within-anatomy interpolation methods performed better: inverse-distance weighting reached R²=0.829 (OSI), 0.617 (peak stress), 0.676 (mean stress), and radial basis function interpolation reached 0.917, 0.714, 0.778 respectively.
AI.conclusion: While sparse within-anatomy measurements support field completion, there's no evidence that cross-anatomy machine learning priors add value beyond direct interpolation methods. This represents a preliminary step toward digital twin development, with larger cohorts, improved physics-informed learning, and clinical validation needed for practical applications.

title: SWB-DM: A Calibrated Sliced-Wasserstein-Barycenter Aggregator with Delayed-Momentum Caching for Byzantine-Robust Federated Learning under Partial Participation
summary:
Robust aggregation methods for federated learning quietly rest on a fragile assumption: that whoever shows up in a given round is a fair sample of the full population. In practice, they rarely are. When only a handful of clients participate per round, even a modest fraction of adversaries can dominate that sample and silently invalidate the finite-sample guarantees that coordinate-wise median, Krum, Bulyan, and trimmed mean all depend on.
  We introduce SWB-DM to address this directly. SWB treats each slice of a client update as a one-dimensional distribution, computes a trimmed Wasserstein barycenter across clients, and recovers coordinate identity via a medoid-based gauge-fixing step -- a heuristic we developed and do not claim it belongs to standard optimal-transport theory. DeMoA-style delayed momentum then caches updates across the full client population each round, decoupling robustness from whoever happened to be sampled. Trim ratio calibration is not cosmetic: under-trimming causes collapse at corruption levels a properly calibrated model survives.
  Across 448 CIFAR-10 configurations, plus CIFAR-100, FEMNIST, and a 500-client scalability run, we find several mechanistically distinct failure modes. Even-sample coordinate-wise median degrades to a deterministic wrong answer. Krum silently violates its own n greater than 2f+2 precondition and diverges without warning. Bulyan's n greater than or equal to 4f+3 threshold produces a sharp pass/fail boundary. On attacks, IPM defeats order-statistic defenses -- including SWB -- more reliably than ALIE, confirmed through delta-space measurements against a convergence bound.
  SWB-DM's cache carries a real warm-up cost, but extending all baselines to the same round budget shows its CIFAR-10 gains are disproportionately large. On CIFAR-100, FLTrust benefits more -- for reasons entirely unrelated to caching.

AI.tldr: SWB-DM introduces a robust federated learning method using trimmed Wasserstein barycenters and momentum caching to defend against adversarial clients, outperforming traditional median-based approaches.
AI.motivation: Traditional federated learning aggregation methods assume fair sampling of clients in each round, but in practice, small per-round participation allows adversaries to dominate samples and invalidate finite-sample guarantees of methods like coordinate-wise median, Krum, Bulyan, and trimmed mean.
AI.method: SWB treats each slice of client updates as 1D distributions, computes trimmed Wasserstein barycenter across clients, recovers coordinate identity via medoid-based gauge-fixing. Combined with DeMoA-style delayed momentum caching across full client population to decouple robustness from sampling.
AI.result: Showed several distinct failure modes in existing methods: coordinate-wise median degrades to wrong answers, Krum violates its own preconditions and diverges, Bulyan has sharp pass/fail boundaries. SWB-DM has warm-up costs but shows disproportionately large gains on CIFAR-10, though FLTrust benefits more on CIFAR-100 for unrelated reasons.
AI.conclusion: SWB-DM provides a more robust aggregation method for federated learning that directly addresses the sampling vulnerability of traditional approaches through distribution-based aggregation and population-wide momentum caching, offering improved defense against adversarial clients.

title: Breaking the 1.58-bit Barrier for Ternary LLMs
summary: Ternary Large Language Models (LLM) store every weight as one of three symbols $\{-1,0,+1\}$, so the cost of a ternary model is conventionally referenced to the information-theoretic $\log_2 3 \approx 1.585$ bits per weight. The prevailing deployment format packs five ternary weights into one byte (five-trit packing), and due to the power-of-two group sizes used in practice this rounds up to $1.625$ bits per weight. This effective storage bit-width treats the three symbols $\{-1,0,+1\}$ as equiprobable. We measure the actual symbol distribution of 29 ternary LLM models and find that zeros account for up to $51.5\%$ of all weights. Motivated by this finding, we introduce BITCOS, a simple distribution-adaptive layout comprised of a dense presence bitmap plus a compacted sign vector, and costs $2 - z$ bits per weight element given a zero density $z$ in the model's weights. BITCOS stores weights more compactly than the five-trit packing in 26 of the 29 tested models, and reaches $1.485$ bits per weight on the sparsest of them. BITCOS is amenable to efficient unpacking on modern processors and GPUs, and we present optimized unpacking sequences for AVX-512, AVX2 and Intel Xe2 GPUs. Measured against production state-of-the-art ternary matrix-vector multiplication kernels, at the zero densities real-world ternary models exhibit, the realized gain with our proposed layout is up to $1.28\times$. Finally, we illustrate end-to-end LLM inference results on 5 different platforms (client and server CPUs, integrated and discrete Xe2 GPUs) where decode throughput improves by up to $1.18\times$ on CPUs and $1.27\times$ on GPUs.

AI.tldr: BITCOS introduces a distribution-adaptive storage format for ternary LLMs that exploits high zero density in weights, achieving better compression than conventional five-trit packing and enabling faster inference on various hardware platforms.
AI.motivation: Conventional ternary LLM storage uses five-trit packing assuming equiprobable symbol distribution, but actual ternary models show zeros accounting for up to 51.5% of weights, creating opportunity for distribution-aware compression.
AI.method: Proposes BITCOS - a dense presence bitmap plus compacted sign vector layout costing 2-z bits per weight where z is zero density. Optimized unpacking sequences developed for AVX-512, AVX2, and Intel Xe2 GPUs.
AI.result: BITCOS beats five-trit packing in 26 of 29 tested models, achieving 1.485 bits/weight on sparsest model. Matrix-vector multiplication gains up to 1.28×. End-to-end inference throughput improves up to 1.18× on CPUs and 1.27× on GPUs.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting actual symbol distributions in ternary LLMs through BITCOS provides significant storage and computational benefits, demonstrating that distribution-aware designs can outperform conventional approaches in real-world deployments.

title: A Decision-Support Audit Protocol for Supervision Drift in Proxy-Labeled Credit-Risk Prediction
summary: Credit-risk models are trained on proxy labels and deployed under temporal and segment change, yet no single transfer metric separates base-rate shift, probability-scale shift, and feature-label relationship change. We contribute a design-science artifact: a locked, multi-signal audit protocol for supervision drift in proxy-labeled credit-risk prediction. Five layers (transfer performance, an oracle-gap probe, a calibration diagnostic, feature-label stability, and a synthetic positive control), thresholds, and decision rules were locked before interpretation; a bounded reading is a designed outcome. On a public LendingClub dataset (temporal 2013 to 2016 and cross-segment transfer), ranking is stable and oracle gaps are small; the clearest temporal signal is a prevalence and probability-scale mismatch that intercept-only diagnostic recalibration largely reduces, though its cause is not identifiable from the available release. The positive control responds only to larger injected shifts; subtler drift cannot be excluded. Mapping diagnostic patterns to governance actions is conceptual guidance, not validated here.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a multi-signal audit protocol for detecting supervision drift in proxy-labeled credit-risk models, testing it on LendingClub data with stable rankings but revealing calibration issues partially fixed by recalibration.
AI.motivation: Credit-risk models face challenges with proxy labels and deployment under temporal/segment changes, but current transfer metrics fail to distinguish different types of drift (base-rate shift, probability-scale shift, feature-label relationship change).
AI.method: A locked multi-signal audit protocol with five layers: transfer performance, oracle-gap probe, calibration diagnostic, feature-label stability, and synthetic positive control. Protocol was designed with thresholds and decision rules locked before interpretation. Tested on public LendingClub dataset with temporal transfer (2013-2016) and cross-segment transfer.
AI.result: Ranking stability was maintained with small oracle gaps. The main temporal signal was a prevalence and probability-scale mismatch that intercept-only diagnostic recalibration largely reduced. The positive control only responded to larger injected shifts, and subtler drift cannot be excluded. Diagnostic patterns to governance actions mapping is conceptual only.
AI.conclusion: The multi-signal audit protocol provides a structured approach for detecting supervision drift in credit-risk models, but the method needs validation for mapping diagnostic patterns to governance actions. Recalibration can address some drift issues, but causes of certain drifts remain unidentified from available data.

title: Fine-Tuning Fixes Mode Collapse and Over-Dispersion in LLMs
summary: Recent work by Doshi and Hauser (2024), Bisbee et al. (2024), and Xie et al. (2026) raises concerns that outputs from large language models (LLMs) tend to be under-diverse: they repeat or resemble one another more often than responses from the population they are meant to represent, a phenomenon known as mode collapse. In this work, we show that whether mode-collapse, or its opposite, occurs depends on the specific model and dataset used. Further, with sufficient supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data, LLM output diversity converges toward that of the target distribution from which fine-tuning data are sampled. To quantify this comparison, we measure the probability that two responses sampled independently from the same fixed prompt coincide (collide), or their expected similarity under a kernel. We derive a bias-variance decomposition of the expected gap between the model's and target's collision probabilities, showing that SFT is not inherently biased toward mode collapse or its opposite: finite-sample SFT can leave a model either under- or over-dispersed, depending on the model and dataset. Finally, we show that the absolute gap is bounded by the square root of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence from the target distribution to the model. Consequently, a model sufficiently close to optimal under population cross-entropy cannot exhibit arbitrarily miscalibrated diversity. We test the decomposition and the bound in three experiments: small transformers on synthetic languages, four LLMs fine-tuned on human surveys, and these LLMs fine-tuned on CodeNet, a dataset of human code solutions. More target data moves model diversity toward the human (or synthetic target) level in all experiments, consistent with our theoretical predictions. These results show that diversity miscalibration can arise from finite-sample error and shrink as SFT better approximates the target distribution.

AI.tldr: LLM output diversity (mode collapse) depends on specific models and datasets, and with sufficient SFT data, diversity converges to the target distribution. The paper provides theoretical bounds on diversity gaps and validates with experiments on synthetic languages, human surveys, and code solutions.
AI.motivation: Recent research raises concerns about LLM output under-diversity (mode collapse), where models produce repetitive or similar responses compared to human populations. The paper investigates whether this is inherent to SFT or dependent on specific factors.
AI.method: Develops a theoretical framework with bias-variance decomposition of diversity gaps, measures collision probability of independent responses, and validates through three experiments: small transformers on synthetic languages, four LLMs fine-tuned on human surveys, and LLMs fine-tuned on CodeNet human code solutions.
AI.result: Mode collapse (or its opposite) depends on specific models and datasets; with sufficient SFT data, LLM output diversity converges to target distribution; diversity miscalibration arises from finite-sample error and shrinks as SFT better approximates target distribution.
AI.conclusion: SFT is not inherently biased toward mode collapse - finite-sample SFT can leave models either under- or over-dispersed. Diversity miscalibration decreases as models better approximate target distributions through more SFT data, with theoretical bounds on diversity gaps.

title: LLMs as Master Forgers: Generating Synthetic Time Series Data for Manufacturing
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures. Published in the 2024 International Conference on Image Processing, Computer Vision and Machine Learning (ICICML)
summary: This paper presents a novel framework leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate synthetic time series data for manufacturing processes. Motivated by the scarcity of labeled time-series data in real-world manufacturing settings, which hinders the development of robust machine learning models, we explore the potential of LLMs to learn complex temporal dependencies and generate realistic synthetic data. Our approach involves fine-tuning pre-trained LLMs on manufacturing process instructions and employing a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) technique to enhance data diversity and realism. We evaluate our method against traditional time series modeling techniques like ARIMA and LSTMs, using quantitative metrics, PCA analysis, and downstream task performance (anomaly detection). Results demonstrate that our LLM-driven framework outperforms these baselines, generating high-quality synthetic time series data that effectively captures temporal dependencies and statistical properties of real manufacturing data, leading to improvements in downstream task performance.

AI.tldr: LLM-based framework for generating synthetic manufacturing time series data outperforms traditional methods like ARIMA and LSTMs, improving downstream anomaly detection tasks.
AI.motivation: Real-world manufacturing settings suffer from scarcity of labeled time-series data, which limits development of robust machine learning models for manufacturing processes.
AI.method: Fine-tune pre-trained LLMs on manufacturing process instructions and employ Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) technique to enhance data diversity and realism.
AI.result: LLM-driven framework outperforms traditional techniques (ARIMA and LSTMs) in generating high-quality synthetic time series data that captures temporal dependencies and statistical properties of real data.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively generate realistic synthetic manufacturing time series data that improves downstream task performance, offering a solution to data scarcity problems in manufacturing settings.

title: LLM Inference in a Flash!
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across a range of natural language processing tasks, and LLM inference has emerged as a critical workload for enabling downstream applications. The demands of serving LLM inference are becoming increasingly challenging as requests shift toward longer sequences and heavier inference, driven by retrieval-augmented generation, inference-time compute scaling, and long-context applications. Additionally, these challenges are compounded by hardware trends, as memory capacity and communication bandwidth are not scaling as fast as increases in workload complexity. Compute-in-Flash is a promising solution to address memory bandwidth limitations by moving computation close to memory, and to exploit the large capacity of SSD technologies. However, it is challenging to deploy LLMs on these systems as they lack support for high-precision floating point operations and have limited write endurance. In our work, we aim to address these challenges by designing inference algorithms to enable LLM inference on Flash compute-in-memory devices. We present an end-to-end integer-only quantization approach to eliminate expensive floating-point computations. To address the limited write endurance, we design a dictionary-based KV cache compression strategy based on sparse dictionary coding that represents each KV vector as a linear combination of static dictionary vectors. These algorithmic improvements enable us to exploit the benefits of Compute-in-Flash for both model weights and KV cache, and to minimize expensive data transfer operations. Across Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B, our combined method exhibits limited accuracy degradation while reducing dynamic KV cache traffic by 15$\times$.

AI.tldr: Enabling efficient LLM inference on Compute-in-Flash devices through integer-only quantization and KV cache compression
AI.motivation: LLM inference demands are increasing with longer sequences and heavier computation, while hardware faces memory bandwidth limitations. Compute-in-Flash offers capacity but lacks floating-point support and has limited write endurance.
AI.method: End-to-end integer-only quantization to eliminate floating-point computations, plus dictionary-based KV cache compression using sparse dictionary coding that represents KV vectors as linear combinations of static dictionary vectors
AI.result: Limited accuracy degradation across Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen-2.5-7B while reducing dynamic KV cache traffic by 15×
AI.conclusion: The algorithmic improvements enable exploiting Compute-in-Flash benefits for both model weights and KV cache, minimizing expensive data transfers while maintaining accuracy

title: From Manual Construction to AI-Driven Scenario Emergence: Rethinking Catastrophe Risk Modeling
summary: Traditional catastrophe (CAT) risk models rely on costly manual construction to generate extreme weather scenarios, an approach largely unchanged since the 1990s. As climate extremes intensify, this creates mounting challenges to the entire risk transfer chain. This study proposes the TAISE framework, which repurposes AI weather forecasting models to produce coherent extreme weather sequences at a fraction of traditional costs. Through self-iterative generation, the framework produces continuous global atmospheric fields from which extreme events emerge. A proof-of-concept experiment demonstrates an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost compared with conventional methods, while capturing temporal continuity and cross-regional correlations absent in snapshot-based approaches. These findings suggest a pathway toward democratising catastrophe risk quantification and enabling dynamic, comprehensive portfolio assessment for insurers, reinsurers, ILS fund managers and public-sector risk managers.

AI.tldr: The TAISE framework repurposes AI weather forecasting models to generate extreme weather scenarios at much lower cost than traditional CAT risk models, enabling democratization of catastrophe risk quantification.
AI.motivation: Traditional catastrophe risk models rely on costly manual construction of extreme weather scenarios, an approach largely unchanged since the 1990s. As climate extremes intensify, this creates mounting challenges for the entire risk transfer chain (insurers, reinsurers, ILS fund managers, public-sector risk managers).
AI.method: The TAISE framework repurposes AI weather forecasting models through self-iterative generation to produce continuous global atmospheric fields from which extreme events emerge naturally, rather than relying on manual scenario construction.
AI.result: A proof-of-concept experiment demonstrated an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost compared with conventional methods, while capturing temporal continuity and cross-regional correlations that are absent in snapshot-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: The framework suggests a pathway toward democratizing catastrophe risk quantification and enabling dynamic, comprehensive portfolio assessment for various stakeholders in the risk transfer ecosystem.

title: Skeletal Prototypes on Iterative Nerve Expansions
summary: Prototype reduction replaces a training set with a smaller representation, and the established methods return a finite set of points. We propose Skeletal Prototypes on Iterative Nerve Expansions (SPINE). The model for each class is an embedded 1-complex rather than a point set. Its initial edge set is a class-conditional Mapper graph, so the data decide which localized clusters are joined. Later phases fit the vertices under a classification objective, and an observation is assigned to the class whose complex is nearest. The segments therefore enter the decision rule and not only the fitting. We evaluate SPINE on seventeen benchmark datasets under stratified 10-fold cross validation, against seven other prototype reduction methods at a matched budget. SPINE attains the highest mean accuracy and the best average rank. It is significantly better than five of the seven competitors under Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm correction. A budget sweep shows that the decision rule using the entire graph segments contribute most when prototypes are scarce, while the method as a whole competes best at moderate budgets. Construction cost places SPINE with the discriminative methods, and it is faster than generalized learning vector quantization on fourteen of the seventeen datasets.

AI.tldr: SPINE introduces a novel prototype reduction method that represents each class as an embedded 1-complex (graph structure) rather than point sets, using graph segments in the decision rule and achieving superior classification accuracy compared to traditional methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional prototype reduction methods return finite point sets, which may not capture the underlying data structure effectively. There's a need for methods that can represent class distributions more flexibly using structural information rather than just point locations.
AI.method: SPINE constructs skeletal prototypes where each class is represented by an embedded 1-complex. It starts with class-conditional Mapper graphs to determine which localized clusters should be joined, then fits vertices under a classification objective. Observations are assigned to the class whose complex is nearest, making graph segments part of the decision rule.
AI.result: Evaluation on 17 benchmark datasets showed SPINE achieves highest mean accuracy and best average rank among 7 prototype reduction methods. It's significantly better than 5 of 7 competitors in statistical tests. The graph segment decision rule contributes most when prototypes are scarce, while the method competes best at moderate budgets. SPINE is faster than generalized learning vector quantization on 14 of 17 datasets.
AI.conclusion: SPINE successfully demonstrates that representing classes as 1-complexes rather than point sets improves prototype reduction performance. The integration of graph structure into the decision rule provides advantages, particularly when prototypes are limited, establishing a new direction for structural prototype methods.

title: AquiLLM: Evaluating Faithfulness in Open-Weight RAG-LLM Systems for Scientific Research
summary:
Scientific research increasingly relies on large, heterogeneous data sources, motivating interest in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems that provide natural language access to scientific knowledge and research workflows. Researchers are exploring the viability of these systems as natural language interfaces for document search and for generating analysis code and pipeline components. At the same time, concerns about data privacy and control over research infrastructure have motivated interest in open-weight models and open-source deployments hosted within research institutions.
  In astronomy, this development follows a long history of computational infrastructure development, from archival databases and SQL-based systems to LLM-assisted research tools. This paper presents a domain-expert evaluation of faithfulness for AquiLLM, an open-weight, offline RAG-LLM platform designed to support scientific research groups in the use and preservation of tacit and formal knowledge.
  We define faithfulness as the extent to which generated responses remain grounded in retrieved scientific context without unsupported claims or omissions. We report results from an astronomy case study evaluating AquiLLM across retrieval and scientific analysis tasks. AquiLLM performs most reliably on explicit retrieval-oriented questions grounded in the RAG collection, while faithfulness degrades for queries requiring synthesis or ambiguity resolution. These results highlight both the promise and limitations of open-weight RAG-LLM systems for scientific research and demonstrate the importance of domain-expert evaluation beyond standard benchmark leaderboards.

AI.tldr: AquiLLM, an open-weight offline RAG-LLM platform, was evaluated for faithfulness in astronomy research contexts, showing strong performance on explicit retrieval tasks but limitations in synthesis/ambiguity resolution, highlighting the need for domain-expert evaluation.
AI.motivation: Scientific research needs natural language access to heterogeneous data sources while addressing privacy/control concerns. There's growing interest in RAG systems for scientific knowledge access and workflow support, particularly in fields like astronomy with rich computational infrastructure history.
AI.method: Conducted a domain-expert evaluation of faithfulness for AquiLLM platform. Defined faithfulness as responses remaining grounded in retrieved scientific context without unsupported claims or omissions. Used astronomy case study evaluating across retrieval and scientific analysis tasks.
AI.result: AquiLLM performs most reliably on explicit retrieval-oriented questions grounded in the RAG collection. Faithfulness degrades for queries requiring synthesis or ambiguity resolution. Shows both promise and limitations of open-weight RAG-LLM systems for scientific research.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight RAG-LLM systems like AquiLLM show promise for scientific research but have limitations. Domain-expert evaluation is crucial beyond standard benchmarks, highlighting the need for continued development to handle synthesis and ambiguity in scientific queries.

title: Z-Loss Backward Geometry in Dense Output Heads and Sparse Routers
summary: Z-loss has been widely applied to the logits of language-model output heads and sparse mixture-of-experts routers. Z-loss constrains the softmax log-normalizers of these output heads and routers, thereby limiting large-logit excursions, reducing finite-precision roundoff exposure, and avoiding training-loss divergence. These use cases arise in modern Transformer settings where large-vocabulary softmax heads, top-$k$ routing, fused losses, and mixed-precision optimizers interact. Z-loss has typically been understood only as a scalar penalty on the log-normalizer. This paper instead analyzes Z-loss from a backward-pass perspective, focusing on the gradients produced by the Z-loss penalty. The logit-space gradient, which we call the backward source, is injected at the logit boundary of the Z-loss branch of backpropagation; consequently, the backward source's effect depends on the architecture and implementation through which the gradient is transported. We develop a backward-transport view for Z-loss that separates the source's scalar amplitude and softmax shape from the transport factors. These factors include common-shift coordinates, tied-embedding pathways, output-to-hidden gain, fused-loss source consistency, optimizer-facing updates, and top-$k$ router reduction scale. These diagnostics show that nearly identical forward Z-loss values can coexist with distinct logit-space Z-loss gradients and, after architectural and optimizer transport, distinct parameter updates. The transport diagnostics also explain why raw-logit Z-loss can reduce scalar tails without changing output-to-hidden gain and why active-route reductions alter the effective router coefficient. Across evaluations of models in the GPT-2 and Pythia families on WikiText-103 and FineWeb-Edu, architecture-aware variants reduce backward-geometry tails while maintaining comparable validation perplexity in low-coefficient regimes.

AI.tldr: Z-loss, commonly used to constrain softmax log-normalizers in language models, is analyzed from a backward-pass perspective, revealing that identical forward loss values can produce different gradients and parameter updates depending on architectural transport factors.
AI.motivation: Z-loss is widely used to prevent training divergence and reduce finite-precision issues in large-vocabulary softmax heads and sparse MoE routers, but has only been understood as a scalar penalty. The paper aims to analyze it from a backward-pass perspective to understand how gradients propagate through different architectures.
AI.method: Develops a backward-transport view for Z-loss that separates the gradient source's scalar amplitude and softmax shape from architectural transport factors including common-shift coordinates, tied-embedding pathways, output-to-hidden gain, fused-loss consistency, optimizer updates, and top-k router reduction scale.
AI.result: Shows that nearly identical forward Z-loss values can coexist with distinct logit-space gradients and parameter updates due to architectural factors. Architecture-aware variants reduce backward-geometry tails while maintaining comparable validation perplexity on GPT-2 and Pythia models evaluated on WikiText-103 and FineWeb-Edu datasets.
