Based on the correctness of intermediate steps, we construct preference data that guide the model toward more efficient and correct reasoning by leveraging DPO. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively improves reasoning compression while mitigating performance degradation after fine-tuning. Besides, SKIP shows strong generalization ability on out-of-distribution datasets. We further conducted ablation studies on the component parameters of our framework.

AI.tldr: SKIP is a self-knowledge-guided step-wise preference learning framework that improves Chain-of-Thought reasoning by reducing overthinking while maintaining accuracy through intermediate step evaluation and DPO-based optimization.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning leads to overthinking, causing computational overhead, inference latency, and degraded performance in LLMs. Existing concise reasoning frameworks significantly compromise accuracy when compressing output length.
AI.method: SKIP uses lightweight fine-tuning to adjust output style, introduces a knowledge probing mechanism to guide models to output answers at each reasoning step, constructs preference data based on intermediate step correctness, and leverages DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) to guide models toward more efficient and correct reasoning.
AI.result: The method effectively improves reasoning compression while mitigating performance degradation after fine-tuning. SKIP shows strong generalization ability on out-of-distribution datasets. Ablation studies were conducted on component parameters.
AI.conclusion: SKIP successfully addresses the overthinking problem in CoT reasoning by balancing computational efficiency and accuracy through step-wise preference learning, demonstrating practical improvements in reasoning compression and generalization.

title: FlowATC: Aircraft Trajectory Prediction via Flow Matching
summary: Building accurate decision-support tools for next-generation air traffic control requires robust trajectory prediction models. We present a flow-matching architecture trained exclusively on historical aircraft trajectories, with no route labels or chart supervision. Trained on 1.15 million Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast trajectory windows collected over the San Francisco Bay Area, the model generates aircraft trajectory distributions that closely match historical traffic, reproducing known airspace structure around San Francisco Airport such as the shape of SFO's published NIITE FOUR departure procedure. Our model is trained directly on the native, irregular ADS-B sampling interval. Trajectory prediction is cast as sequence inpainting using a block-causal Transformer that denoises future state tokens conditioned on the observed history using Conditional Flow Matching or Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models. We compare our architecture against constant-velocity, deterministic-Long Short Term Memory, and Conditional Variational Autoencoders baselines. At matched parameter count, CFM outperforms DDPM by 11-26% in minADE@20, and both generative objectives surpass the CVAE baseline by 31-41%. We further show that the error degrades gracefully with prediction horizon, and the architecture remains effective when retrained on temporally decimated feeds. Lastly, we sample $K$ independent completions, yielding spatial probabilistic occupancy estimates that can serve as input to downstream conflict-risk estimation.

AI.tldr: A flow-matching architecture for aircraft trajectory prediction trained on historical ADS-B data without route labels, outperforming baselines in accuracy and providing spatial probabilistic occupancy estimates for conflict-risk assessment.
AI.motivation: To build accurate decision-support tools for next-generation air traffic control by developing robust trajectory prediction models that can operate without route labels or chart supervision, using only historical aircraft trajectory data.
AI.method: Flow-matching architecture using a block-causal Transformer for sequence inpainting, trained on 1.15 million ADS-B trajectory windows from the San Francisco Bay Area. The model uses Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) or Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) to denoise future state tokens conditioned on observed history, working directly with the native irregular ADS-B sampling interval.
AI.result: The model generates trajectory distributions closely matching historical traffic, reproducing known airspace structures. CFM outperforms DDPM by 11-26% in minADE@20, and both generative objectives surpass CVAE baseline by 31-41%. The architecture remains effective with temporally decimated data and produces spatial probabilistic occupancy estimates from independent completions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed flow-matching architecture trained exclusively on historical ADS-B trajectories provides accurate probabilistic trajectory predictions without requiring route labels, offering a robust foundation for downstream conflict-risk estimation tools in air traffic control.

title: Sparse MLLM Anchors, Dense Adaptation: Breaking the Self-Referential Loop in Wild Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Wild test-time adaptation (WTTA) updates a source model online under small test batches, concurrent distribution shifts, and time-varying class imbalance. Most WTTA methods derive their adaptation signals, including predictive uncertainty, sample reliability, and local feature geometry, from the model being adapted. When the source model is unreliable under shift, these signals can reinforce its own errors, forming a self-referential loop. We introduce MASA (Multimodal-LLM-Anchored Semantic Adaptation), which complements model-internal evidence with structured semantic descriptions from a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM). To limit inference cost, MASA queries the MLLM only for a small set of diverse, reliability-ranked anchors. The resulting descriptions capture the object family and nuisance factors such as style, viewpoint, and occlusion. MASA encodes these descriptions, propagates them to neighboring test samples, and stores the resulting visual-semantic information in an online prototype memory. Descriptor-aware retrieval from this memory provides an auxiliary target for lightweight adaptation of normalization-affine parameters. We evaluate MASA on the WTTA ImageNet-C benchmark under limited-batch, mixed-domain, and imbalanced-label-shift settings with ResNet and ViT backbones.

AI.tldr: MASA is a novel WTTA method that uses a frozen multimodal LLM to provide semantic descriptions as external evidence, preventing self-referential error loops in test-time adaptation under distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Existing WTTA methods rely on model-internal signals (predictive uncertainty, sample reliability, local feature geometry) which can create self-referential error loops when the source model is unreliable under distribution shift - the model reinforces its own errors.
AI.method: MASA queries a frozen multimodal LLM for structured semantic descriptions of diverse, reliability-ranked anchor samples. It encodes these descriptions, propagates them to neighboring test samples, stores visual-semantic info in online prototype memory, and uses descriptor-aware retrieval for lightweight adaptation of normalization-affine parameters.
AI.result: MASA is evaluated on WTTA ImageNet-C benchmark under limited-batch, mixed-domain, and imbalanced-label-shift settings with ResNet and ViT backbones, showing improved adaptation by preventing self-referential error loops.
AI.conclusion: By complementing model-internal evidence with external semantic descriptions from a frozen MLLM, MASA breaks the self-referential error loop in WTTA, enabling more robust adaptation under challenging test-time conditions with distribution shifts and class imbalance.

title: What Does Layer-Importance Reveal About Transformers and State-Space Models?
summary: Transformers and state-space models (SSMs) are the two dominant families of sequence models, and a central open question is how far the analytical knowledge built for transformers transfers to SSMs. We address this through the lens of layer importance which underpins compression, selective fine-tuning, and interpretability across both families. We decompose layer importance into two distinct notions. \emph{Necessity} captures how much the pretrained model depends on a layer's existing contribution, measured by the loss increase from bypassing it. \emph{Plasticity} captures where the model absorbs new information during fine-tuning, measured by the magnitude of task-specific weight updates. Our analysis reveals that the two families behave fundamentally differently: in every evaluated residual transformer up to $14$B parameters, Necessity and Plasticity anti-align across depth, whereas in the evaluated Mamba-style SSMs they point to overlapping regions. The sign of this alignment also predicts downstream adaptation behavior. In the evaluated transformers, concentrating updates in the most plastic layers increases catastrophic forgetting, while this tier-dependent effect disappears in the evaluated Mamba-style SSMs.

AI.tldr: Transformers and SSMs differ fundamentally in layer importance alignment: transformers show Necessity and Plasticity anti-align across depth while Mamba-style SSMs show overlapping alignment, affecting downstream adaptation differently.
AI.motivation: To understand how analytical knowledge built for transformers transfers to state-space models (SSMs) by examining layer importance, which is crucial for compression, selective fine-tuning, and interpretability in both model families.
AI.method: Decompose layer importance into two notions: Necessity (measures loss increase from bypassing a layer to capture pretrained model dependence) and Plasticity (measures magnitude of task-specific weight updates during fine-tuning to capture where new information is absorbed). Analyze these across various residual transformers (up to 14B parameters) and Mamba-style SSMs.
AI.result: Transformers show Necessity and Plasticity anti-align across depth - they point to different layers. In Mamba-style SSMs, they point to overlapping regions. This alignment sign predicts downstream adaptation: in transformers, concentrating updates in most plastic layers increases catastrophic forgetting, while this effect disappears in Mamba-style SSMs.
AI.conclusion: Transformers and SSMs behave fundamentally differently in layer importance alignment, suggesting analytical knowledge from transformers doesn't directly transfer to SSMs. The alignment between Necessity and Plasticity predicts adaptation behavior and has practical implications for selective fine-tuning strategies.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Hierarchical Intention Anticipation in Human Behavior
summary: Assistive autonomous systems must anticipate human goals before an observed behavior is complete. This article formulates anticipation as goal inference from a partially observed multimodal episode together with structured prediction of the remaining behavior, rather than exact motor forecasting. A compact Hierarchical Planning Decoder (HPD) is attached to a frozen neuro-symbolic recognition encoder and predicts, at four ontological levels, the next actions, the remaining activities and low-level intentions, and the episode high-level intention(HLI). The decoder is trained with soft neuro-symbolic regularization combining transition-coherence and hierarchical continuity losses, and is decoded with hard reachability masks that enforce ontological validity at inference. On a compositional four-level benchmark of 15,002 multimodal episodes built over NTU RGB+D 120 features, three headline properties are observed together. The advantage over the strongest sequential baseline grows with the anticipation horizon, from +1.7 points at step 1 to +7.3 points at step 3 (top-5). Under compositional generalization, where one parent association per multi-parent low level intention is held out, this advantage widens to +4.9 points at step 1. At the episode level, 96.8% of anticipated trajectories satisfy the joint logic constraints, above the 88.1% strongest-baseline value and the 73.9% ground-truth floor; soft logic terms alone account for a 59.8 to 71.1% relative reduction of HLI-reachability violations, and the hard masks then eliminate them entirely. Neural generation supplies predictive ranking, symbolic constraints supply onto logical validity, and their combination yields coherent hierarchical anticipation while exposing remaining challenges in compositional goal generalization and unordered set prediction.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical planning decoder (HPD) for multimodal behavior anticipation using neuro-symbolic regularization and hard reachability masks to predict future actions and intentions at four ontological levels.
AI.motivation: Assistive autonomous systems need to anticipate human goals before behaviors are complete, requiring early goal inference rather than exact motor forecasting to enable timely assistance.
AI.method: Attaches compact HPD to frozen neuro-symbolic recognition encoder; uses soft neuro-symbolic regularization (transition-coherence + hierarchical continuity losses) and hard reachability masks for ontological validity; predicts at four levels: next actions, remaining activities, low-level intentions, and high-level intention.
AI.result: Advantage over strongest baseline grows with anticipation horizon (+1.7 to +7.3 points); handles compositional generalization (+4.9 points improvement); 96.8% of anticipated trajectories satisfy joint logic constraints; soft logic reduces HLI-reachability violations 59.8-71.1%; hard masks eliminate remaining violations.
AI.conclusion: Combining neural generation (predictive ranking) with symbolic constraints (ontological validity) yields coherent hierarchical anticipation while revealing challenges in compositional goal generalization and unordered set prediction.

title: On the Importance of Gating: Memorization vs. In-Context Learning in State Space Models
summary: State Space Models (SSMs) have emerged as a compelling alternative to Transformers, enabling sequence modeling with constant memory and linear compute. Although SSMs exhibit reasonable performance and favorable computational characteristics, they continue to lag behind Transformers on tasks that require in-context learning and precise retrieval, slowing their adoption for large-scale language modeling. In this work, we demonstrate that both the success and failure of SSMs in these domains can be explained by studying the role of the gating mechanism, a prevalent component in modern recurrent networks. Specifically, we show through theory and experiments that this gating mechanism causes SSMs to first learn an in-weights "memorization" solution, while delaying, or even preventing, convergence to a correct in-context learning solution. Importantly, this happens even in cases where there are no fundamental limitations due to the architecture or its memory capacity. On the other hand, we find that gating is often beneficial for improving generalization to long sequence lengths. Our results illuminate the crucial role of the gating mechanism in shaping both the training dynamics and generalization of SSMs, and provide a basis for understanding and improving linear-time models.

AI.tldr: Gating mechanisms in State Space Models cause them to learn weight-based memorization first, delaying or preventing proper in-context learning solutions, while helping generalization to long sequences.
AI.motivation: SSMs are promising alternatives to Transformers but underperform on tasks requiring in-context learning and precise retrieval. The authors aim to understand why SSMs succeed or fail in these domains by studying the role of gating mechanisms.
AI.method: The study uses both theoretical analysis and experimental investigation to examine how gating mechanisms in modern recurrent networks affect SSM behavior. They analyze training dynamics and generalization properties.
AI.result: Gating causes SSMs to initially learn an in-weights "memorization" solution, delaying or preventing convergence to correct in-context learning solutions. However, gating is beneficial for improving generalization to long sequence lengths.
AI.conclusion: The gating mechanism plays a crucial role in shaping both training dynamics and generalization of SSMs, providing insights for understanding and improving linear-time models.

title: Sample-Conditioned Representation Selection for Audio Few-Shot Learning
summary: Few-shot audio classifiers may rely on foreground-background co-occurrences and fail when those correlations shift. On SpurAudio, the resulting representation shift is concentrated and class dependent: for ResNet12, the top 10 percent of channels explain 82.80 percent of the null-corrected shift contribution. We propose SAMPLESELECT, which predicts a fixed-budget feature mask independently for each input while keeping the encoder and source classifier frozen. Training uses differentiable Gumbel Top-k selection with foreground classification and cross-background contrastive losses; inference uses deterministic Top-k masks and support-only linear adaptation. Across ResNet12 and Conv64 in 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot evaluation, SAMPLESELECT gives the best OOD accuracy among the compared methods and improves the matched full-representation control by 4.90-8.38 percentage points. Ablations and representation analyses further support the learned selection mechanism. Code is available at https://github.com/Cross-Innovation-Lab/SAMPLESELECT/

AI.tldr: SAMPLESELECT is a few-shot audio classification method that learns to selectively mask spurious background features to improve out-of-distribution generalization by focusing on robust foreground features.
AI.motivation: Few-shot audio classifiers often fail due to spurious correlations between foreground and background features that shift in out-of-distribution settings. The representation shift is concentrated in specific channels (e.g., top 10% explain 82.80% of shift), indicating class-dependent spur correlations.
AI.method: SAMPLESELECT learns to predict fixed-budget feature masks for each input while keeping encoder and source classifier frozen. Training uses differentiable Gumbel Top-k selection with foreground classification and cross-background contrastive losses. Inference uses deterministic Top-k masks with support-only linear adaptation.
AI.result: SAMPLESELECT achieves best OOD accuracy among compared methods across ResNet12 and Conv64 in 5-way 1-shot and 5-shot evaluation, improving matched full-representation control by 4.90-8.38 percentage points. Ablations and representation analyses support the learned selection mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Selective feature masking effectively mitigates spurious background correlations in few-shot audio classification, enabling better out-of-distribution generalization by focusing on robust foreground features.

title: AsyncCouple-Flow: Asynchronous Cross-Modal Coupling and Flow Matching for Spatio-Temporal Forecasting
comment: Accepted at the International Conference on Neural Information Processing (ICONIP 2026)
summary: Multi-modal spatio-temporal forecasting (MM-STF) supports weather nowcasting, traffic prediction, and earth-system modeling by combining heterogeneous sources such as physical fields, satellite imagery, and in-situ sensors. Three obstacles persist: (i) modalities have different spatio-temporal sampling rates, forcing lossy interpolation onto a unified grid; (ii) modalities are frequently missing at deployment due to sensor outages or revisit gaps, while most methods train with full availability; and (iii) autoregressive decoders accumulate errors over long horizons, amplified by multi-modal conditioning. We propose AsyncCouple-Flow to address these issues jointly. A Modality-Aware Token Sparsification (MATS) module performs scale-aware tokenization and uses a shared importance scorer to select top-k tokens per timestep, producing equal-length sequences. An Asynchronous Cross-Modal Coupling Graph (ACCG) replaces fixed cross-attention with a learnable graph whose edges encode time offsets, semantic similarity, and modality-specific physical priors, enabling fusion under arbitrary asynchrony and missingness. A Flow-Matching Forecasting Head models multi-step prediction as a conditional ODE, trained with stochastic modality dropout and integrated jointly to avoid autoregressive drift. Experiments on ERA5+GOES+ISD weather forecasting and PEMS-BAY traffic prediction with multi-source side information show that AsyncCouple-Flow outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and remains robust with up to two missing modalities. The code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: AsyncCouple-Flow is a novel multi-modal spatio-temporal forecasting method that addresses three key challenges: handling different sampling rates, missing modalities at deployment, and avoiding autoregressive error accumulation, outperforming SOTA methods while remaining robust to missing modalities.
AI.motivation: Multi-modal spatio-temporal forecasting faces three persistent obstacles: 1) modalities have different spatio-temporal sampling rates requiring lossy interpolation, 2) modalities are frequently missing at deployment due to sensor outages while most methods assume full availability, and 3) autoregressive decoders accumulate errors over long horizons, amplified by multi-modal conditioning.
AI.method: The proposed AsyncCouple-Flow consists of three main components: 1) Modality-Aware Token Sparsification (MATS) module that performs scale-aware tokenization and selects top-k tokens per timestep using a shared importance scorer, 2) Asynchronous Cross-Modal Coupling Graph (ACCG) that replaces fixed cross-attention with a learnable graph encoding time offsets, semantic similarity, and modality-specific physical priors, and 3) Flow-Matching Forecasting Head that models multi-step prediction as a conditional ODE, trained with stochastic modality dropout to avoid autoregressive drift.
AI.result: Experiments on ERA5+GOES+ISD weather forecasting and PEMS-BAY traffic prediction with multi-source side information show that AsyncCouple-Flow outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and remains robust with up to two missing modalities.
AI.conclusion: AsyncCouple-Flow effectively addresses the key challenges in multi-modal spatio-temporal forecasting by jointly handling asynchronous modalities, missing data, and error accumulation, providing a robust solution for real-world applications where sensor outages and sampling rate differences are common.

title: Interactive Memory Learning for Long-Term Conversations
summary: Recent advancements in large language models have significantly enhanced the capabilities of agents in modeling long-term conversations. Despite these successes, existing approaches typically adopt a static heuristic paradigm, where information is passively archived without adaptive memory valuation. Consequently, these methods fail to self-evolve or align their memory management with evolving user needs. To address this, we propose ICML (InteraCtive Memory Learning), a multi-agent framework that transforms the memory mechanism from a passive archive into a learnable, interactive memory policy. Specifically, we first employ a session synthesis pipeline to generate expert data, facilitating rapid test-time adaptation in unseen scenarios. Building on this, ICML utilizes an online reinforcement learning mechanism where a Planner agent selectively encodes high-value information and a Trigger agent dynamically retrieves it to optimize response quality, whereby the two agents co-evolve through continuous interaction feedback. Crucially, both agents are synchronized through a delayed reward mechanism that propagates future feedback back to earlier storage decisions, ensuring memory policies are precisely aligned with user expectations. Experimental results demonstrate that ICML significantly outperforms strong baselines, exhibiting the unique capability to continuously improve response quality as interactions accumulate.

AI.tldr: ICML is a multi-agent framework that transforms static memory management into learnable, interactive memory policies using reinforcement learning, enabling agents to continuously improve conversation quality through adaptive memory valuation and retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing large language model agents use static heuristic paradigms for memory management, passively archiving information without adaptive valuation. They fail to self-evolve or align with changing user needs, creating inefficient memory systems that don't improve with interaction.
AI.method: ICML uses a multi-agent framework with: 1) Session synthesis pipeline to generate expert data for rapid test-time adaptation; 2) Online reinforcement learning with Planner agent (selectively encodes high-value information) and Trigger agent (dynamically retrieves information); 3) Delayed reward mechanism synchronizing both agents by propagating future feedback to earlier storage decisions.
AI.result: ICML significantly outperforms strong baselines and exhibits unique capability to continuously improve response quality as interactions accumulate, demonstrating effective adaptive memory management aligned with user expectations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed ICML framework successfully transforms memory mechanisms from passive archives into learnable, interactive policies, enabling agents to co-evolve through continuous interaction and achieve superior conversation quality through adaptive memory valuation and retrieval.

title: Recovering Physical Parameters from Fragmented Observations via Exact Distributed Spline Merging
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 1 table. Under review at ICLR 2027
summary: Scientific measurements are frequently distributed across locations, time periods, and institutions. Combining such fragments into a continuous, differentiable field enables recovering governing physical parameters from its derivatives. This paper makes two contributions toward that goal. First, the established additive structure of fixed-basis ridge-regression statistics is applied to tensor-product spline fields: each data holder computes a local Gram matrix and moment vector, and the merged solution is mathematically identical to centralized fitting, with no raw data shared and no iterative synchronization. This property is specific to the fixed-feature squared-error setting; the present derivation does not establish an analogous guarantee for general jointly trained multilayer networks. Second, a complete pipeline connects distributed observations to physical parameter inference through field reconstruction, derivative extraction, and linear regression. The diffusion coefficient is recovered to 0.11% error and wave speed to 0.12% error; in both cases, distributed merging introduces zero degradation relative to centralized fitting. Application to 41 years of NOAA sea-surface temperature data confirms the result on real spatiotemporal observations.

AI.tldr: Distributed data can be combined into continuous fields using tensor-product splines with privacy-preserving local computations; the merged solution matches centralized fitting exactly, enabling accurate physical parameter recovery from derivatives.
AI.motivation: Scientific measurements are often distributed across locations, times, and institutions, making it difficult to combine them into continuous differentiable fields needed to recover governing physical parameters from derivatives.
AI.method: Apply additive structure of fixed-basis ridge regression to tensor-product spline fields: each data holder computes local Gram matrix and moment vector without sharing raw data; complete pipeline includes field reconstruction, derivative extraction, and linear regression for parameter inference.
AI.result: Diffusion coefficient recovered to 0.11% error, wave speed to 0.12% error; distributed merging introduces zero degradation relative to centralized fitting; validated on 41 years of NOAA sea-surface temperature data.
AI.conclusion: Tensor-product spline fields enable privacy-preserving distributed data analysis with mathematically identical results to centralized fitting, facilitating accurate physical parameter recovery from distributed observations through derivative-based inference.

title: Scaling-Score Conformal Prediction for Multi-Target Regression
summary: Multi-target regression requires a model to simultaneously predict several related outputs. Conformal prediction provides distribution-free, finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees, but extending these to joint multi-dimensional regions in a model-agnostic, sample-efficient manner remains challenging: max-aggregation ignores scale differences, copula-based methods are only asymptotically valid, rectangular methods typically split the calibration set, and quantile or density-based methods require training a specialised model beyond a plain point predictor. We propose the scaling-score conformal method, which is model-agnostic (requires only component-wise absolute residuals), uses a single calibration set, and yields four nested output types: an outer rectangle (SCO) with valid joint coverage, the exact set R $α$ , a staircase (SC 2 ) over approximation of R $α$ , and an inner rectangle (SCI). A single hyperparameter $γ$ $\in$ (0, 1) controls the base-rectangle quantile level independently of $α$. We prove downward-closedness and a rectangular sandwich bound and derive a closed-form outer rectangle. Experiments on 29 realworld datasets confirm valid joint coverage; SC 2 with $γ$ = 1-$α$ consistently achieves competitive volume relative to baselines, with the advantage growing with output dimension d.

AI.tldr: Scaling-score conformal method for multi-target regression provides joint coverage guarantees using component-wise residuals, producing nested output regions with valid joint coverage.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for extending conformal prediction to multi-dimensional joint coverage have limitations: max-aggregation ignores scale differences, copula methods are only asymptotically valid, rectangular methods split calibration data, and specialized models are required for quantile/density methods.
AI.method: Proposes scaling-score conformal method using only component-wise absolute residuals from a single calibration set. It yields four nested output types: outer rectangle (SCO) with valid joint coverage, exact set Rα, staircase approximation (SC2), and inner rectangle (SCI). Uses hyperparameter γ to control base-rectangle quantile level independently of α.
AI.result: The method achieves valid joint coverage on 29 real-world datasets. SC2 with γ = 1-α consistently achieves competitive prediction set volume relative to baselines, with advantage growing with output dimension d. Theoretical properties include downward-closedness and rectangular sandwich bound.
AI.conclusion: Scaling-score conformal method provides a practical, model-agnostic solution for joint multi-target conformal prediction with finite-sample guarantees, single calibration set usage, and competitive performance especially in higher dimensions.

title: A Weighted Kernel Method for Approximation that Adapts to Learned Multivariable Structure
summary: Approximating the input-output behavior of a multivariable black-box function from limited data is challenging when blind to the importance of its inputs and their interactions. We introduce total sensitivity kernels (TSKs), a method based on families of weighted ANOVA kernels that learn and adapt to this multivariable structure. TSKs parameterize the weights on each multivariable component of the target function by factors for each input. We propose learning these factors directly from function evaluations by selecting the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) in which the target function has minimum norm. Under suitable conditions, we show that this norm-minimization problem admits a unique solution, and we establish consistency of a finite-data formulation based on minimum-norm interpolation. The learned TSK factors characterize the participation of individual inputs across interactions and main effects, providing a kernel-dependent notion of input sensitivity related to total Sobol indices. Numerical experiments demonstrate that adapting the kernel to learned multivariable structure can substantially improve approximation accuracy over a standard product kernel.

AI.tldr: TSKs adapt kernel weights to multivariable structure by learning input importance from limited data, improving approximation accuracy over standard kernels.
AI.motivation: Approximating black-box multivariable functions from limited data is challenging when the importance of inputs and their interactions is unknown.
AI.method: Introduce Total Sensitivity Kernels (TSKs) using families of weighted ANOVA kernels that learn input-specific factors by selecting the RKHS where the target function has minimum norm.
AI.result: TSKs provide a unique solution under suitable conditions, show consistency in finite-data formulations, characterize input participation across interactions, and improve accuracy over standard kernels.
AI.conclusion: Adapting kernels to learned multivariable structure significantly enhances approximation performance and provides interpretable input sensitivity measures related to Sobol indices.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning-Based Genetic Biomarkers Dataset for Multiple-Stage Hepatocellular Carcinoma Prediction
comment: 6 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables, published at the 18th International Conference Series on Developments in eSystems Engineering
summary: Liver cancer is a complex disease responsible for a high number of deaths across the globe each year, making automated solutions for liver cancer classification urgent. The most common form of liver cancer is hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), accounting for over 90% of liver cancer cases. There is a distinct lack of publicly available HCC datasets utilizing genomic data, which is necessary for training artificial intelligence (AI) models for automated HCC classification. This study proposes constructing a multi-stage HCC dataset using XGBoost and Semi-Supervised learning on three separate datasets of genomic biomarkers, utilizing their existing labels in the Semi-Supervised learning process to label the proposed dataset. The proposed dataset consists of 770 patient samples in total, categorized into five classes that represent normal tissue alongside different stages of HCC. Each sample in the dataset consists of 11,150 different gene expression levels. The XGBoost model demonstrated a final classification accuracy of 96.5% during the Semi-Supervised learning process.

AI.tldr: This paper creates a new multi-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) dataset using genomic data and semi-supervised learning with XGBoost to address the lack of public HCC datasets for AI model training.
AI.motivation: There's a critical need for automated liver cancer classification solutions due to high mortality rates, but a lack of publicly available HCC datasets with genomic data needed for training AI models.
AI.method: The authors constructed a multi-stage HCC dataset using XGBoost and semi-supervised learning on three existing genomic biomarker datasets, leveraging their existing labels in the semi-supervised process to label the proposed dataset.
AI.result: The resulting dataset contains 770 patient samples categorized into five classes (normal tissue plus different HCC stages), with each sample having 11,150 gene expression levels. The XGBoost model achieved 96.5% classification accuracy during semi-supervised learning.
AI.conclusion: The study successfully created a valuable public HCC dataset with genomic data and demonstrated high classification accuracy using XGBoost and semi-supervised learning, addressing the critical gap in resources for automated liver cancer classification research.

title: Divergence Timing and Cumulative Disagreement under KV-Cache Eviction
summary: KV-cache eviction perturbs the conditional token distributions governing autoregressive generation. We investigate how first-divergence timing and subsequent token mismatch determine cumulative disagreement. We derive an exact decomposition under a specified stepwise maximal coupling: the expected mismatch fraction equals a first-mismatch contribution plus post-divergence exposure multiplied by its mismatch rate. An explicit construction over unrestricted autoregressive kernel pairs realizes the sharp interval of risks compatible with a finite divergence-aligned observation window. Residual-branch conditional Monte Carlo provides unbiased joint estimates of occurrence, occupation, and window/tail contributions, with per-replicate variance dominance for total token loss. Complete trajectories from Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that SnapKV at 50% retention enters divergence later and less often than SnapKV-512 or recent-token retention with the same 50% prompt-cache budget, while post-divergence total variation (TV) remains high. In an exploratory analysis of 288 documents, post-divergence exposure accounts for 85-90% of four aggregate mismatch gaps. On 288 independent documents at 90% retention, prespecified comparisons show higher branch-aligned TV in the late than in the early window in both models.

AI.tldr: KV-cache eviction causes token distribution divergence in autoregressive generation; the paper analyzes timing and cumulative mismatch, finding that post-divergence exposure accounts for most disagreement.
AI.motivation: KV-cache eviction during autoregressive generation perturbs conditional token distributions, leading to disagreements between evicted and full-cache trajectories. Understanding the timing and extent of these divergences is crucial for efficient cache management in large language models.
AI.method: The paper develops a theoretical decomposition of cumulative disagreement, uses stepwise maximal coupling to analyze first-divergence timing, and employs residual-branch conditional Monte Carlo for unbiased estimation. Experiments use Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 288 documents to evaluate SnapKV and recent-token retention strategies.
AI.result: SnapKV at 50% retention diverges later and less often than SnapKV-512 or recent-token retention with the same budget. Post-divergence total variation remains high, and post-divergence exposure accounts for 85-90% of aggregate mismatch gaps. At 90% retention, late window shows higher branch-aligned TV than early window in both models.
AI.conclusion: KV-cache eviction significantly affects generation quality through timing and magnitude of divergences, with post-divergence period being the dominant source of cumulative mismatch. Efficient cache eviction strategies need to minimize both divergence occurrence and post-divergence exposure to maintain generation fidelity.

title: Symbolic Separation: Grounding Deep Agents in Knowledge Graphs for Trustworthy Operational Data Analytics
summary: Generative AI promises natural language access to the massive numerical telemetry of data centers and Industry 4.0 installations, yet text-to-query and tool-using agents stay unreliable: even frontier models answer little more than half of real-world database questions, and far fewer of the multi-step, operational ones, because the LLM must compose how heterogeneous sources relate and hallucinates the relations, not just the fields. We propose symbolic separation: a deep agent reasons freely but may act on data only through an ontology-constrained Virtual Knowledge Graph with deterministic pre-execution validation. Unlike a tool API's interface contract, this domain-semantic contract turns a complex question into one validated graph traversal instead of LLM-inferred joins. Instantiated as the Neurosymbolic Deep Analyst and evaluated on 49.9 TB of superconputer telemetry against a rigid workflow and a non-symbolic ablation, it raises end-to-end task success from 43% to 86%, prevents silent data-integrity errors that no syntactic check catches, and cuts token cost by 2.4x, letting a smaller on-premise model outperform a larger one.

AI.tldr: A neurosymbolic system combining LLM reasoning with ontology-constrained virtual knowledge graphs improves database query accuracy from 43% to 86% while preventing data integrity errors and reducing costs.
AI.motivation: Current generative AI systems for database querying are unreliable, with frontier models answering little more than half of real-world database questions. The problem is worse for multi-step operational queries where LLMs must understand heterogeneous data relationships and often hallucinate incorrect relations.
AI.method: Proposes symbolic separation: a deep agent reasons freely but can only act on data through an ontology-constrained Virtual Knowledge Graph with deterministic pre-execution validation. Unlike traditional tool APIs, this domain-semantic contract turns complex questions into validated graph traversals instead of LLM-inferred joins.
AI.result: Instantiated as Neurosymbolic Deep Analyst and evaluated on 49.9 TB of supercomputer telemetry, the system raises end-to-end task success from 43% to 86%, prevents silent data-integrity errors that syntactic checks miss, cuts token cost by 2.4x, and enables smaller on-premise models to outperform larger ones.
AI.conclusion: The neurosymbolic approach combining symbolic validation with LLM reasoning significantly improves reliability, accuracy, and efficiency of natural language database querying, addressing fundamental limitations of current text-to-query systems.

title: Stable by Construction: Variational Latent Markov Operators for Long-Horizon PDE Prediction
summary: Neural PDE solvers provide efficient surrogates for time-dependent physical systems, but autoregressive prediction over long horizons remains challenging because local errors can induce distribution shift and accumulate under recursive deployment. We develop a variational approach to this problem by introducing latent Markov dynamics in which physical states are represented by latent distributions and evolved through probabilistic transitions. The framework is formulated directly on function spaces and specialized to functional Gaussian models, where structured latent perturbations induce a spectral geometry and variational transition alignment regularizes the learned dynamics. We further analyze how these mechanisms affect autoregressive error propagation, providing a theoretical connection between variational training and long-horizon prediction. We instantiate the framework as the Variational Autoencoding Markov Operator (VAMO), which combines spatially resolved latent fields, structured Gaussian perturbations, and a neural-operator transition. Empirically, we demonstrate the effectiveness of VAMO on several fluid-dynamics benchmarks with prediction horizons extending substantially beyond those represented during training, where it consistently reduces error accumulation and improves rollout stability over several deterministic and noise-injection baselines. Overall, these results highlight variational modeling as a complementary approach to robust long-horizon neural PDE dynamics.

AI.tldr: VAMO introduces variational Markov dynamics with latent Gaussian fields to reduce error accumulation in neural PDE solvers for long-horizon predictions.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive neural PDE solvers struggle with long-horizon predictions due to error accumulation from distribution shift during recursive deployment.
AI.method: Develops variational Markov framework with latent distributions for physical states, using functional Gaussian models with structured perturbations and variational transition alignment. Instantiates as VAMO with spatially resolved latent fields and neural-operator transitions.
AI.result: VAMO demonstrates reduced error accumulation and improved rollout stability on fluid-dynamics benchmarks, achieving predictions substantially beyond training horizons and outperforming deterministic and noise-injection baselines.
AI.conclusion: Variational modeling provides a complementary approach to robust long-horizon neural PDE dynamics by addressing error propagation through latent Markov dynamics.

title: Shared-Prefix KV Reuse Across Standard LoRA Adapters: Quality and Serving Tradeoffs
summary: A common small-model deployment runs one shared backbone with several LoRA specialists that answer over the same context. Serving them naively re-prefills that shared context once per specialist. We study a narrow, practical question: for already-trained standard LoRA adapters -- not adapters retrained for cache compatibility -- how much task quality is preserved if the backbone's prefill KV cache is computed once and reused across specialists, and what does that buy in serving cost? On a Qwen3-1.7B backbone with two adapters (extractive QA on HotpotQA, arithmetic reasoning on GSM8K), we sweep the boundary at which the specialist takes over from the reused base cache and measure paired quality differences and serving cost. Full-prefix reuse had the lowest prefill cost and a small quality difference on held-out GSM8K (Delta = -4.6 EM at a 160-token budget; -3.0 at 320 tokens; -0.8 under a second training seed -- all favoring native, only the first excluding zero, and the magnitude not consistent). Partial recomputation provided no demonstrated advantage. Neither quality equivalence nor a general boundary-selection rule is established. We also report a closed-form ridge KV translator that did not beat direct reuse, and specialist-dependence contrasts whose intervals all include zero. The measured serving benefit is warm-cache time-to-first-token, which grows with context (~16x at 8K); two-branch peak memory was only 12% lower and, on inspection, the prefix was never physically shared across branches -- this implementation reuses KV values but copies their storage, so shared-cache memory savings are not achieved.

AI.tldr: Studying KV cache reuse for LoRA specialists with same backbone shows partial quality degradation but significant time savings in warm-cache scenarios, though memory savings not achieved due to implementation copying.
AI.motivation: Current LoRA specialist serving requires recomputing shared backbone context for each specialist, which is inefficient. The paper investigates whether pre-trained LoRA adapters (not retrained for cache compatibility) can reuse the backbone's prefill KV cache across specialists without significant quality loss, to reduce serving costs.
AI.method: Experiments on Qwen3-1.7B backbone with two adapters (HotpotQA extractive QA, GSM8K arithmetic reasoning). Swept the boundary where specialist takes over from reused base cache. Measured quality differences and serving costs. Also tested a closed-form ridge KV translator and examined implementation details of cache sharing.
AI.result: Full-prefix reuse showed lowest prefill cost with small quality degradation on GSM8K (Delta = -4.6 EM at 160-token budget; -3.0 at 320 tokens; -0.8 under different training seed). Partial recomputation provided no advantage. No general boundary-selection rule established. Ridge KV translator didn't beat direct reuse. Serving benefit was warm-cache time-to-first-token growth with context (~16x at 8K), but memory savings weren't achieved due to KV value copying rather than physical sharing.
AI.conclusion: KV cache reuse for pre-trained LoRA specialists offers practical serving time benefits in warm-cache scenarios despite some quality degradation, but current implementations don't achieve memory savings due to storage copying. The approach shows promise but requires better implementation and clearer quality-preserving strategies.

title: GrowMTP: Can RL Grow Its Own Draft Head?
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training drives the frontier capabilities of large language models, with its wall-clock dominated by autoregressive rollout generation. Speculative decoding is an established remedy for this bottleneck, but existing draft heads must be pretrained or warmed up before RL, introducing substantial training cost outside the RL run to be accelerated. We observe that RL training itself provides both conditions required for online draft-head training: its rollout distribution is far narrower than that of pretraining, and its verification step continuously produces supervision signals aligned with this distribution. Building on these observations, we propose GrowMTP, which uses this supervision to train a draft head from scratch entirely within the RL loop, with all head updates detached from the policy backbone. On Qwen3-4B (no draft head), MiMo-7B-SFT (weak head), and Qwen3.5-4B-Base (strong head), GrowMTP achieves rollout speedups of 2.13x, 1.93x, and 1.36x, and end-to-end speedups of 1.60x, 1.41x, and 1.20x, respectively. GrowMTP therefore serves existing RL training frameworks as a modular component, particularly offering a from-scratch acceleration path for models without pretrained draft heads.

AI.tldr: GrowMTP is a novel approach that trains speculative decoding draft heads entirely within RL training loops, eliminating the need for pretraining or warmup while achieving significant speedups in autoregressive rollout generation.
AI.motivation: Current RL post-training for large language models suffers from slow autoregressive rollout generation. While speculative decoding helps, existing methods require costly pretraining or warmup of draft heads outside the RL training process, adding substantial overhead to the very system being accelerated.
AI.method: GrowMPP trains draft heads from scratch within the RL training loop by leveraging two key observations: 1) RL rollout distributions are much narrower than pretraining distributions, and 2) RL verification steps continuously produce aligned supervision signals. The method trains draft heads with all updates detached from the policy backbone, making it a modular component.
AI.result: The method achieves rollout speedups of 2.13x, 1.93x, and 1.36x on Qwen3-4B, MiMo-7B-SFT, and Qwen3.5-4B-Base respectively, with end-to-end speedups of 1.60x, 1.41x, and 1.20x. It works with models regardless of their existing draft head capabilities.
AI.conclusion: GrowMTP successfully demonstrates that draft heads can be trained entirely within RL loops without external pretraining, offering a modular, from-scratch acceleration solution that integrates seamlessly with existing RL training frameworks, particularly valuable for models lacking pretrained draft heads.

title: FirmCORe: A Benchmark for Structured Reasoning about Inter-Firm Collaboration Opportunities
summary: Comprehensive structured data on inter-firm relationships is often scarce or inaccessible because many relationships are privately negotiated, selectively disclosed, and fragmented across proprietary databases. This scarcity hinders the discovery of collaboration opportunities, particularly for startups and small and medium-sized enterprises. Firm profiles are readily available, but collaboration potential cannot be inferred from business similarity alone, since similar firms may be competitors, whereas dissimilar firms may offer complementary products, technologies, channels, capabilities, or capital. We present FirmCORe (Inter-Firm Collaboration Opportunity Reasoning), a human-annotated benchmark for pairwise reasoning over weakly structured firm profiles, comprising 2,805 labeled firm pairs. Given two firm profiles, a model must determine whether the available evidence supports a collaboration opportunity and, for positive pairs, jointly predict its strength, primary collaboration type, and role direction. FirmCORe also provides parallel Chinese- and English-language evaluation sets containing identical instances and gold labels, enabling controlled analysis of input-language sensitivity. Experiments with representative locally deployed and hosted large language models (LLMs) show that the strongest model achieves a macro-F1 score of 74.51 for opportunity detection but only 61.57% exact match across all four output fields. Language effects vary across models, and high cross-language agreement can mask errors shared across languages. These results indicate that current LLMs are substantially more reliable at detecting broad collaboration opportunities than at identifying their specific types and role directions.

AI.tldr: FirmCORe is a new benchmark for evaluating LLMs' ability to identify collaboration opportunities between firms using weakly structured profile data, showing current models are better at detecting opportunities than specifying their details.
AI.motivation: Comprehensive data on inter-firm relationships is scarce due to private negotiations and selective disclosure, hindering discovery of collaboration opportunities especially for startups and SMEs. While firm profiles are available, collaboration potential can't be inferred from business similarity alone since similar firms may be competitors while dissimilar ones may complement each other.
AI.method: Created FirmCORe, a human-annotated benchmark with 2,805 labeled firm pairs. Given two firm profiles, models must determine if evidence supports collaboration opportunity, and for positive pairs, jointly predict strength, primary collaboration type, and role direction. Includes parallel Chinese- and English-language evaluation sets with identical instances for controlled language sensitivity analysis.
AI.result: Experiments with representative LLMs show strongest model achieves 74.51 macro-F1 for opportunity detection but only 61.57% exact match across all four output fields. Language effects vary across models, and high cross-language agreement can mask errors shared across languages.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs are substantially more reliable at detecting broad collaboration opportunities than at identifying their specific types and role directions, indicating limitations in fine-grained reasoning about inter-firm relationships from profile data.

title: Right Direction, Wrong Step: Geometric Analysis of Finite-Step Failure in Looped Transformers
summary: Looped Transformers offer a parameter-efficient route to test-time scaling by reusing shared layers for iterative latent reasoning. However, additional iterations can reduce support for a reference answer, leaving unclear whether an update's direction is locally unhelpful or its full displacement moves too far. We study this distinction by analysing reference utility, which measures this support, along the model's own update direction, varying the fraction of the proposed displacement supplied to the readout. This reveals finite-step failures in which a locally improving direction produces a harmful full update. A pathwise curvature decomposition characterises how initial progress is lost, while a local quadratic model predicts full-step gains and useful step scales. Bounds based on accumulated curvature variation characterise the approximation error of these predictions. Experiments across two model families reveal this separation on mathematical and commonsense tasks. A fixed quarter step produces positive gains in reference utility for 72.2--83.2% of selected failures across four settings. These findings identify a mismatch between update direction and step scale as a mechanism of lost progress, explaining how some harmful updates retain useful computation.

AI.tldr: Looped Transformers show harmful updates despite locally improving directions due to step scale mismatches; using quarter-step scaling recovers positive gains for 72-83% of failures.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers enable parameter-efficient test-time scaling via iterative latent reasoning, but additional iterations sometimes reduce support for correct answers, making it unclear whether update directions are locally unhelpful or step displacements are too large.
AI.method: Study reference utility along update directions with varying displacement fractions; use pathwise curvature decomposition to analyze lost progress; develop local quadratic models to predict full-step gains; establish bounds on prediction errors based on accumulated curvature variation.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical and commonsense tasks across two model families show finite-step failures where locally improving directions produce harmful full updates; fixed quarter-step scaling produces positive gains in reference utility for 72.2-83.2% of selected failures across four settings.
AI.conclusion: The mismatch between update direction and step scale is identified as a mechanism for lost progress, explaining how some harmful updates retain useful computation; step scaling can recover benefits from initially promising directions.

title: MOCC-R1: Reinforcing Reasoning-Response Consistency for Multimodal Counselor Response Generation
summary: Multimodal counselor response generation (MCRG) aims to generate an appropriate counselor response from multimodal dialogue histories. Progress is limited by two gaps: first, existing datasets rarely capture sustained, human-recorded counseling interactions conducted by qualified counselors; Second, existing methods do not explicitly optimize consistency between counseling reasoning and the generated response, potentially undermining the reliability of MCRG systems. Thus, we introduce MOCC, a multimodal counseling conversation corpus containing over 200 hours of interactions involving 154 credential-verified counselors. Based on MOCC, we propose MOCC-R1, a two-stage framework for optimizing reasoning-response consistency. Cold-start supervised fine-tuning trains the model to generate a structured trajectory consisting of client-state understanding, a response intent that links a counseling principle to a planned action, and the final response. Reinforcement learning (RL) then rewards grounded plan coherence and plan execution, encouraging the inferred state and plan to be supported by the dialogue context and the response to realize that plan. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed MOCC-R1.

AI.tldr: Proposes MOCC-R1, a two-stage framework for multimodal counselor response generation that improves reasoning-response consistency using a new counseling conversation dataset and reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Two main gaps in current MCRG: 1) lack of high-quality multimodal counseling datasets with verified counselors, and 2) failure to explicitly optimize consistency between counseling reasoning and generated responses, compromising system reliability.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: 1) Cold-start supervised fine-tuning to generate structured trajectory (client-state understanding, response intent linking counseling principle to action, final response), 2) Reinforcement learning that rewards grounded plan coherence and execution.
AI.result: Introduces MOCC dataset (200+ hours with 154 credential-verified counselors) and shows effectiveness of MOCC-R1 framework through experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed MOCC-R1 framework effectively addresses reasoning-response consistency in multimodal counselor response generation using structured reasoning trajectories and RL-based optimization.

title: Continuous-Time Machine Learning: A Unified Mathematical Perspective
summary: Continuous-time (CT) machine learning has emerged as a principled framework for modeling temporal dynamics as a continuous process, particularly when observations are sampled at arbitrary time points or span long-range horizons. However, major branches of CT machine learning have matured in separate research communities, leaving their mathematical relationships and design trade-offs insufficiently characterized. In this survey, we develop a unified, concept-driven view of major CT machine learning branches through a taxonomy that organizes families according to their underlying base mathematical formulations. We present a canonical mathematical formulation that relates these families through different architectural choices of vector-field parameterization, stochasticity, memory mechanisms, and discretization. We compare training algorithms, optimization strategies, and failure modes, highlighting the trade-offs across families. We further provide a comparative analysis of theoretical computational complexity alongside an illustrative architecture-controlled benchmark analysis on representative architectures from each family. We also review software ecosystems supporting their implementation. Finally, we identify open challenges in approximation theory, training stability, hardware-efficient implementations, benchmarking, foundation models, and scientific machine learning, and discuss an agenda for future research.

AI.tldr: A survey paper that unifies continuous-time machine learning through a taxonomy based on mathematical formulations, comparing architectural choices, training algorithms, computational complexity, and software ecosystems.
AI.motivation: Continuous-time ML has matured in separate communities, leaving mathematical relationships and design trade-offs insufficiently characterized. There's a need for a unified view to understand connections between different CT ML approaches.
AI.method: Develops a unified taxonomy organizing CT ML families by underlying mathematical formulations. Presents a canonical formulation that relates families through architectural choices (vector-field parameterization, stochasticity, memory, discretization). Compares training algorithms, optimization strategies, and provides theoretical complexity analysis with benchmark studies.
AI.result: Provides a comprehensive framework for understanding CT ML, enabling comparison of trade-offs across families. The taxonomy reveals relationships between different approaches, and benchmark analysis offers practical insights into performance characteristics.
AI.conclusion: The survey successfully unifies CT ML through mathematical foundations and identifies key open challenges in approximation theory, training stability, hardware efficiency, benchmarking, foundation models, and scientific ML, setting an agenda for future research.

title: End-to-End Latency-Minimizing and Load-Balanced Request Scheduling for Edge LLM Inference in Agentic AI Services
summary: Large language model (LLM)-powered agentic AI services increasingly demand low-latency inference, motivating the deployment of LLMs across distributed edge servers. However, heterogeneous communication and computing capabilities, together with dynamically evolving inference states, make the edge server selection for each incoming request time-varying and tightly coupled across slots. In this paper, we investigate an online request scheduling framework for edge LLM inference that jointly minimizes long-term average end-to-end latency and regulates workload distribution across heterogeneous edge servers. Two main challenges arise in this context. First, conventional latency models cannot accurately capture the fine-grained dynamics of multi-stage LLM execution. Second, the latency consequence of a scheduling decision is observed only after request completion, making immediate decision evaluation difficult. To address these challenges, we develop a cross-slot inference model that captures transmission, prefill, iteration-level decoding, and key-value (KV) cache evolution for each diverse request, and characterize server workload through a KV cache memory-time consumption metric. We propose the LYREO approach that transforms the long-term load-balancing constraint via Lyapunov optimization and employs reward redistribution with sequencebased return prediction to convert delayed outcomes into timely learning signals for earlier decisions. Simulations under various configurations demonstrate that LYREO consistently achieves lower latency and more balanced load distribution than representative learning-based and heuristic baseline schemes.

AI.tldr: LYREO: An online request scheduling framework for edge LLM inference that jointly minimizes latency and balances workload using cross-slot inference modeling and Lyapunov optimization with reward redistribution.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered AI services need low-latency inference, prompting deployment across distributed edge servers. However, heterogeneous communication/computing capabilities and dynamic inference states make server selection complex and time-varying. Existing approaches struggle with accurate latency modeling and delayed outcome evaluation.
AI.method: Developed cross-slot inference model capturing transmission, prefill, iteration-level decoding, and KV cache evolution. Characterized server workload using KV cache memory-time consumption. Proposed LYREO approach using Lyapunov optimization to handle long-term constraints and reward redistribution with sequence-based return prediction to convert delayed outcomes into timely learning signals.
AI.result: Simulations under various configurations show LYREO consistently achieves lower latency and more balanced load distribution than representative learning-based and heuristic baseline schemes.
AI.conclusion: LYREO effectively addresses the challenges of accurate latency modeling and delayed decision evaluation in edge LLM inference scheduling, providing a practical solution for optimizing performance in distributed edge environments.

title: A Systematic Evaluation of Machine Learning Methods for Fault Detection and Line Identification in Electrical Power Grids
comment: Accepted at ICASSP 2025. 5 pages, 4 figures. Published version: DOI 10.1109/ICASSP49660.2025.10890544
summary: The integration of renewable energy sources into the electrical grid introduces complex challenges in fault detection and coordination of grid recovery mechanisms. Traditional relay protection systems, which operate based on static rules and predefined thresholds, are inadequate for addressing these challenges, particularly in detecting and isolating faults such as short circuits. Consequently, the conventional methodologies applied to electrical network protection frequently fail to achieve optimal performance in fault detection, especially in terms of adherence to safety standards and the selective limitation of damage. Recent research indicates that machine learning (ML)-based approaches can effectively tackle these issues; however, variations in grid configurations and analysis windows have impeded consistent comparative assessments. In this study, we assess the efficacy of various ML models in detecting electrical faults and pinpointing defective transmission lines within a 10 ms measurement interval - a critical time-frame for real-time operational viability, for the first time. The most effective model attained an F1 score of 0.991 +/- 0.018 and demonstrated a processing time of 0.342ms +/- 0.509ms.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates machine learning models for electrical fault detection in renewable energy grids, achieving high F1 scores and fast processing times within 10ms measurement windows.
AI.motivation: Renewable energy integration creates complex fault detection challenges. Traditional relay protection systems with static rules are inadequate for detecting faults like short circuits. Conventional methods fail to achieve optimal performance in safety standards and damage limitation. While ML approaches show promise, grid configuration variations and analysis windows hinder consistent comparative assessments.
AI.method: The study assesses various machine learning models for detecting electrical faults and identifying defective transmission lines. Evaluation focuses on a 10ms measurement interval, which is critical for real-time operational viability. This is the first time such comprehensive assessment is done within this specific timeframe.
AI.result: The most effective model achieved an F1 score of 0.991 +/- 0.018 with a processing time of 0.342ms +/- 0.509ms. This demonstrates high accuracy and fast performance within the critical 10ms timeframe required for real-time grid operation.
AI.conclusion: Machine learning models can effectively address electrical fault detection challenges in renewable energy-integrated grids, particularly within the critical 10ms timeframe needed for real-time operation. The high accuracy and fast processing times show potential for practical implementation in grid protection systems.

title: Extracting ontology-compliant knowledge from scientific text describing irradiated materials using large language models
summary: The quest for new materials increasingly relies on predictive models and comprehensive simulations that span scales from atomic to macroscopic levels. However, essential data necessary for these models and simulations are often embedded in scientific literature as unstructured text, limiting reusability and posing challenges for researchers seeking to leverage existing knowledge effectively. While extracting structured data from unstructured text using large language models is gaining popularity, traditional methods typically generate key-value pairs data with straightforward schemas. In contrast, we introduce eolas, a modular pipeline that uses large language models to automatically transform scientific documents into knowledge graphs aligned with a specified ontology. We demonstrate eolas effectiveness in extracting useful information for scientists studying materials designed to endure the extreme temperatures and radiation levels found in fusion reactors. While a human expert might spend between thirty to ninety minutes extracting relevant data from an article, eolas can generate high-quality knowledge graphs in just a few minutes. These are presented in a tabular format with faceted navigation for easy human validation. Additionally, we introduce the first benchmark dataset designed to assess large language models capabilities in constructing knowledge graphs within the domain of irradiated materials. The analysis of 168 experiments using our dataset, various large language models and prompting techniques provides key insights that we summarize into practical guidelines for effectively extracting knowledge graphs aligned with an input ontology.

AI.tldr: eolas is a modular pipeline using LLMs to automatically transform scientific documents into ontology-aligned knowledge graphs, enabling rapid extraction of structured data from materials science literature with human-validatable results.
AI.motivation: Essential materials science data is embedded in unstructured scientific literature, limiting reusability and making knowledge extraction time-consuming for researchers. Traditional LLM-based extraction methods only produce simple key-value pairs, lacking complex structured representations needed for comprehensive materials modeling.
AI.method: The authors introduce eolas, a modular pipeline using large language models to automatically transform scientific documents into knowledge graphs aligned with specified ontologies. They demonstrate its effectiveness in extracting information about irradiated materials for fusion reactors. The system produces knowledge graphs in minutes (vs 30-90 minutes for human experts) and presents results in tabular format with faceted navigation for validation.
AI.result: eolas successfully generates high-quality knowledge graphs for irradiated materials research. The authors also create the first benchmark dataset for assessing LLM capabilities in constructing knowledge graphs for irradiated materials. Analysis of 168 experiments using various LLMs and prompting techniques provides practical guidelines for effective ontology-aligned knowledge graph extraction.
AI.conclusion: The eolas pipeline demonstrates that LLMs can effectively transform scientific documents into structured knowledge graphs aligned with ontologies, dramatically reducing extraction time while maintaining quality. The benchmark dataset and practical guidelines provide valuable resources for the research community in knowledge extraction from scientific literature.

title: TAME: Token Attribution and Masking for Emergent misalignment
summary: Fine-tuning an aligned language model on narrow, flawed data can induce harmful behavior far outside the training domain, known as emergent misalignment (EM). Prior work has localized EM in model weights, activations, and training documents, but it remains unclear which training tokens carry the relevant fine-tuning signal. We introduce TAME (Token Attribution and Masking for Emergent Misalignment), a three-stage framework: token attribution scores how strongly the fine-tuning update raises each response token's likelihood, using forward passes through a released LoRA adapter; signal characterization finds patterns among high-attribution tokens; and causal validation tests them by attribution-guided loss masking. On released EM organisms and a 6,849-example medical-advice split, attribution is concentrated (the top 5% of tokens hold 32% of the mass) and, in Llama, depleted for medical vocabulary but enriched for a register of unwarranted certainty, even after controlling for token rarity. Masking high-attribution tokens during fresh fine-tuning cuts EM by 23x in Llama and 36x in Qwen, with the perplexity cost concentrated on the targeted register rather than on medical content; an equal random mask leaves EM unchanged. In Llama, the attribution pattern suggests that EM-relevant signal lies more in how confidently flawed content is expressed than in its domain vocabulary; the causal masking effect itself holds across both model families.

AI.tldr: TAME framework identifies harmful training tokens in language model fine-tuning that cause emergent misalignment, showing confidence patterns rather than domain vocabulary are key.
AI.motivation: Previous work localized emergent misalignment in model weights, activations, and training documents, but it remained unclear which specific training tokens carry the harmful fine-tuning signal that causes models to generate harmful outputs far outside their training domain.
AI.method: Introduces TAME (Token Attribution and Masking for Emergent Misalignment) - a three-stage framework: 1) Token attribution scores fine-tuning updates' effect on response token likelihoods using forward passes through released LoRA adapters, 2) Signal characterization finds patterns among high-attribution tokens, 3) Causal validation tests patterns via attribution-guided loss masking during fresh fine-tuning.
AI.result: Attribution is highly concentrated (top 5% of tokens hold 32% of mass). In Llama, medical vocabulary is depleted while "unwarranted certainty" register is enriched. Masking high-attribution tokens reduces emergent misalignment by 23x in Llama and 36x in Qwen, while random masking has no effect. Perplexity cost concentrates on targeted register, not medical content.
AI.conclusion: Emergent misalignment signal lies more in how confidently flawed content is expressed (register/style) than in domain vocabulary itself. The causal masking effect works across model families, providing a practical mitigation strategy for harmful fine-tuning.

title: Intrinsic Motivation in Reinforcement Learning: A Research Agenda for Adaptive Self-Organisation
summary: Biological cells can be viewed as individual, interacting agents whose collective dynamics give rise to adaptive behaviour at multiple levels of organisation, from individual cells through tissues to whole multicellular organisms. In this perspective and tutorial article we discuss whether intrinsic rewards in artificial neural systems can support adaptation, functional specialisation and higher-level self-organisation without a shared external objective. We review empowerment, curiosity, learning progress, information gain, unsupervised skill discovery, mutual information estimation and the use of world models for intrinsic reward computation. Particular attention is given to failure modes showing when such objectives do not produce sustained exploration or increasingly complex behaviour. We argue that more capable systems may require complementary objectives, communication, memory, learning at multiple temporal scales and environmental constraints. Based on this perspective, we outline three experimental directions. These include a resource-constrained environment in which otherwise stable behavioural attractors become unsustainable, allowing us to test whether environmental constraints can mitigate characteristic failure modes of intrinsic objectives. The network of recurrent agents with per-agent intrinsic rewards, and a hierarchical world-model agent in which exploratory motor competence develops before goal-directed behaviour. These experiments are intended to test whether intrinsic learning can lead to adaptive organisation at progressively higher levels.

AI.tldr: Intrinsic rewards (empowerment, curiosity, learning progress, etc.) may enable artificial neural systems to achieve adaptive, self-organized behavior without external objectives, but they often fail to sustain exploration or produce complex behavior, requiring complementary approaches.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by biological cells' ability to achieve adaptive collective dynamics without centralized control. The authors explore whether artificial neural systems can achieve similar self-organization and functional specialization using intrinsic rewards rather than external objectives.
AI.method: The paper presents a perspective and tutorial review of intrinsic reward approaches including empowerment, curiosity, learning progress, information gain, unsupervised skill discovery, and mutual information estimation. It analyzes their failure modes and proposes complementary approaches including communication, memory, multi-timescale learning, and environmental constraints.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that pure intrinsic objectives often fail to produce sustained exploration or increasingly complex behavior. The authors propose three experimental directions: (1) resource-constrained environments to destabilize stable behavioral attractors, (2) networks of recurrent agents with per-agent intrinsic rewards, and (3) hierarchical world-model agents where motor competence develops before goal-directed behavior.
AI.conclusion: More capable self-organizing systems require a combination of approaches beyond pure intrinsic rewards, including complementary objectives, communication mechanisms, memory systems, hierarchical learning, and environmental constraints to achieve adaptive organization at progressively higher levels.

title: Noise2Noise Revisited: Training Pair Distributions Dominate Loss Choice in Self-Supervised Denoising
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Accepted to The 8th International Conference on Video, Signal and Image Processing (VSIP 2026). Code and data: https://github.com/dyshang/noise2noise-revisited
summary: Noise2Noise (N2N) trains denoisers on pairs of independently corrupted observations, eliminating clean references. We stress-test two natural conjectures about why the L1 loss outperforms L2 here. First, the hypothesis that the L1 loss confers robustness via parameter sparsity confuses the loss with Lasso regularization: an explicit Lasso penalty produces the predicted sparsity yet fails to reproduce L1's cross-noise behavior, while L1- and L2-trained weight distributions are indistinguishable. Second, the population optima of the two losses coincide exactly for symmetric signal posteriors and nearly so for concentrated ones.
