summary: Continual learning must balance the learning of new knowledge with the retention of previously learned knowledge to incrementally learn tasks from a data stream without catastrophic forgetting. While leveraging pretrained models has significantly advanced continual learning, existing methods exhibit a scalability bottleneck when trained sequentially on many tasks, suffering from performance degradation due to inter-task interference and loss of plasticity. Inspired by evidence that sparse fine-tuning achieves performance comparable to full fine-tuning, this paper presents a novel sparsity-driven continual learning framework. Our continual learning method, termed CLARE, operates in two stages: it first identifies a sparse, task-critical parameter mask via a sparsity-inducing objective, then performs mask-constrained fine-tuning by only optimizing parameters selected by the mask. This two-stage sparse adapter mechanism enables all tasks to be accumulated within a shared adapter space while reducing destructive interference across tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate the scalability of CLARE. On the long task-sequence benchmark Omnibenchmark-1k, CLARE outperforms strong baselines in final accuracy by a large margin, e.g, improving EASE by 4.64% and 13.34% after learning 100 tasks, respectively.

AI.tldr: CLARE introduces a sparsity-driven continual learning framework that uses two-stage sparse adapters to prevent catastrophic forgetting in long task sequences.
AI.motivation: Existing continual learning methods suffer from scalability bottlenecks when trained on many tasks sequentially, experiencing performance degradation due to inter-task interference and loss of plasticity. While leveraging pretrained models helps, there's a need for approaches that can handle long task sequences without catastrophic forgetting.
AI.method: CLARE uses a two-stage approach: (1) identifies a sparse, task-critical parameter mask via a sparsity-inducing objective, and (2) performs mask-constrained fine-tuning by only optimizing parameters selected by the mask. This creates sparse adapters that accumulate tasks within shared adapter space while minimizing interference.
AI.result: CLARE demonstrates superior scalability on long task sequences. On Omnibenchmark-1k, it outperforms strong baselines significantly, improving EASE by 4.64% and 13.34% after learning 100 tasks respectively.
AI.conclusion: The sparsity-driven continual learning framework CLARE effectively addresses scalability challenges in continual learning by reducing inter-task interference through sparse adapters, enabling successful learning across long task sequences without catastrophic forgetting.

title: Distributed JEPA: A Self-Supervised Framework for Energy Forecasting
summary: Traditional energy forecasting solutions rely on task-specific supervision and energy asset representations, limiting transferability and the ability to capture general temporal dynamics across heterogeneous assets. We address this by proposing a distributed Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for self-supervised learning from heterogeneous energy time-series. The framework predicts latent representations of masked temporal segments while integrating temporal observations and contextual information within a shared embedding space. To prevent representation collapse, training combines a latent-space predictive objective with covariance and temporal variance regularization. The evaluation was conducted on energy consumption and generation datasets under data-degradation scenarios and compared with a Transformer forecasting baseline. The learned representations remained stable (cosine similarity $\approx 0.98$; effective rank 185-235). JEPA achieved performance comparable to a Transformer on building energy data, higher $R^2$ in 3/5 consumer clusters, and outperformed the baseline on 9/10 unseen PVs ($R^2$=0.73-0.88 vs. <0.45), while showing greater robustness to missing data.

AI.tldr: Distributed JEPA framework enables self-supervised learning on heterogeneous energy time-series, achieving robust forecasting with transferable representations and outperforming Transformers on unseen data.
AI.motivation: Traditional energy forecasting solutions have limitations in transferability and capturing general temporal dynamics across heterogeneous energy assets due to task-specific supervision and limited asset representations.
AI.method: Proposed distributed Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for self-supervised learning, predicting latent representations of masked temporal segments while integrating temporal observations and contextual information. Uses covariance and temporal variance regularization to prevent representation collapse.
AI.result: JEPA maintained stable representations (cosine similarity ≈0.98; effective rank 185-235). Achieved comparable performance to Transformer on building energy data, higher R² in 3/5 consumer clusters, and significantly outperformed baseline on 9/10 unseen PV systems (R²=0.73-0.88 vs. <0.45), with greater robustness to missing data.
AI.conclusion: The distributed JEPA framework enables effective self-supervised learning from heterogeneous energy time-series, producing transferable representations that generalize well to unseen assets and demonstrate robustness to data degradation.

title: Learning Options for Compositional Motor Control with Adapter Banks
summary: Learning flexible motor primitives is a hallmark of skilled motor control. Recent neuroscience theory proposes that motor primitives may be implemented as low-rank perturbations of a shared recurrent network, but leaves open how such a system is learned. We translate this principle into a novel architecture for learning motor skills end-to-end: a shared recurrent core modulated by a bank of residual adapters, each selected by a discrete latent code. Trained on closed-loop biomechanical control, the adapters develop emergent low-rank perturbations of the recurrent dynamics despite no architectural rank constraint, placing task representations in disparate subspaces of the shared core network. A simple high-level policy over the learned options, optimized while the whole network is frozen, sequences the low-rank adapters to produce novel out-of-distribution movements. We demonstrate the ability to generalize to novel motor sequences within the closed-loop control setting, improving on the generalization error of a task-input-conditioned multitask baseline by upto order of magnitude.

AI.tldr: A novel neural architecture learns motor skills as low-rank perturbations to a shared recurrent network, enabling flexible sequencing of motor primitives with strong generalization to novel movements.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to translate neuroscience theory about motor primitives implemented as low-rank perturbations in shared recurrent networks into a practical learning system for motor control.
AI.method: Proposes a shared recurrent core modulated by residual adapters selected via discrete latent codes, trained end-to-end on closed-loop biomechanical control without architectural rank constraints.
AI.result: Adapters develop emergent low-rank perturbations of recurrent dynamics, creating task representations in disparate subspaces. Simple high-level policy sequences adapters for novel out-of-distribution movements with order-of-magnitude better generalization than baselines.
AI.conclusion: The architecture successfully implements neuroscience principles for motor learning, enabling flexible composition of learned motor primitives and strong generalization to novel motor sequences.

title: Repurposing Unified Topological Signatures for Graph Representation Learning
summary: Message-passing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) iteratively propagate and aggregate local neighborhood information followed by global readout to learn graph representations. However, their discriminative power is upper-bounded by the Weisfeiler--Lehman (1-WL) graph isomorphism test. This prevents GNNs from distinguishing certain non-isomorphic graphs with identical local neighborhood structures, often leading to similar graph representations. Unified Topological Signatures (UTS) capture compact, multi-scale representation of global graph topology derived from persistent homology. We introduce two complementary UTS signatures: Graph_UTS- a static signature of the input graph topology, and Embedding_UTS- a dynamic signature of the evolving embedding topology. They encode structural information inaccessible to 1-WL-based message-passing GNNs, yet their capabilities are explored solely for post-hoc embedding-space analysis. We integrate UTS into GNN training across three architectural interventions: (i) UTS-Aug: augmenting with standard readout feature that encodes graph's true topology; (ii) UTS-Reg: topological regularizer that constrains representation collapse; (iii) UTS-Pool: topology-guided pooling that retains structurally critical nodes. We further leverage UTS as a layer-wise diagnostic to quantify oversmoothing during GNN training. Theoretically, we show that integrating UTS into GNN optimization strictly extends GNN expressivity beyond the 1-WL hierarchy. Experiments on three graph classification benchmarks show consistent benefits: Graph-UTS, Dual-UTS, and UTS-Pool improve accuracy across all three datasets, Embedding-UTS provides smaller but similarly consistent gains, and UTS-Reg's benefit varies across graph domains. Accuracy improves by up to 5.8% with Graph-UTS augmentation, by up to 1.9% with UTS-Reg, and achieves comparable performance to TOGL with UTS-Pool.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Unified Topological Signatures (UTS) that capture multi-scale global graph topology from persistent homology, and integrates them into GNN training through three architectural interventions to overcome GNNs' expressivity limitations bounded by the 1-WL test.
AI.motivation: Message-passing GNNs are limited by the 1-WL graph isomorphism test, preventing them from distinguishing certain non-isomorphic graphs with identical local neighborhood structures. This leads to similar graph representations and reduced discriminative power.
AI.method: Proposes two UTS signatures: Graph_UTS (static signature of input graph topology) and Embedding_UTS (dynamic signature of evolving embedding topology). Integrates UTS into GNN training via three interventions: UTS-Aug (augmentation with topology-encoded readout features), UTS-Reg (topological regularizer to prevent representation collapse), and UTS-Pool (topology-guided pooling to retain critical nodes).
AI.result: Experiments on three graph classification benchmarks show consistent improvements: Graph-UTS, Dual-UTS, and UTS-Pool improve accuracy across all datasets. Accuracy improves by up to 5.8% with Graph-UTS augmentation, by up to 1.9% with UTS-Reg, and achieves comparable performance to TOGL with UTS-Pool. Embedding-UTS provides smaller but consistent gains.
AI.conclusion: Integrating Unified Topological Signatures into GNN optimization theoretically extends GNN expressivity beyond the 1-WL hierarchy and consistently improves performance across graph classification tasks, with different UTS interventions offering varying benefits depending on graph domains.

title: High-Fidelity Digital Twin Data Models by Randomized Dynamic Mode Decomposition and Deep Learning with Applications in Fluid Dynamics
summary: The purpose of this paper is the identification of high-fidelity digital twin data models from numerical code outputs by non-intrusive techniques (i.e., not requiring Galerkin projection of the governing equations onto the reduced modes basis). In this paper the author defines the concept of the digital twin data model (DTM) as a model of reduced complexity that has the main feature of mirroring the original process behavior. The significant advantage of a DTM is to reproduce the dynamics with high accuracy and reduced costs in CPU time and hardware for settings difficult to explore because of the complexity of the dynamics over time. This paper introduces a new framework for creating efficient digital twin data models by combining two state-of-the-art tools: randomized dynamic mode decomposition and deep learning artificial intelligence. It is shown that the outputs are consistent with the original source data with the advantage of reduced complexity. The DTMs are investigated in the numerical simulation of three shock wave phenomena with increasing complexity. The author performs a thorough assessment of the performance of the new digital twin data models in terms of numerical accuracy and computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: Non-intrusive creation of high-fidelity digital twin data models from numerical code outputs using randomized dynamic mode decomposition combined with deep learning AI, validated on shock wave simulations.
AI.motivation: Need to identify high-fidelity digital twin data models from numerical simulations without requiring intrusive Galerkin projection methods, to reproduce complex dynamics with high accuracy while reducing computational costs.
AI.method: Combines randomized dynamic mode decomposition (randomized DMD) with deep learning artificial intelligence to create efficient digital twin data models non-intrusively from numerical code outputs.
AI.result: Digital twin data models successfully reproduce original process behavior with high accuracy and reduced computational complexity, validated on three shock wave phenomena simulations with increasing complexity.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables creation of efficient digital twin data models that maintain high fidelity to original simulations while significantly reducing computational costs, demonstrating practical utility for complex dynamical systems.

title: Neural Field Ensembles for Aerodynamic Surface Prediction: Winning Solution to the ONERA CRM Wall Distribution 2025 Challenge
summary: Machine-learning surrogate models offer a promising alternative to high-fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations for aerodynamic analysis and design. However, constructing accurate surrogates for realistic aircraft configurations remain challenging due to complex geometries, multiple flow regimes, and limited training data. This work presents the methodology that achieved first place in the ONERA CRM Wall Distribution Regression Challenge, which focuses on predicting pressure and skin-friction coefficient distributions over the NASA Common Research Model wing-body-pylon-nacelle configuration under different operating conditions. The proposed approach formulates the problem as a conditional neural field mapping spatial coordinates, surface normals, and operating conditions to aerodynamic wall quantities. Fourier feature encoding, a relative squared error objective aligned with the challenge metric, ensemble learning, and $k$-fold cross-validation are progressively introduced to improve prediction accuracy and exploit the limited training data. Beyond presenting the final methodology, the paper documents the successive model design choices that led to the winning solution through a comprehensive ablation study and discusses several alternative approaches that were investigated but ultimately discarded. On the hidden competition test set, the proposed methodology achieves an overall score of 8.81, outperforming the strongest organizer-provided baseline, which achieved a score of 8.64, while requiring approximately three orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters. These results illustrate that carefully designed coordinate-based neural fields constitute an efficient and robust framework for aerodynamic surrogate modeling on complex geometries under limited-data conditions.

AI.tldr: Neural field method wins aerodynamic regression challenge using coordinate-based ML to predict wall distributions on complex aircraft geometry with limited data.
AI.motivation: Machine learning surrogates can replace costly CFD simulations but struggle with complex aircraft geometries, multiple flow regimes, and limited training data. The ONERA CRM Wall Distribution Regression Challenge provides a concrete test case for developing effective surrogates.
AI.method: Formulates the problem as conditional neural field mapping spatial coordinates, surface normals, and operating conditions to aerodynamic wall quantities. Uses Fourier feature encoding, relative squared error objective aligned with challenge metric, ensemble learning, and k-fold cross-validation to improve prediction accuracy with limited data.
AI.result: Achieved first place in the competition with overall score of 8.81, outperforming organizer-provided baseline (score: 8.64) while using approximately 1000x fewer trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: Carefully designed coordinate-based neural fields provide an efficient and robust framework for aerodynamic surrogate modeling on complex geometries under limited-data conditions, demonstrating superior performance with far fewer parameters than traditional approaches.

title: A unified framework for global and local interpretability using adaptive derivative-ordered random explanation
summary: The interpretability of complex machine learning models is of paramount importance, especially in real-world high-stakes domains such as healthcare and finance. However, existing post-hoc interpretability methods suffer from inherent limitations: fragmented analytical processes, inadequate capacity to model nonlinear feature interactions, computational inefficiencies, and over-reliance on specific model architectures. To address these challenges, this paper provides a novel method - Adaptive Derivative-Ordered Random Explanation (ADORE) - that leverages first- and second-order derivatives to accommodate nonlinear model complexities, while enabling effective capture of feature-sample interactions within a unified analytical framework. ADORE integrates global feature importance with local sample contributions, precisely quantifying feature impact by capturing both magnitude and direction, and identifying critical samples influencing model decisions. Furthermore, it achieves computational efficiency through randomized singular value decomposition (SVD) and dynamic sparsity detection, making it scalable to large, high-dimensional datasets. Experiments across three data modalities - tabular, text, and image - demonstrate that ADORE outperforms existing methods such as LIME and SHAP in handling complex interactions and computational efficiency, while providing detailed and reliable explanations. To facilitate adoption and reproducibility, ADORE has been released as an open-source Python package, hosted on GitHub, enabling researchers and practitioners to readily adapt and apply our approach to their specific tasks, models, and datasets.

AI.tldr: ADORE is a novel interpretability method that uses first- and second-order derivatives to model nonlinear feature interactions, integrating global feature importance with local sample contributions for comprehensive explanations across different data modalities.
AI.motivation: Existing post-hoc interpretability methods have limitations: fragmented analytical processes, inability to model nonlinear feature interactions, computational inefficiency, and over-reliance on specific model architectures, especially problematic for high-stakes domains like healthcare and finance.
AI.method: ADORE uses first- and second-order derivatives to accommodate nonlinear model complexities, captures feature-sample interactions in a unified framework, integrates global feature importance with local contributions, and achieves efficiency through randomized SVD and dynamic sparsity detection.
AI.result: Experiments across tabular, text, and image data demonstrate ADORE outperforms existing methods (LIME, SHAP) in handling complex interactions and computational efficiency while providing detailed, reliable explanations. The method is scalable to large, high-dimensional datasets.
AI.conclusion: ADORE successfully addresses limitations of existing interpretability methods by providing a unified, efficient framework for modeling nonlinear interactions. The open-source Python package facilitates adoption and reproducibility for researchers and practitioners.

title: IRENE: A Convolutional GRU Ensemble Model for Radar Precipitation Nowcasting over Italy
summary: We present IRENE (Italian Radar Ensemble Nowcasting Experiment), a deep learning model for probabilistic short-range precipitation nowcasting over the Italian domain at \SI{1}{km} spatial and 5 min temporal resolution. IRENE adopts an encoder--forecaster architecture built on multi-scale Convolutional Gated Recurrent Units (ConvGRUs), trained on the national radar composite produced by the Italian Civil Protection Department (DPC). An importance-sampling scheme focuses training on precipitation-relevant events, while the almost-fair Continuous Ranked Probability Score (afCRPS) is adopted as the primary probabilistic loss function. Two additional training configurations are proposed: an adversarial (GAN) variant, IRENE-GAN, designed to improve the spatial sharpness of the generated forecasts, and a spectrally constrained variant, IRENE-GAN-RAPSD, in which the adversarial objective is complemented by an explicit penalty on the radially averaged power spectral density. The three configurations are evaluated against the stochastic extrapolation method STEPS and the pre-trained deep learning model DGMR. All IRENE configurations attain a lower Continuous Ranked Probability Score than both benchmarks at every lead time and rank histograms closer to uniformity, indicating better probabilistic skill and ensemble calibration. In terms of ensemble-mean mean absolute error the advantage is confined to the first 90 min, beyond which the strongly damped DGMR fields and, to a lesser extent, STEPS become competitive. Spectral analysis shows that the adversarial training removes the progressive loss of small-scale variance exhibited by IRENE, at the cost of an excess of fine-scale power at long lead times that the spectral penalty only partially controls.

AI.tldr: IRENE is a deep learning model for 1km-resolution precipitation nowcasting over Italy using ConvGRU architecture with three variants (standard, GAN, and spectrally-constrained GAN), outperforming existing methods in probabilistic forecasting skill.
AI.motivation: Need for accurate probabilistic short-range precipitation forecasting over Italy at high spatial (1km) and temporal (5min) resolution, improving upon existing stochastic extrapolation (STEPS) and deep learning (DGMR) methods.
AI.method: Encoder-forecaster architecture using multi-scale ConvGRUs trained on Italian radar data, with importance sampling for precipitation events and afCRPS as main loss. Three variants: standard IRENE, adversarial IRENE-GAN for spatial sharpness, and spectrally-constrained IRENE-GAN-RAPSD.
AI.result: All IRENE variants achieve lower Continuous Ranked Probability Score than benchmarks at all lead times with better calibration. Ensemble-mean MAE advantage lasts 90 minutes. Adversarial training improves small-scale variance but causes excess fine-scale power at long lead times.
AI.conclusion: IRENE demonstrates superior probabilistic forecasting skill over existing methods, though trade-offs exist between probabilistic accuracy, spatial sharpness, and spectral characteristics that need optimization for different applications.

title: LoopSpec: Pipelined Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
summary: Looped Transformers achieve strong performance with compact parameter sizes by repeatedly applying a shared stack of Transformer blocks across recurrent depths. However, they incur higher decoding latency than standard Transformer models of comparable parameter size because shared weights are accessed at every recurrent depth. To improve decoding efficiency, self-speculative decoding is particularly well suited to Looped Transformers, as their intermediate recurrent states can directly provide draft predictions without an auxiliary draft model. We therefore propose LoopSpec, a training-free self-speculative decoding framework tailored for Looped Transformers. LoopSpec extracts draft tokens from early recurrent states and operates in a pipelined manner, overlapping draft generation of future tokens with target verification of the current token. To improve draft accuracy without excessive compute overhead, we introduce a selective second proposal from deeper recurrent depth while ensuring lossless decoding under both greedy and sampling regimes. Furthermore, we derive the optimal proposal depths in closed form and show the prediction matches measurement. Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, LoopSpec achieves up to 6.83$\times$ inference speedup across diverse Looped Transformers.

AI.tldr: LoopSpec: A training-free self-speculative decoding framework for Looped Transformers that uses intermediate recurrent states for draft predictions and pipelining to achieve up to 6.83× speedup.
AI.motivation: Looped Transformers achieve strong performance with compact parameter sizes but suffer from higher decoding latency than standard Transformers because shared weights are accessed at every recurrent depth. Self-speculative decoding is well-suited to Looped Transformers since their intermediate recurrent states can directly provide draft predictions without needing an auxiliary draft model.
AI.method: LoopSpec extracts draft tokens from early recurrent states and operates in a pipelined manner, overlapping draft generation of future tokens with target verification of the current token. Introduces selective second proposal from deeper recurrent depth to improve draft accuracy while ensuring lossless decoding. Derives optimal proposal depths in closed form.
AI.result: Across reasoning and coding benchmarks, LoopSpec achieves up to 6.83× inference speedup across diverse Looped Transformers.
AI.conclusion: LoopSpec provides an efficient training-free self-speculative decoding framework that leverages the inherent properties of Looped Transformers to significantly improve inference speed while maintaining lossless decoding under both greedy and sampling regimes.

title: MyoFlow: Anchor-Tied Rectified Flow for HD-sEMG Gesture Recognition Across Sessions and Subjects
summary: High-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG) gesture recognition supports prosthetic control, assistive robotics, and rehabilitation, but electrode re-donning and physiological variability cause distribution shifts that degrade accuracy across sessions and subjects. Generative HD-sEMG models primarily synthesize signals for augmentation; although diffusion models enhance representation learning, prediction still relies on a separate classifier. To tie learned dynamics to the decision rule, we propose MyoFlow, the first discriminative flow-matching framework for HD-sEMG recognition across sessions and subjects. It recasts classification as anchor-tied transport: a domain-conditioned rectified flow moves encoded windows toward gesture anchors that serve as transport targets and define the nearest-anchor decision geometry, enabling zero-shot prediction without an independent head. On the Hyser dataset, MyoFlow improves mean cross-session and cross-subject accuracy over the strongest diffusion-based baseline by 4.24\% and 6.37\%, respectively, and achieves 91.71\% mean zero-shot accuracy and 97.39\% mean few-shot accuracy across multiple days on the CEMHSEY dataset.

AI.tldr: MyoFlow is a discriminative flow-matching framework for HD-sEMG gesture recognition that treats classification as anchor-tied transport, enabling zero-shot prediction across sessions and subjects without a separate classifier head.
AI.motivation: HD-sEMG gesture recognition suffers from accuracy degradation due to electrode re-donning and physiological variability causing distribution shifts across sessions and subjects. Existing generative models only synthesize signals for augmentation and rely on separate classifiers, failing to tie learned dynamics to decision rules.
AI.method: MyoFlow is a discriminative flow-matching framework that recasts classification as anchor-tied transport. It uses a domain-conditioned rectified flow that moves encoded HD-sEMG windows toward gesture anchors, which serve as transport targets and define the nearest-anchor decision geometry. This eliminates the need for a separate classifier head and enables zero-shot prediction.
AI.result: On Hyser dataset: improved mean cross-session accuracy by 4.24% and cross-subject accuracy by 6.37% over strongest diffusion-based baseline. On CEMHSEY dataset: achieved 91.71% mean zero-shot accuracy and 97.39% mean few-shot accuracy across multiple days.
AI.conclusion: MyoFlow is the first discriminative flow-matching framework for HD-sEMG recognition that successfully addresses distribution shifts across sessions and subjects. By tying learned dynamics directly to decision rules through anchor-tied transport, it enables effective zero-shot and few-shot learning with significant accuracy improvements over existing methods.

title: Memorisation bias in medical AI
summary: Medical AI models hold immense potential to improve patient outcomes, but they are also known to unintentionally memorise individual records from their training datasets. While such memorisation has been linked to targeted privacy attacks, its consequences for clinical deployment, where patients may be assessed by a model that saw their historical data during training, remain poorly understood. Here we show that predictions on a patient's unseen future data can change significantly if a model observed that same patient's anonymised historical data during training, a phenomenon we term "memorisation bias". We demonstrate that this bias exists across diverse data modalities and model architectures, and over prolonged time spans: in some cases, memorisation bias persists on future records acquired decades after the historical records used for training. Moreover, in simulated prospective deployment, memorisation bias has asymmetric effects on the diagnostic accuracy of returning data contributors. When a patient returned with a de novo condition absent from their historical records in the training dataset, diagnostic sensitivity decreased significantly compared to an otherwise identical model not trained on their historical data. Conversely, when their health state was unchanged, both sensitivity and specificity were significantly inflated. Our findings reveal a previously uncharacterised risk in medical AI that arises when a model is deployed on patients who contributed to its training data. This exposes a shortcoming of current model development practice: the de-identification measures designed to protect patients' privacy make it difficult to identify returning contributors and exclude them from the AI-assisted interpretation of their own future data. Mitigating memorisation risks may thus require changes to current model training and deployment protocols.

AI.tldr: Medical AI models can develop "memorisation bias" where predictions on a patient's future data change significantly if the model saw that patient's anonymized historical data during training, creating diagnostic accuracy risks for returning patients.
AI.motivation: Medical AI models unintentionally memorize individual patient records from training data, but the clinical consequences when these models are deployed on patients whose historical data was used in training remain poorly understood. This poses risks in real-world clinical deployment scenarios.
AI.method: The study investigates memorization bias across diverse data modalities and model architectures, examining how predictions change when models are tested on future data from patients whose historical records were in the training set. They analyze bias persistence over prolonged time spans (decades) and conduct simulated prospective deployment scenarios.
AI.result: Memorisation bias exists across all tested data modalities and model architectures and persists on future records acquired decades after training. In simulated deployments, bias has asymmetric effects: for returning patients with new conditions absent from historical records, diagnostic sensitivity significantly decreases; for patients with unchanged health states, both sensitivity and specificity are significantly inflated.
AI.conclusion: Memorisation bias represents a previously uncharacterized risk in medical AI deployment, particularly affecting returning patients who contributed to training data. Current de-identification practices paradoxically make it difficult to identify returning contributors and exclude them from AI interpretation of their own future data, requiring changes to model training and deployment protocols.

title: Easy to Catch a Liar, Hard to Clear an Honest One: Language Models Diagnosing a Corrupted Reward Channel from a Verified Record
comment: 15 pages, 9 tables. Code, prompts, answer keys, and every scored output: https://github.com/IamArmanNikkhah/easy-to-catch-a-liar
summary: An agent that learns from rewards has to trust whatever reports those rewards. When the reports suddenly change, either the world changed or the reporter broke. From the reports alone these are indistinguishable, and reinforcement learning theory shows that no amount of further experience separates them. The prescribed escape is richer data about the reporter itself. We ask whether a frozen language model, handed exactly that data, uses it. We build a two-option game in which a payout swap and a lying reporter produce byte-identical histories. Then we add one verified record: an independent check of one round's real result, printed beside what the reporter said about that round. That single line settles the case. We ask three large models, from two families, to answer one question with one letter. Is the reporter honest or lying? They catch a lying reporter almost perfectly. At the 70B class that holds in every condition we tried; the 32B model slips in one wording. They clear an honest reporter far less often, and how often depends on things that should not matter. Averaged over rounds, letters, and wordings, a 72B model calls an honest reporter a liar 38% of the time when nothing has changed at all, and 58% of the time when the payouts moved. A 70B model from a second family calls an honest reporter a liar 26% and 48% of the time. The failure is not one of reading, because in the situation where nothing changed the same models score 0.96 to 1.00 with the answer printed in the prompt. Which surface feature drives it differs by family. For the Qwen models it is which round the record names, and for Llama it is which letter stands for "honest." Adding the record to a prompt that already states the answer makes Llama less likely to give that answer. We had registered a prediction for that 58% before the run: 35%. The failure is larger than we expected.

AI.tldr: Large language models can detect lying reporters almost perfectly when given verified evidence, but they falsely accuse honest reporters of lying at high rates (26-58%), showing systematic bias rather than comprehension failure.
AI.motivation: When an agent learns from reward reports and those reports change, it's impossible to tell from the reports alone whether the world changed or the reporter started lying. The theoretical solution is richer data about the reporter itself, but the question is whether frozen language models actually use such verification data effectively.
AI.method: Researchers created a two-option game where payout changes and lying reporters produce identical histories. They added one verified record - an independent check of one round's real result printed beside what the reporter said. They tested three large models (70B and 32B classes from two families) with a simple binary question: "Is the reporter honest or lying?"
AI.result: Models catch lying reporters almost perfectly (70B class works in all conditions, 32B slips in one wording). However, they falsely accuse honest reporters of lying at high rates (38-58% when nothing changed, 26-48% when payouts moved). When the answer is printed in the prompt, the same models score 0.96-1.00, showing they can read correctly. The failure patterns differ by model family: Qwen models are sensitive to which round the record names, Llama models to which letter represents "honest."
AI.conclusion: Large language models have systematic biases in evaluating reporter honesty that go beyond simple reading comprehension. They exhibit asymmetric performance: excellent at detecting lies but prone to false accusations of dishonesty, with failure rates higher than expected (58% vs predicted 35%). The specific biases differ by model architecture, suggesting deeper issues in how models process verification evidence.

authors: José Mairton Barros da Silva Júnior
title: Personalized Federated Learning through Global Knowledge Distillation and Local Head Adaptation
summary: Statistical heterogeneity limits federated learning when a single global classifier cannot represent client-specific label distributions. In this work, we propose Personalized Federated Knowledge Distillation with Head Adaptation (pFedKDH), which aggregates only the shared backbone, keeps persistent client-specific heads, and uses a recalibrated global head as a teacher during local training. Across MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 under class-wise Dirichlet partitions, pFedKDH obtains the best accuracy in most settings, with accuracy gaps up to 37.67\% over the weakest baseline and consistently low standard deviation across repetitions. Component-wise diagnostics and convergence results support the role of persistent heads and distillation-guided local optimization under label-skewed data.

AI.tldr: pFedKDH improves personalized federated learning by keeping client-specific heads permanent, aggregating only shared backbones, and using a recalibrated global head as a teacher via knowledge distillation.
AI.motivation: Statistical heterogeneity in federated learning where a single global classifier fails to represent diverse client-specific label distributions, especially under label-skewed data partitions.
AI.method: Proposed Personalized Federated Knowledge Distillation with Head Adaptation (pFedKDH): aggregates only the shared backbone network, keeps persistent client-specific heads, uses a recalibrated global head as teacher during local training, and employs knowledge distillation guidance.
AI.result: Achieved best accuracy on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 under class-wise Dirichlet partitions, with accuracy gaps up to 37.67% over weakest baselines and consistently low standard deviation across repetitions.
AI.conclusion: pFedKDH effectively addresses statistical heterogeneity in federated learning through persistent client heads and distillation-guided optimization, demonstrating superior performance and stability across diverse datasets and label-skewed scenarios.

title: Same Flow, Different Paths: Variance Reduction in Flow Matching
summary: In flow matching (FM), a velocity model $v_θ$ is trained using a predefined path $g_t$ that connects data and noise samples (e.g., $g_t(x_0, x_1) = (1 - t) x_0 + t x_1$). In this work, we study the choice of this path from an optimization perspective by analyzing the variance of stochastic gradients. We consider the class $G(p_t,v^\star_t)$ of paths that induce the same marginal distributions $p_t$ and marginal velocity field $v^\star_t$, and therefore the same FM objective. Our main finding is that the choice of path $g_t$ can fundamentally change the convergence rate of SGD, even when the FM objective remains exactly the same. (i) For a linear velocity model and one-dimensional Gaussian data, we derive a tight bound on the SGD iteration complexity up to logarithmic factors and find an analytically optimal path that minimizes this bound among linear paths inducing the same FM problem. (ii) We then extend the variance analysis to general FM problems and formulate path selection at a fixed $θ$ as the variance-minimization problem PathOpt$_θ$, constrained to $g_t\in G(p_t,v^\star_t)$. We show that this constraint is essential: reducing variance without it can lead to slower convergence. (iii) Since the constraint $g_t \in G(p_t,v^\star_t)$ cannot generally be verified directly, we derive an equivalent formulation with constraints that can be estimated from samples, allowing paths to be found numerically. Our theoretical results are supported by experiments with Gaussian data, Gaussian mixture models, and real datasets.

AI.tldr: Flow matching path selection affects SGD convergence rate despite identical objectives. Optimal paths minimize gradient variance, with analysis showing linear paths optimal for 1D Gaussians and general formulation for numerical optimization.
AI.motivation: While flow matching uses predefined paths connecting data and noise, the choice of path is typically made without consideration of optimization efficiency. The authors study whether different paths (that induce identical flow matching objectives) affect SGD convergence rates, motivated by improving training efficiency.
AI.method: Analyze variance of stochastic gradients in flow matching. For 1D Gaussian data with linear velocity models, derive tight SGD iteration complexity bound and find analytically optimal linear path. Formulate general PathOpt problem minimizing gradient variance constrained to paths inducing same FM objective, with equivalent sample-estimatable constraints.
AI.result: Path choice fundamentally changes SGD convergence rate even with identical FM objectives. Found optimal linear path for 1D Gaussian case. Showed constraint g_t∈G(p_t,v*_t) is essential - variance reduction without it can slow convergence. Derived practical formulation allowing numerical path optimization.
AI.conclusion: Path selection in flow matching is crucial for optimization efficiency. The proposed variance-minimizing path optimization framework offers both theoretical insights (optimal paths for simple cases) and practical methods (numerical optimization) for improving training convergence.

title: Hybrid Variational Quantum Circuits for Multivariate Regression and High-Dimensional Data Reconstruction
summary: Variational quantum circuits (VQCs) are parameterized quantum circuits optimized classically. We propose a hybrid variational quantum circuit (HVQC) extending VQCs with a classical affine post-measurement layer, enabling vector-valued regression without the linear overhead of independent scalar circuits. Theoretically, we show that elementary one-and two-qubit circuits can approximate quadratic functions and products via data re-uploading and entanglement, providing the foundations of the full architecture. Experimentally, on two synthetic image reconstruction datasets and the Friedman1 benchmark (40,568 test samples), our HVQC matches Gaussian Process Regression and outperforms XGBoost and Random Forest. An ablation study confirms that both quantum and classical components are essential, and results highlight the central role of the feature map in hybrid quantum-classical models.

AI.tldr: HVQC extends VQCs with classical affine post-measurement layer, enabling efficient vector-valued regression, outperforming classical ML methods on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Variational quantum circuits are limited to scalar regression, requiring linear overhead for vector-valued tasks. There's a need for quantum circuits that can handle multi-output regression efficiently without the overhead of running independent scalar circuits.
AI.method: Proposes Hybrid Variational Quantum Circuit (HVQC) that extends VQCs with a classical affine post-measurement layer. Uses data re-uploading and entanglement in one- and two-qubit circuits to approximate quadratic functions and products, forming the foundation for the full architecture.
AI.result: On synthetic image reconstruction datasets and Friedman1 benchmark (40,568 test samples), HVQC matches Gaussian Process Regression and outperforms XGBoost and Random Forest. Ablation study confirms both quantum and classical components are essential, highlighting the importance of feature maps.
AI.conclusion: HVQC provides an efficient quantum-classical architecture for vector-valued regression, demonstrating competitive performance against classical ML methods and emphasizing the crucial role of feature maps in hybrid quantum-classical models.

title: Large Language Models Develop Belief State Geometry In-Context
summary: Large language models (LLMs) trained on next-token prediction exhibit remarkable in-context learning (ICL) abilities, yet the representations that support ICL remain poorly understood. We consider such representations in a controlled setting: prompting LLMs with data emitted from hidden Markov models (HMMs) and probing for the corresponding belief state -- the posterior distribution over the HMM's hidden states given the observed token history. Across six open-source LLMs prompted with data from 40 HMMs selected for non-trivial belief structure, we find that belief states are linearly decodable from residual stream activations, with peak probe $R^2$-values from 0.83-0.99 across HMM and LLM combinations, ranging from early to late layers. To establish functional relevance, we intervene directly on the probe-identified subspace via patching and steering, resulting in downstream prediction quality on the order of the untampered model, while controls degrade performance substantially. Together, these results provide representation-level evidence that ICL in open-source LLMs approximates optimal Bayesian prediction over a context-inferred generative model. More broadly, our findings extend prior results linking input-distribution structure to activation geometry: from toy networks trained explicitly on HMM data to production-scale LLMs.

AI.tldr: LLMs linearly encode hidden belief states from HMM-generated data, and manipulating these representations functionally affects predictions, suggesting ICL implements approximate Bayesian inference.
AI.motivation: Despite impressive in-context learning abilities of LLMs, the underlying representations supporting ICL remain poorly understood, especially how LLMs might implement probabilistic reasoning over hidden structure in observed data.
AI.method: Probed six open-source LLMs with data from 40 carefully selected HMMs, used linear probes to decode belief states from residual stream activations, and performed interventions (patching and steering) on probe-identified subspaces to test functional relevance.
AI.result: Belief states are linearly decodable with high accuracy (R² 0.83-0.99 across models), across early to late layers. Interventions on identified subspaces maintained prediction quality near untampered model levels, while controls substantially degraded performance.
AI.conclusion: ICL in LLMs approximates optimal Bayesian prediction over a context-inferred generative model, extending prior theoretical links between input structure and activation geometry to production-scale models.

title: OPEN-1B: A Fully Auditable Training Run
summary:
Open-source language models have a reproducibility problem. Despite releasing weights, training data, and recipes, none of them are provably reproducible due to the non-associativity of floating-point arithmetic. Deep learning frameworks often offer a deterministic execution mode, allowing reproducible operations on the same machines. Unfortunately, this determinism does not carry across hardware such that a user can verify that a released checkpoint was actually produced using the declared training recipe. This leaves room for undisclosed data, injected biases, or backdoors that existing techniques such as proof-of-learning or proof-of-training-data cannot rule out.
  We introduce a new tier of model transparency, fully auditable, in which every operation on every data sample during training is independently reproducible on heterogeneous commodity hardware with bitwise certainty. By imposing a definite order on the sources of training nondeterminism, GPU kernel reductions, data batch ordering across a data-parallel cluster, and inter/intra-node collective communication, we make it possible to replay any individual step of a large, distributed training run on a single piece of commodity hardware and check it against the published trajectory.
  Because replaying an entire run on one machine is infeasible, we support this with a collective verification scheme in which many independent auditors each certify individual steps, together covering the whole run. We release Open-1B, a model trained under this regime, together with its full pretraining dataset, every intermediate checkpoint, the training codebase, and the audit harness needed to reproduce and verify any step of its training.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces fully auditable language models where every training operation is bitwise reproducible on any hardware, enabling independent verification of training processes to ensure transparency and rule out undisclosed data or backdoors.
AI.motivation: Current open-source language models lack true reproducibility - even with released weights, data, and recipes, they're not provably reproducible due to floating-point non-associativity and hardware-dependent determinism. This creates vulnerabilities where undisclosed data, biases, or backdoors could be introduced without detection.
AI.method: The authors impose a definite order on sources of training nondeterminism (GPU kernel reductions, data batch ordering across clusters, and collective communication) to enable bitwise reproducible training. They use a collective verification scheme where multiple independent auditors each certify individual training steps, covering the entire run.
AI.result: The authors release Open-1B, a 1B-parameter model trained under this fully auditable regime, including its full pretraining dataset, all intermediate checkpoints, training codebase, and audit harness needed to reproduce and verify any step of training.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a new tier of model transparency (fully auditable) that enables independent verification of training processes on heterogeneous commodity hardware, addressing the reproducibility problem in open-source language models and providing stronger guarantees against undisclosed modifications.

title: Bridging the Confidence Gap: Temperature Scaling for Calibrating Test-Time Prompt Tuning
summary: Test-time prompt tuning (TPT) enables adaptation on a single test instance, achieving improved accuracy but often sacrificing calibration performance. Most existing calibration methods introduce additional regularization terms to promote dispersion across text embeddings and reduce calibration error, yet these methods often suffer from a drop in accuracy. Motivated by the well-calibrated nature of zero-shot predictions, we propose CoTS, a simple yet effective post-hoc calibration method that preserves accuracy. Specifically, CoTS applies temperature scaling to minimize the confidence gap between adapted and zero-shot predictions. To fully exploit the potential of multiple augmentations during adaptation, we introduce a weak-strong ensemble strategy that further boosts accuracy. We then apply CoTS to this ensemble, termed E-CoTS, to maintain its well-calibrated property. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets and backbones show that our approaches effectively mitigate miscalibration without compromising primary accuracy. For instance, E-CoTS reduces the average expected calibration error of TPT from 11.90% to 5.38% on ImageNet variants, while even increasing accuracy from 60.74% to 62.95%. Moreover, when integrated with existing calibration methods, E-CoTS usually enhances both accuracy and calibration simultaneously.

AI.tldr: CoTS: A post-hoc calibration method for test-time prompt tuning that preserves accuracy by minimizing confidence gap between adapted and zero-shot predictions, with E-CoTS extending it to ensemble methods for improved calibration and accuracy.
AI.motivation: Test-time prompt tuning improves accuracy but sacrifices calibration performance. Existing calibration methods often hurt accuracy when trying to improve calibration. Zero-shot predictions are well-calibrated, suggesting they could guide calibration.
AI.method: CoTS applies temperature scaling to minimize confidence gap between adapted and zero-shot predictions. For multiple augmentations, introduce weak-strong ensemble strategy for accuracy boost, then apply CoTS to create E-CoTS to maintain calibration.
AI.result: CoTS/E-CoTS effectively mitigate miscalibration without compromising accuracy. E-CoTS reduces average expected calibration error from 11.90% to 5.38% on ImageNet variants while increasing accuracy from 60.74% to 62.95%. Works with existing calibration methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CoTS and E-CoTS methods provide simple yet effective post-hoc calibration that preserves accuracy, leveraging zero-shot predictions as calibration guidance, with strong empirical results across diverse datasets and backbones.

title: Knowledge as Orbit: Finite Collections as Phases of an Exactly Periodic Latent Generator
summary: Finite knowledge is usually stored extensionally, one code or vector per item. We ask whether a finite collection can instead be stored intensionally, as the decoded orbit of one compact law that returns exactly to its start. For X objects, we encode item i as the i-th phase of a fixed rotation in a learned latent space and decode all phases with a shared network; the latent advances through a bank of rotations at integer harmonics of the cycle, a real discrete Fourier operator, so that R^X equals the identity and exact closure is guaranteed rather than learned. Images are a controlled carrier; looping video is the case where the phase order is the content's own temporal structure. Holding the decoder fixed and varying only the operator, a general learned operator diverges, a norm-preserving but non-periodic one degrades around the loop, and the exactly periodic operator is flat; on real images the gap widens. Capacity is then the decoder's budget: dense decoders carry a structural overhead per crisp image that no size reconciles with compression, while a small convolutional decoder on objects that share a manifold reaches crisp and compressed. A codebook control shows the generative law is free in reconstruction terms while multiplying the latent store many-fold. On seven benchmark clips, against a matched frame-index baseline, the cycle reaches equal or better fidelity at equal parameters while wrapping at machine precision, where the baseline leaves a visible seam; pinning the baseline's frequencies to loop harmonics closes its seam too, confirming that exact periodicity is the operative constraint. Finite cyclic knowledge can be stored as dynamics rather than independent instances, with exact recurrence supplied by algebra and content by a shared decoder.

AI.tldr: Finite collections can be stored intensionally as decoded orbits of compact periodic laws rather than extensional storage, achieving exact recurrence via algebraic constraints and content via shared decoders.
AI.motivation: Traditional finite knowledge storage is extensional (one vector per item), which is inefficient. The paper explores whether collections can be stored intensionally as periodic dynamics where items are phases of a learned cyclic law.
AI.method: Encode items as phases of a fixed rotation in learned latent space; decode all phases with a shared network. Use a discrete Fourier operator with integer harmonics to guarantee exact periodicity (R^X = identity). Images serve as controlled carriers, and looping video represents temporal structure.
AI.result: The exactly periodic operator maintains flat error around the loop while other methods degrade. On seven benchmark clips, cyclic storage achieves equal/better fidelity than frame-index baselines while wrapping perfectly at machine precision. Pinning baseline frequencies to loop harmonics confirms exact periodicity is key.
AI.conclusion: Finite knowledge can be stored as dynamics rather than independent instances, with exact recurrence ensured algebraically and content provided by shared decoders, enabling compression while maintaining crisp reconstruction.

title: Learning-Guided Planning in Large Dynamic Action Spaces: Budgeted Tree Search for One-to-Many Mobile Charging
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures. Learning-guided planning, budgeted tree search, PUCT, and sequential decision-making in large dynamic action spaces
summary: Many learned sequential decision systems map the current state directly to an action. That shortcut becomes brittle when candidate actions are numerous, geometrically structured, and rebuilt with the state. One-to-many mobile charging makes this setting concrete: with N=250 sensors, the initial state induces about 1,125 candidate charging-stop actions; each chosen stop simultaneously serves its in-range sensors, and the action universe changes as sensors die. LP-BTS is a learning-guided planning architecture: a graph proposal policy concentrates a small candidate support, a learned value critic evaluates leaves, and edge-budgeted PUCT compares short simulated futures before committing an action. Because the policy scores this set without a fixed output head, a single frozen checkpoint covers every evaluated setting, spanning action universes from 736 to 2,813 stops. Matched ablations reveal complementary effects: uniform sampling costs 8.8 survival percentage points, while, with targeted support fixed, PUCT jointly retains 1.4 points (about 3.5 of 250 sensors) and direct policy selection travels 23% farther. On a prospectively specified, sealed 30-scenario confirmatory bank evaluated once, LP-BTS attains the highest observed survival (0.4545) and alive-AUC (0.8031). Its estimated survival advantage over the strongest domain-engineered comparator is +0.0066 (95% CI [-0.0037, +0.0184]), an unresolved difference, while it exceeds a deadline heuristic and two source-derived direct-policy reconstructions on every paired scenario. Both learned rows are trained, source-derived reconstructions of variants reported by Gong et al. In this setting, the results provide controlled evidence about learning-guided planning in a large, dynamic action space.

AI.tldr: LP-BTS is a learning-guided planning architecture for mobile charging in large, dynamic action spaces that uses graph proposal policy, learned value critic, and edge-budgeted PUCT to select actions efficiently.
AI.motivation: Traditional direct state-to-action mapping becomes brittle when dealing with numerous, geometrically structured actions that change dynamically with the state, as in one-to-many mobile charging with 250 sensors where action universes range from 736 to 2,813 stops.
AI.method: LP-BTS combines three components: 1) a graph proposal policy that concentrates a small candidate support, 2) a learned value critic that evaluates leaves, and 3) edge-budgeted PUCT that compares short simulated futures before committing an action. The policy scores actions without a fixed output head, enabling a single frozen checkpoint to cover all settings.
AI.result: LP-BTS achieves highest observed survival (0.4545) and alive-AUC (0.8031) on a 30-scenario confirmatory bank. It outperforms uniform sampling by 8.8 survival percentage points, and with targeted support fixed, PUCT retains 1.4 points while direct policy selection travels 23% farther. Estimated survival advantage over strongest domain-engineered comparator is +0.0066.
AI.conclusion: The results provide controlled evidence for learning-guided planning in large, dynamic action spaces, demonstrating that LP-BTS effectively addresses challenges of numerous, geometrically structured actions that change with state in mobile charging scenarios.

title: Reduced-Space Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization of Process Simulation Models
comment: Accepted at the 20th Learning and Intelligent Optimization Conference (LION 20), 2026. Corrected author version. This version corrects a typo in the mathematical description of the multi-fidelity covariance kernel in Section 3.2
summary: Optimizing industrial process flowsheets is often computationally prohibitive due to the high cost of rigorous simulations and the curse of dimensionality inherent in complex design spaces. To address these challenges, we present a reduced-space multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (RS-MFBO) framework designed for high-dimensional, expensive black-box functions. The approach integrates Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA) for dimensionality reduction with a fidelity-augmented Gaussian process that captures correlations between low-cost approximations and expensive high-fidelity evaluations. A cost-aware acquisition strategy, augmented with cooldown and promotion mechanisms, adaptively guides the allocation of samples across fidelities. The framework is validated on two distinct industrial process simulators: a plasmid DNA bioprocess in SuperPro Designer and a green fuel synthesis plant in Aspen HYSYS. Results across diverse economic and physical objectives demonstrate that the proposed method substantially reduces the number of high-fidelity simulator evaluations while maintaining competitive optimization performance compared to single-fidelity baselines. These results highlight RS-MFBO as a scalable, simulator-agnostic approach for cost-constrained black-box optimization.

AI.tldr: RS-MFBO framework combines dimensionality reduction with multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization to efficiently optimize expensive industrial process flowsheets using adaptive fidelity allocation.
AI.motivation: Industrial process flowsheet optimization is computationally prohibitive due to expensive rigorous simulations and high-dimensional design spaces, requiring efficient methods to reduce computational costs while maintaining performance.
AI.method: Proposes reduced-space multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (RS-MFBO) integrating Global Sensitivity Analysis for dimensionality reduction with fidelity-augmented Gaussian processes, plus cost-aware acquisition strategy with cooldown and promotion mechanisms for adaptive fidelity allocation.
AI.result: RS-MFBO substantially reduces number of high-fidelity simulator evaluations while maintaining competitive optimization performance compared to single-fidelity baselines, validated on plasmid DNA bioprocess and green fuel synthesis plant simulators.
AI.conclusion: RS-MFBO provides a scalable, simulator-agnostic approach for cost-constrained black-box optimization of industrial processes, effectively balancing computational efficiency with optimization performance.

title: Coupled Calibration and Learning: Mitigating Teacher Bias in LLM Distillation without Target-Domain Reward Feedback
summary: Large language model (LLM) distillation aims to transfer the capabilities of a powerful teacher to a smaller student. Direct imitation, however, can also transfer the teacher's systematic bias and errors. This challenge is particularly pronounced under covariate shift, when the teacher's reliability on target questions is uncertain and target-domain reward feedback is unavailable. We propose Coupled Calibration and Learning (CCL), an LLM distillation algorithm that couples teacher calibration with student updates through token-level branching, using reward feedback only on source questions. Each iteration calibrates the teacher using source feedback and then uses the calibrated teacher to train the student on target questions. The updated student, in turn, informs subsequent calibration. In an autoregressive policy framework, we prove that the output student's expected average Kullback-Leibler divergence to the oracle student converges to zero at a polynomial rate in the number of iterations. The oracle maximizes the true reference-regularized target reward within the student class, which need not represent the unrestricted optimal policy. Our analysis quantifies the progress of projected student gradient updates while controlling the error in teacher calibration. We further establish a separation from regularized direct matching: its error relative to the oracle student can remain bounded away from zero even when the teacher achieves higher regularized target reward than every student policy. These results demonstrate that LLM distillation can overcome persistent teacher bias and recover the optimal student through coupled calibration and learning, without target-domain reward feedback.

AI.tldr: CCL is an LLM distillation algorithm that couples teacher calibration with student learning to overcome teacher bias and errors under covariate shift, achieving optimal student performance without target-domain reward feedback.
AI.motivation: Direct LLM distillation transfers both teacher capabilities and systematic bias/errors to students. This is problematic under covariate shift where teacher reliability on target questions is uncertain and target-domain reward feedback is unavailable.
AI.method: Coupled Calibration and Learning (CCL) algorithm that iteratively calibrates the teacher using source feedback, then uses the calibrated teacher to train the student on target questions. The updated student informs subsequent calibration through token-level branching in an autoregressive policy framework.
AI.result: Proved convergence where the student's expected average KL divergence to the oracle student converges to zero at polynomial rate. Established separation from regularized direct matching which can fail even when teacher outperforms all student policies.
AI.conclusion: LLM distillation can overcome persistent teacher bias and recover the optimal student through coupled calibration and learning without target-domain reward feedback, addressing the covariate shift challenge.

title: FreqSpaNet: Frequency and Spatial Learning of SFPF for Physical Layer Hardware Integrity Detection
summary: Unauthorized hardware replacement can preserve a wireless device's logical identity while altering its physical implementation, posing a challenge to hardware integrity verification. Spatio-frequency polarization fingerprints (SFPFs) capture device-dependent responses across multiple frequencies and directions, but their frequency and spatial dimensions exhibit different structural dependencies. We propose FreqSpaNet, an SFPF representation learning network for open set hardware anomaly detection. A frequency branch captures local variations among neighboring frequencies, while a geometry-aware spatial branch models directional relationships using angular information. The two representations are combined through adaptive fusion, and complementary pretraining further captures shared information while preserving the distinct characteristics of the frequency and spatial representations. Experiments show that FreqSpaNet achieves a mean AUROC of 96.31\%, 9.05 points above the baseline. Results under seven hardware replacement scenarios further verify the effectiveness of FreqSpaNet.

AI.tldr: FreqSpaNet is a neural network for detecting unauthorized hardware replacements in wireless devices by analyzing spatio-frequency polarization fingerprints using dual-branch architecture with frequency and spatial branches combined through adaptive fusion.
AI.motivation: Unauthorized hardware replacement can maintain a wireless device's logical identity while changing its physical implementation, making hardware integrity verification challenging. Existing spatio-frequency polarization fingerprints have structural dependencies between frequency and spatial dimensions that need proper modeling.
AI.method: Proposed FreqSpaNet with two branches: frequency branch captures local variations among neighboring frequencies; geometry-aware spatial branch models directional relationships using angular information. Features are combined through adaptive fusion, with complementary pretraining to capture shared information while preserving distinct characteristics of both representations.
AI.result: Achieves mean AUROC of 96.31%, 9.05 points above baseline. Results under seven hardware replacement scenarios further verify effectiveness of the approach for open set hardware anomaly detection.
AI.conclusion: FreqSpaNet successfully addresses the hardware integrity verification challenge by effectively modeling the structural dependencies in spatio-frequency polarization fingerprints through dual-branch architecture with adaptive fusion, demonstrating superior performance in detecting unauthorized hardware replacements.

title: ENCP: Episode-Normalized Conformal Prediction for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Uncertainty estimation for Vision-Language-Navigation (VLN) models is a critical task since it can help identify ambiguous and unreliable predictions, enabling agents to make safer navigation decisions. As one of the most advanced uncertainty estimation frameworks, conformal prediction (CP) offers a promising approach for uncertainty estimation in VLN. However, given that VLN agent requires a sequence of steps, standard calibration in conformal prediction fails to provide coverage guarantee it promises over a dependent, variable-length VLN episode. To this end, we propose Episode-Normalized Conformal Prediction (ENCP), which rescales a nonconformity score by the policy's residual confidence and calibrates one maximum score per episode. Under exchangeable calibration and test episodes, this construction covers the ground truth at every step with probability at least $1 - α$, while allowing dependence among steps within an episode. Across four VLN policies and three nonconformity scores on R2R and REVERIE dataset, ENCP meets all reported empirical step-coverage targets on the seen-to-unseen evaluation. These results demonstrate that ENCP can provide model-agnostic uncertainty estimates, which might be useful for determining when a VLN agent should defer to a more capable predictor, including human assistance.

AI.tldr: ENCP (Episode-Normalized Conformal Prediction) provides reliable uncertainty estimation for Vision-Language-Navigation by normalizing nonconformity scores per episode, ensuring step-coverage guarantees despite dependencies between navigation steps.
AI.motivation: Standard conformal prediction methods fail to provide reliable uncertainty estimation in VLN tasks because they don't account for the sequential, dependent nature of navigation episodes and variable episode lengths. This limitation prevents VLN agents from safely identifying ambiguous situations where they should defer to more capable predictors.
AI.method: The authors propose Episode-Normalized Conformal Prediction (ENCP) which: 1) rescales nonconformity scores by the policy's residual confidence, 2) calibrates one maximum score per entire episode rather than per step, and 3) maintains coverage guarantees under exchangeable calibration/test episodes while allowing dependence among steps within an episode.
AI.result: ENCP successfully meets all empirical step-coverage targets on seen-to-unseen evaluation across four VLN policies and three nonconformity scores on R2R and REVERIE datasets, demonstrating reliable uncertainty estimation that covers ground truth at every step with probability at least 1-α.
AI.conclusion: ENCP provides model-agnostic uncertainty estimates for VLN that maintain proper coverage guarantees despite sequential dependencies, enabling safer navigation decisions and determining when agents should defer to more capable predictors or human assistance.
